article_title: Reporting What Readers Need to Know About Education Research Measures: A Guide
citation: Kimberly Boller, Ellen Eliason Kisker. (2014). Reporting What Readers Need to Know About Education Research Measures: A Guide. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov
title: Five-checklist framework for complete reporting of education research measures
description: This brief organizes complete reporting of education research measures into five checklists covering, in the authors' words, "their study's measures; (2) data collection training and quality; (3) the study's reference population, study sample, and measurement timing; (4) evidence of the reliability and construct validity of the measures; and (5) missing data and descriptive statistics." The checklists function as a reusable reporting pattern that researchers apply when drafting or reviewing methods sections.
requirements: Researchers applying the checklists must have carried out data collection and measurement for the study being reported
constraints: The guide addresses reporting of measures in education research reports, not study design itself
target_learners: education researchers preparing reports of studies using measures
target_learning_goals: complete and transparent reporting of measures in education research
examples: The brief includes an example of parts of a report's methods and results section illustrating checklist use
key_sources: Kimberly Boller, Ellen Eliason Kisker. (2014). Reporting What Readers Need to Know About Education Research Measures: A Guide. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/reporting-what-readers-need-to-know-about-education-research-measures-a-guide

article_title: CCSR: A New Model for the Role of Research in Supporting Urban School Reform
citation: Melissa Roderick, John Q. Easton, and Penny Bender Sebring. (2009). A New Model for the Role of Research in Supporting Urban School Reform. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago Urban Education Institute. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Five organizational commitments for research that builds district capacity
description: CCSR's three themes for capacity-building research are institutionalized in five commitments that organize how the organization conducts and communicates research: 'developing an extensive data archive on CPs, (2) extensive stakeholder engagement and strong ongoing relationships with the district, (3) conducting scientifically rigorous research while making findings broadly accessible, (4) building knowledge of core problems across time and across studies, and (5) an extensive outreach of providing information to the public.' The pattern treats the how of research—interaction, organization, dissemination—as capacity-building mechanisms in their own right.
requirements: An ongoing data-sharing agreement with the district
Governance structures (steering committee) that institutionalize stakeholder consultation
High internal standards of quality and review
constraints: The report notes technical quality can interfere with accessibility, requiring deliberate translation of rigorous analysis into public reports
target_learners: Practitioners, principals, district leaders, and the broader civic reform community in a single urban district
target_learning_goals: Making research findings usable for school improvement planning and policy dialogue
examples: Biennial CCSR surveys of principals, teachers, and students in grades six through twelve, with individual school reports benchmarking each school against similar schools
key_sources: Melissa Roderick, John Q. Easton, and Penny Bender Sebring. (2009). A New Model for the Role of Research in Supporting Urban School Reform. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago Urban Education Institute. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/ccsr-new-model-role-research-supporting-urban-school-reform

article_title: Infographic: Adopting and Adapting
citation: Adopting & Adapting: Skyline ELA curriculum launch infographic. (2021). University of Chicago Consortium. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Five organizational capacity levers leaders used to support Skyline ELA implementation
description: The infographic identifies five domains of strategic investment through which school leaders strengthened organizational capacity for curriculum implementation: "Championed professional learning", "Protected teacher time", "Expanded staff support", "Engaged external support", and "Strengthened collaboration structures". Leaders who targeted these key organizational levers supported teachers' engagement with the Skyline ELA curriculum. The pattern organizes implementation support as leadership investment across these five domains rather than as a single intervention.
requirements: Leaders must have discretion to allocate resources across professional learning, teacher time, staffing, external support, and collaboration structures.
constraints: Documented in the context of the K-2 Skyline ELA curriculum launch in Chicago Public Schools.
target_learners: Elementary school teachers in grades K-2
target_learning_goals: Implementation of a new literacy (ELA) curriculum with instructional change
examples: Leaders in the studied schools made strategic investments across the five domains during the 2021 Skyline launch.
key_sources: Adopting & Adapting: Skyline ELA curriculum launch infographic. (2021). University of Chicago Consortium. https://consortium.uchicago.edu

article_title: Computing in rural America: Developing K-8 coding pathways for Kentucky Appalachia
citation: Computing in Rural America: Developing K-8 Coding Pathways for Kentucky Appalachia. (2020). Presentation slides, December 2nd 2020.
title: Build a CT pathway from five key components: district-wide vision, annotated grade-band competencies, curated resources, competency-based PD, and formative assessment
description: The presentation enumerates the key components of a pathway: "Develop a district-wide vision for curricular integration of CT & CS in each grade band, including attention to the 'why' in the eyes of students, teachers and parents"; clear competency statements annotated with "short, illustrative examples or videos"; "Identification & adaptation of useful curricular resources"; identification of teacher professional development needs "based on stated competencies & curricula resources"; and "Articulation of formative assessment for students & teachers, guiding improvement."
requirements: Competencies must be stated per grade band and PD must be derived from those competencies and the chosen curricular resources
target_learning_goals: district-wide computational thinking and computer science integration
examples: The project's three central outputs — competencies, curricula, and credentialing — map onto these components

article_title: Unveiling the Value of Exploration: Insights from NSF-Funded Research on Emerging Technologies for Teaching and Learning
citation: Prado, Y.; Ouyang, S.; Risha, Z.; Ferguson, C.; Gardner, S.; Mallavarapu A.; Kelley, C.; Martin, W.; Glazer, K.; Hampton, S.; Fusco, J.; Pillai, S.; Walker, E.; Roschelle, J. (2024). Unveiling the Value of Exploration: Insights from NSF-Funded Research on Emerging Technologies for Teaching and Learning [Report]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/230
title: Five recurring innovation themes in NSF EXP project outcomes: accessibility, alternative CS modalities, VR/AR for STEM and workforce, broadening participation, and educator-centered AI
description: Qualitative analysis of 51 Project Information Pages submitted by RETTL PIs yielded recurring themes of project innovations. These include "Expanding accessibility for learners through digital tools," such as the SAIL 2 project's gamified virtual reality with signing avatars for ASL learning; alternative modalities in CS education using AI, AR/VR, tangible computing, and interdisciplinary learning; VR/AR tools for STEM education and workforce development; broadening participation of marginalized groups through technology; and centering educators in AI/ML tools so teachers remain at the forefront of decision making. Co-design with youths and LLM limitations and successes were cross-cutting themes discussed within the others.
requirements: Project teams showcasing key findings and technical and learning innovations via Project Information Pages developed in collaboration with NSF
constraints: Themes derive from 51 pages submitted by RETTL PIs, a self-selected subset of the portfolio
target_learners: underrepresented students in CS and STEM
target_learning_goals: Accessible and inclusive learning
computational thinking and CS entry
STEM concept understanding
critical data literacy
teacher-supported instruction
examples: SAIL 2 immerses learners in gamified VR with signing avatars to learn ASL; NeuroVivid co-designs with neurodivergent teenagers building their own EEGs; mTeam builds a debriefing system capturing multimodal data from a multi-user VR cardiac arrest resuscitation platform

article_title: Scaling Up Design of Inquiry Environments
citation: Roschelle, J., Mazziotti, C. & Means, B. (2021). Scaling Up Design of Inquiry Environments. In C. Chinn & R.G. Duncan et al (Eds.), International Handbook on Learning and Inquiry. Routledge. ISBN 9781138922600. https://isbnsearch.org/isbn/9781138922600
title: Five complementary strategies for scaling inquiry environments: understand context, engage expertise, build a coherent system, work with practitioners, measure and iterate
description: From reflections on six scaled inquiry environments (including SimCalc, GLOBE, LASER, WISE, River City, and Building Blocks), the chapter distills five strategies: "Through our review of each team’s reflections on these cases, we identified five useful scaling strategies. We see these as complementary strategies, not alternatives." The strategies are understanding the context and niche, engaging a breadth of expertise, developing a coherent learning activity system aligning curriculum, technology, professional development, and assessment, working with practitioners through co-design and partnerships, and measuring and iterating with aligned learning measures and implementation indicators.
requirements: Teams must explicitly take on scaling themselves and organize leadership to manage it, as all six case teams did
constraints: The chapter did not have space for a comprehensive review of every case
target_learners: K-12 students in science and mathematics inquiry programs
target_learning_goals: Inquiry learning outcomes sustained at scale across diverse settings
examples: The GLOBE program mapped its curriculum onto accountability standards and developed GLOBE books for early readers to win school-schedule time
The Scaling Up SimCalc project synchronized teacher professional development tightly to the curriculum workbooks and technology use

article_title: Using Research on Homework to Improve Remote and Hybrid Learning
citation: Roschelle, J. & Hodkowski, N.M. (2020). Using Research on Homework to Improve Remote and Hybrid Learning [White Paper]. San Mateo, CA: Digital Promise. http://hdl.handle.net/20.500.12265/107
title: Five essentials of effective homework: purpose, efficiency, ownership, competence, and aesthetic appeal
description: The paper identifies five fundamental qualities research has found in effective homework (Carr, 2013): "Purpose: Homework should be meaningful for learning; it should not be 'busy work.'" along with efficiency, ownership, competence, and aesthetic appeal. Teachers pressed for time are advised to start by getting purpose right, with clear directions explaining why the assignment helps learning.
requirements: Homework must be meaningful for learning rather than busy work, with clear and concise directions helping students understand why the assignment will help them learn
target_learners: K-12 students learning remotely or in hybrid models
target_learning_goals: Independent learning during non-instructional time
examples: Purpose statements such as 'I am making notes so I can participate in tomorrow's discussion.'

citation: Digital Promise. (2021). Nurturing an Innovative District: Inclusive Computing Pathways in Talladega County Schools. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/132
title: Five key computational thinking competencies organizing K-12 content

This gives the district a common competency spine for vertically and horizontally aligning CT across grades, from Pre-K through high school, and a frame students can use to articulate how CT integrates into classroom practice.

Mapping of competencies to state standards (Alabama DLCS) and vertical/horizontal alignment

examples: Talladega customized a competency map template, mapped it to Alabama DLCS standards, and aligned competencies vertically and horizontally across grade bands.

article_title: The Promotion Power Impacts of Louisiana High Schools
citation: Jonah Deutsch, Matthew Johnson, Brian Gill. (2020). The Promotion Power Impacts of Louisiana High Schools. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/the-promotion-power-impacts-of-louisiana-high-schools
title: Five-outcome long-term success framework for school impact measurement
description: The report organizes school effectiveness measurement around five long-term student outcomes: "On-time high school graduation", "Completion of a college or career readiness credential", "College enrollment", "Persistence in college", and "Earnings at age 26". This multi-outcome structure lets a state assess schools' contributions to long-term success rather than short-term test performance alone, and supports comparing school effectiveness across different outcome domains.
requirements: Requires statewide longitudinal data linking students to high school, postsecondary, and workforce records
constraints: Outcome window extends to earnings at age 26, requiring long follow-up periods
target_learning_goals: Graduation
College and career readiness
College persistence
Early-career earnings
examples: Louisiana used this framework to become one of the first states to identify its high schools' contributions to students' long-term success separately from other factors.

article_title: AI Literacy in Postsecondary Education
citation: Zachariah, I., Peters Hinton, V., Ruiz, P., Dallas, D., Liberman, B., & Karim, S. (2025). AI Literacy in Postsecondary Education. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/270
title: Five-domain taxonomy of AI skills and competencies for postsecondary educators and students
description: Through a literature review, the brief organizes postsecondary AI literacy into five domains: technical knowledge, ethical evaluation, analytical and adaptive skills, interpersonal and collaborative skills, and practical implementation. The article states that "five domains emerged" and details skills in each, such as "Understanding key technical terms, including large language model, machine learning, generative AI" and applying human judgment to evaluate AI outputs. It uses this taxonomy as the foundation for identifying implementation gaps and recommendations.

Responsibly evaluating AI systems
Using AI effectively as a human-centered tool

article_title: Integrating AI-Enabled EdTech in PK16 Education: Five Recommendations
citation: Ruiz, P., Peters Hinton, V., Prado, Y., Noakes, S., Liberman, B., Chillmon, C., Van Nostrand, P., Shell, A., Karim, S., Dallas, D., & Zachariah, I. (2025). Integrating AI-enabled edtech in PK16 education: Five recommendations for state and district leaders. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/273
title: Five EdTech Quality Indicators: Safe, Evidence-Based, Inclusive, Usable, and Interoperable
description: The brief presents the Five Edtech Quality Indicators—developed by 1EdTech, CAST, CoSN, Digital Promise, InnovateEDU, ISTE+ASCD, and SETDA—as core criteria for building AI-enabled edtech evaluation and accountability systems. Each indicator names a requirement: AI-enabled edtech must protect data and be "Safe," grounded in ESSA evidence tiers, "Inclusive" in prioritizing accessibility and equitable design, "Usable" by educators and students, and "Interoperable" through established interoperability standards for secure data exchange. Districts are encouraged to use these frameworks rather than start from scratch.

constraints: The brief notes many third-party validations still require research on product quality

examples: SETDA's 2025 guide integrates the five indicators into state procurement processes with adaptable model questions

article_title: Supporting School Improvement
citation: Hart, H., Young, C., Chen, A., Zou, A., & Allensworth, E.M. (2020). Supporting school improvement: Early findings from reexamination of the 5Essentials survey. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://www.5-essentials.org/
title: Five Essential Supports framework: five organizational essentials that influence students' learning
description: The framework identifies five key elements of school organization that influence students' learning: Effective Leaders, Collaborative Teachers, Involved Families, Supportive Environment, and Ambitious Instruction. The report states the framework "identified five key elements, or “essential supports,” of a school that influenced its students' learning". Each essential is defined behaviorally: Effective Leaders are "the driver for change"; a Supportive Environment is "safe, nurturing, stimulating, and focused on learning for all students"; Ambitious Instruction "challenges students through well-organized curricula". The 5Essentials Survey operationalizes the framework, and this study revalidates it in elementary and high schools.
requirements: Strength in multiple essentials: in the original validation, schools strong in at least three of the five supports were 10 times more likely to improve reading and math gains than schools weak in three to five supports
constraints: The authors note the framework encompasses more than school climate and prefer to describe schools strong in the essentials as having strong organizations rather than strong climates
target_learners: K-12 students in Chicago Public Schools (elementary and high schools)
target_learning_goals: Student achievement growth (reading and math)
Attendance
GPA
Freshman OnTrack and college enrollment
examples: The framework was crafted with input from the superintendent, principals, teachers, university professors, community activists, and parents during Chicago's 1990s districtwide reform, then studied with qualitative, survey, and administrative data from 1991–2005
key_sources: Hart, H., Young, C., Chen, A., Zou, A., & Allensworth, E.M. (2020). Supporting school improvement: Early findings from reexamination of the 5Essentials survey. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/supporting-school-improvement

article_title: Practice-Driven Data
citation: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Five characteristics of effective indicators: predictiveness, usability and clarity, right-time availability, direct causal linkage, and malleability
description: A Consortium report cited in the paper outlines five characteristics of effective indicators: predictiveness, usability and clarity, real time/right time availability, direct causal linkage to outcomes, and malleability. Predictiveness alone is insufficient — researchers must also show which indicators are less predictive and therefore poor targets — and even rigorously predictive indicators fail if they are not understandable, simple, and applicable in schools, since complexity that becomes a barrier to action undermines use. Indicators should be available in real time or at the right time, should have a direct causal linkage so that improving them changes the ultimate outcome, and must be malleable, meaning educators can move them with known strategies. The paper grounds the framework in the assumption that indicators' predictive power is practical rather than deterministic: indicators estimate likely outcomes to trigger support, with the goal that the predicted outcome does not correspond with the student's actual outcome.
requirements: Researchers must provide evidence of what indicators are and are not predictive of, and attend to how indicators will be incorporated into daily practice
Indicators must be available at the right time for educators to act, not only once a year
constraints: Establishing direct causal linkage is a complicated task, and indicators like eighth-grade test scores cannot be changed by high school educators
target_learning_goals: identifying students who need support
focusing school improvement strategies on outcomes that matter
examples: The Freshman Success Team at Sarah E. Goode STEM Academy uses a staged intervention flowchart (Figure 5) that first separates students with extremely low attendance, then uses GPA bands to assign classroom instruction, tutoring, or attendance-team support
key_sources: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/practice-driven-data-lessons-chicagos-approach-research-data-and-practice-education

article_title: From High School to the Future
citation: Melissa Roderick, Vanessa Coca, Eliza Moeller, and Thomas Kelley-Kemple. (2013). From High School to the Future: The Challenge of Senior Year in Chicago Public Schools. UChicago CCSR Research Report. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Five distinct senior-year coursetaking patterns characterize CPS seniors' schedules
description: The report typologizes CPS seniors' overall schedules into five named coursetaking patterns: "Making Up Courses," "Vocationally Focused," "Elective Heavy," "Core Concentrators," and "Advanced Placement." The report states that "Their schedules fall into five distinct coursetaking patterns" and that these patterns are not simply a result of achievement differences, since similarly qualified seniors often take different schedules. The typology is used throughout to show that most seniors' schedules focus on completing graduation requirements rather than preparing for college.
requirements: The typology is applied to graduates who took four or more courses in senior year, excluding special education and alternative/charter students
constraints: Patterns were derived from 2003-09 CPS transcript data and may not generalize beyond this district and period
target_learners: twelfth-grade high school students in an urban district
target_learning_goals: college preparatory coursetaking
postsecondary preparation
examples: Figure 13 shows seniors qualified for somewhat selective colleges split roughly across Advanced Placement (25%), Core Concentrators (18%), Elective Heavy (29%), Vocationally Focused (22%), and Making Up Courses (6%)
key_sources: Melissa Roderick, Vanessa Coca, Eliza Moeller, and Thomas Kelley-Kemple. (2013). From High School to the Future: The Challenge of Senior Year in Chicago Public Schools. UChicago CCSR Research Report. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/high-school-future-challenge-senior-year-chicago-public-schools

article_title: From High School to the Future
citation: Melissa Roderick, Jenny Nagaoka, Vanessa Coca, Eliza Moeller. (2009). From High School to the Future: Making Hard Work Pay Off — The Road to College for Students in CPS's Academically Advanced Programs. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago, Urban Education Institute. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: Five-part account of distinctive college-navigation challenges facing academically advanced first-generation students
description: The report draws on qualitative and quantitative analysis to identify five areas where academically advanced CPS students—most first-generation college students—face challenges in the college application process: not understanding the range of accessible colleges, lacking structured support for complicated applications to competitive colleges, competing demands from challenging coursework, and weak financial aid knowledge and participation. The report states "lack of knowledge of financial aid possibilities and lack of effective participation in financial aid prevent them from getting the aid they deserve." It argues high schools "must also fill the gaps in students'—and their parents'—understanding of college search, application, and selection."
requirements: High schools must provide specialized supports for college search and application beyond setting college-going expectations
constraints: The report states it is not intended to be a rigorous evaluation of the efficacy of selective enrollment schools, IB programs, or AP initiatives
target_learners: high-achieving high school students in selective enrollment, IB, and AP programs, most of whom are first-generation college students
target_learning_goals: navigating college search, application, selection, and financial aid
examples: The report compares the colleges students are qualified to attend with those to which they apply and enroll using CPS postsecondary tracking data, alongside qualitative analysis of the application process
key_sources: Melissa Roderick, Jenny Nagaoka, Vanessa Coca, Eliza Moeller. (2009). From High School to the Future: Making Hard Work Pay Off — The Road to College for Students in CPS's Academically Advanced Programs. article_title: School Improvement with External Partners
citation: Fred M. Newmann, Karin Sconzert. (2000). School Improvement with External Partners. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu/sites/default/files/publications/ExternalPartners.pdf
title: Five Essential Supports for Student Learning as analytical framework for assessing external partners
description: The Five Essential Supports is a research-based framework for school improvement that identifies five interconnected conditions: school leadership, professional community, parent and community involvement, student-centered learning climate, and quality instruction. The report uses this framework as its primary analytical lens to assess external partners' accomplishments, stating it was 'derived from a synthesis of research across the country on school improvement.' Each support is elaborated with specific indicators in Figure 1 of the report.
requirements: All five supports must be considered together, as they represent an integrated account of what schools need to improve student learning
constraints: The framework represents a consensus of experienced educators within the Chicago Public Schools and is most applicable to urban school contexts
target_learners: K-12 students in urban public schools
target_learning_goals: School-wide improvement in student achievement and learning conditions
examples: Used to organize the report's assessment of nine external partners' accomplishments and difficulties across 18 schools

equity-centered systems change
inclusive decision-making

article_title: Building Mathematics Teachers' Capacity to Enact Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education
citation: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Building Mathematics Teachers' Capacity to Enact Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Five criteria for mathematics curricular materials that support culturally responsive and sustaining education
description: The brief defines what CRSE-aligned mathematics curricular materials should do, listing five criteria: they should "affirm racial and cultural identities," "cultivate agency and belonging," "build critical consciousness," "center diverse perspectives," and "center student learning and academic success." The brief argues that such materials spare teachers the cognitively demanding and time-consuming task of making ad-hoc curriculum adjustments, enabling them to enact CRSE more effectively.
requirements: Materials must fulfill all five stated criteria: affirming racial and cultural identities, cultivating agency and belonging, building critical consciousness, centering diverse perspectives, and centering student learning and academic success
constraints: If adopting a new curriculum is not possible, the brief offers guiding questions for diversifying existing materials instead
target_learning_goals: Mathematics learning grounded in racial and cultural identity, agency, belonging, and critical consciousness
examples: The brief points readers to the WestEd publication Essential Characteristics of Math Curriculum Materials That Advance Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education for more detail

article_title: Roadmap to the Future for Yolo County Children and Youth Needs Assessment
citation: Roadmap to the Future for Yolo County Children and Youth Needs Assessment. (2024). WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Five-step community needs assessment process with engagement and interagency coordination throughout
description: The Roadmap Needs Assessment Five-Step Process structures the assessment as a pyramid of five sequential steps, with community engagement and interagency coordination as essential components throughout. The report states the team "used the Roadmap Needs Assessment Five-Step Process (see Figure 2) to conduct the needs assessment" and that the process "encompasses all aspects of the methodology." The steps move from identifying existing assets by the Ten Aspects of Community and district, to identifying needs, interviewing key informants, developing recommendations filtered through guiding principles, and aligning systems to achieve desired outcomes.
requirements: Community engagement and interagency coordination throughout the process
Data from multiple sources including asset databases, engagement sessions, interviews, and public quantitative data
constraints: Developed and applied for the Yolo County Roadmap to the Future initiative; recommendations are filtered through the initiative's three guiding principles
target_learners: Children, youth, and families in Yolo County
target_learning_goals: Coordinating and improving community assets and services that support children's and youth's healthy development
examples: Step 1 identified existing community assets and services organized by the Ten Aspects of Community and Supervisorial District; Step 4 developed recommendations and strategic actions filtered through the guiding principles

article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners: Formative Assessment Support for Integrated and Meaningful Language Learning
citation: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., Blitz, J., & Garcia-Arena, P. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Formative Assessment Support for Integrated and Meaningful Language Learning. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Five task characteristics for integrated learning and evidence gathering: rigorous, interactive, authentic, language-rich, and multimodal
description: The brief enumerates characteristics tasks should have when teachers plan to gather evidence and frame learning experiences: "they should be rigorous, interactive, authentic, support language, and offer a choice of modality." Rigorous tasks promote deep higher-order thinking; interactive tasks invite collaboration; authentic tasks address students' lived experiences; language-rich tasks integrate the four domains; multimodal tasks offer choices for accessing learning and representing knowledge.
requirements: Tasks must generate visible or audible student learning outputs that teachers can gather as evidence during tasks
target_learning_goals: Deep conceptual understanding, disciplinary language use, and demonstration of knowledge through multiple modes
examples: In the 5th-grade vignette, students could complete a graphic organizer in pairs, draw pictures with labels, or give oral explanations, and some English learners paired with peers providing home-language support
key_sources: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., Blitz, J., & Garcia-Arena, P. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Formative Assessment Support for Integrated and Meaningful Language Learning. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673604

article_title: How English Learners Are Screened for Risk of Reading Difficulty: Use of English- and Spanish-Language Screeners in the 2023/24 School Year
citation: Soo Ping Chow, A., Faulkner-Bond, M., Lemke, M., LeBeau, B., & Quesen, S. (2025). How English learners are screened for risk of reading difficulty: Use of English- and Spanish-language screeners in the 2023/24 school year. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Five-cluster typology of English learner language-of-assessment screening practices
description: The brief uses k-modes clustering, a technique for identifying natural groups within categorical data, to sort English learners into five screening-practice clusters based on assessment language at each time of year. The solution that best reflected the sample showed "five primary practices in the screening of English learners": English-only at all periods (90%), both languages at all periods (8%), English all periods with Spanish at MOY/EOY (1%), alternating languages (under 1%), and Spanish all periods with English at EOY (under 1%). Clusters were characterized by program enrollment, native language, years in U.S. schools, and ACCESS performance.
requirements: Requires categorical assessment-taking data at each screening period (BOY, MOY, EOY) to assign students to clusters
constraints: Some students do not fit perfectly within a given cluster; students were assigned to the cluster that most closely aligned with their screening practices
Solutions with more than five clusters had redundant or indistinguishable clusters; fewer than five revealed no new meaningful groups
target_learning_goals: Early literacy screening for risk of reading difficulty
examples: Cluster 1 (21,582 students) was screened only in English; cluster 4 (185 students) alternated Spanish at BOY, English at MOY, Spanish at EOY
key_sources: Soo Ping Chow, A., Faulkner-Bond, M., Lemke, M., LeBeau, B., & Quesen, S. (2025). How English learners are screened for risk of reading difficulty: Use of English- and Spanish-language screeners in the 2023/24 school year. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED677598

article_title: Measuring What Matters: Considerations for Measuring the Implementation of High-Quality Instructional Materials in Mathematics
citation: Perry, R., Nucci, D., Walters, K., McKinney, D., Nielsen, S., & Hannan, M. (2026). Measuring what matters: Considerations for measuring the implementation of high-quality instructional materials in mathematics. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Five-dimension framework for operationalizing HQIM implementation fidelity: dosage, adherence, instructional quality, student experience, and support
description: The report defines implementation as "a reduction in the translational difference between the essential, intended design elements of the curriculum and its enactment in classrooms" and operationalizes five dimensions. Dosage captures how much of the official curriculum teachers use; adherence captures following prescribed units, lessons, and sequence; instructional quality captures alignment of instruction with intended interactions; student experience captures students' perceptions of opportunities to learn; and support captures district and school professional learning. The framework treats implementation as contextual, informed by professional learning that shapes teachers' decisions to add, modify, or omit curriculum elements.
requirements: Measuring fidelity requires identifying which dimensions are core to the intervention, and the report notes a minimum fidelity threshold is not always clearly specified
constraints: Classroom-based interventions like HQIM add complexity because teachers make professional decisions in dynamic environments; the framework was designed for middle-grades mathematics and the team did not anticipate generalizing beyond the middle grades
target_learners: middle grades (6–8) mathematics students and their teachers
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of curriculum implementation to attribute student outcomes to programs
examples: Table 1 maps each fidelity dimension to specific teacher-survey items, such as percentage of class time using the core curriculum for dosage and frequency of instructional practices for quality
key_sources: Perry, R., Nucci, D., Walters, K., McKinney, D., Nielsen, S., & Hannan, M. (2026). Measuring what matters: Considerations for measuring the implementation of high-quality instructional materials in mathematics. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED681340

article_title: From the Brink of Closure: Key Factors in One Charter School's Successful Turnaround
citation: Evan, A. (2019). From the brink of closure: Key factors in one charter school's successful turnaround. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://dcpcsb.egnyte.com/dl/hdsUO9pDbh/
title: Five-Component Framework for Systemic School Turnaround
description: TenSquare's framework holds that successful turnaround requires transforming five core components in tandem: board and leadership, talent, teaching and learning, culture, and operations and finance. The report states the approach "centered on transforming five core components" and that working on any one component in isolation "results in turnaround efforts that quickly deteriorate." Each component had defined content, e.g., teaching and learning included curriculum and assessment alignment to standards and evidence-based instructional practices.
requirements: Simultaneous attention to all five components rather than isolated improvement efforts
constraints: The report cautions that "No framework should be a magic bullet" and implementation must fit the school's needs and context
target_learners: School leaders, boards, and turnaround partners in low-performing charter schools
target_learning_goals: Comprehensive organizational transformation supporting student achievement
examples: Perry Street overhauled leadership structure, talent systems, curriculum alignment to PARCC, PBIS behavior systems, and budget reallocation
key_sources: Evan, A. (2019). From the brink of closure: Key factors in one charter school's successful turnaround. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://dcpcsb.egnyte.com/dl/hdsUO9pDbh/

article_title: Lessons Learned about Leading the Implementation of Formative Assessment: A Framework for School Leaders and Leadership Teams
citation: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Five-practice framework for leading formative assessment implementation
description: The brief presents a leadership framework (Exhibit 1) of five synergistic practices for guiding formative assessment implementation: "fostering understanding of formative assessment; communicating a compelling vision...; modeling a culture of learning...; leading site-based professional learning...; and nurturing the conditions necessary for the changes associated with implementing and scaling formative assessment." It was derived from WestEd's site observations and leadership coaching at 12 school campuses in three urban districts during the How I Know project (2017–2020). The practices are described as operating "synergistically to support and strengthen the learning and mindset shifts needed by teachers and their students."
requirements: Leaders must themselves understand formative assessment's grounding principles and the instructional shifts it requires
constraints: Framework derived from one project's observations across 12 campuses in three urban districts
target_learners: school leaders and leadership teams in K-12 sites
target_learning_goals: leading instructional change toward formative assessment practice
examples: WestEd coaches documented five leadership practices that appeared to enhance implementation across 12 school campuses in three districts between 2017 and 2020
key_sources: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606088

article_title: California Special Education Funding System Study, [Part 1]: A Descriptive Analysis of Special Education Funding in California
citation: Jason Willis, Sara Menlove Doutre, Kelsey Krausen, Tyson Barrett, Tye Ripma, and Ruthie Caparas. (2020). Study of California's Special Education Funding System: Phase I Report — A Descriptive Analysis of Special Education Funding in California. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Five-component framework for education funding policymaking: allocation, distribution, expected expenditures, governance, and external accountability
description: The report introduces a framework for conceptualizing any education funding system, built around a funding formula with three components — "allocation (how amounts of funding are calculated), distribution (directing the funds to specific entities), and expected expenditures (requirements for or restrictions on how funds will be spent)" — plus decisions affecting local governance authority and external accountability. The report uses this framework as the lens for describing California's system in Sections 4 and 5 and states the next report will use it to detail implications and options for refining the system.
requirements: Policymakers consider all five components when revising a funding system, as the report states these are the components around which funding and practice decisions are made
constraints: The report notes every design choice in each component has tradeoffs, for example incentivizing overidentification versus underidentification of students with disabilities
target_learners: students with disabilities in California K-12 schools
target_learning_goals: correct, timely identification of students with disabilities; effective and efficient provision of special education services; provision of funding through effective mechanisms and agencies
examples: The report describes California's AB 602 system through this framework: state allocation by ADA with SELPA-specific rates, distribution exclusively through SELPAs, and expected expenditures including required and restricted spending rules
key_sources: Jason Willis, Sara Menlove Doutre, Kelsey Krausen, Tyson Barrett, Tye Ripma, and Ruthie Caparas. (2020). Study of California's Special Education Funding System: Phase I Report — A Descriptive Analysis of Special Education Funding in California. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED616102

article_title: Supporting California's Children through a Whole Child Approach: A Field Guide for Creating Integrated, School-Based Systems of Care
citation: Breaking Barriers, California Alliance of Child and Family Services, Santa Clara County Office of Education, & WestEd. (2022). Supporting California's children through a whole child approach: A field guide for creating integrated, school-based systems of care. https://WestEd.org/permissions
title: Five key elements of a whole child approach
description: The guide enumerates five key elements that constitute a whole child approach: "positive developmental relationships; environments filled with safety and belonging; rich learning experiences and knowledge development; development of skills, habits, and mindsets; and integrated support systems." The fifth element, integrated support systems, is the guide's central focus, operationalized as integrated, school-based systems of care built through cross-sector collaboration. The list is grounded in the science of learning and development literature the guide cites.
requirements: Schools must coordinate policy, process, and practice across health, education, and social service sectors, since frameworks alone are described as insufficient without implementation

article_title: STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis
citation: Fulton, K., Doerr, H., & Britton, T. (2010). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis. National Commission on Teaching & America's Future / WestEd. https://www.nctaf.org/resources/events/STEMWingspreadConference.htm
title: Five-class taxonomy of knowledge sources for synthesizing STEM PLC knowledge
description: The synthesis organizes its evidence into five named classes of knowledge: Type 1, elaborated empirical studies since 1995 mostly in peer-reviewed journals; Type 2, empirical studies reported without method detail and non-empirical work such as theory building; Type 3, published expert knowledge and advice; Type 4, practice-based knowledge from an expert practitioner online panel; and Type 5, published model descriptions often with lessons learned. The authors explain that they "determined it would be useful to add an additional category that would explicitly attend to knowledge about models of conducting PLCs", finding "a considerable body of research in this category, some with “lessons learned” but without formal research". The framework lets the synthesis combine gold-standard and working knowledge while flagging where evidence is thin.
requirements: Restricting the synthesis only to empirical and descriptive studies in peer-reviewed journals would be too incomplete, so the additional non-empirical knowledge classes are needed to capture working knowledge.
constraints: The non-empirical sources may not meet the gold standard of empirical research, though the authors found them generally consistent with findings emerging from the empirical studies.
target_learning_goals: STEM teachers' content and pedagogical content knowledge
STEM instructional practice
student mathematics and science achievement
examples: The corpus profile: 78% qualitative only, 85% focused on inservice, 18% involving online components, twice as many studies in mathematics as in science, and two-thirds published in the last five years.
key_sources: Fulton, K., Doerr, H., & Britton, T. (2010). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis. National Commission on Teaching & America's Future / WestEd. https://www.nctaf.org/resources/events/STEMWingspreadConference.htm

article_title: Solving the Teacher Shortage: How to Attract and Retain Excellent Educators
citation: Podolsky, A., Kini, T., Bishop, J., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2016). Solving the Teacher Shortage: How to Attract and Retain Excellent Educators. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/solving-teacher-shortage
title: Five-factor framework of teacher recruitment and retention
description: The report organizes the research on teacher shortages around five major factors that shape teachers' career decisions: "Salaries and other compensation", "Preparation and costs to entry", "Hiring and personnel management", "Induction and support for new teachers", and "Working conditions". Each factor is treated in its own section, with attention to how it operates in hard-to-staff schools. The authors stress the factors are interrelated and require a comprehensive policy response rather than isolated interventions.
requirements: Policymakers should implement mutually reinforcing policies across the five factors rather than any single policy in isolation
constraints: The authors note the factors are interrelated and the report treats them separately only for analysis
target_learners: policymakers and school and district leaders responsible for staffing classrooms with effective teachers
target_learning_goals: recruiting and retaining an effective, stable teaching workforce, especially in high-need schools

article_title: Improving Education the New Mexico Way: An Evidence-Based Approach
citation: Oakes, J., Espinoza, D., Darling-Hammond, L., Gonzales, C., DePaoli, J., Kini, T., Hoachlander, G., Burns, D., Griffith, M., & Leung, M. (2020). Improving education the New Mexico way: An evidence-based approach. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/improving-education-new-mexico-way
title: Five fundamental elements of a high-quality education system
description: The report organizes its recommendations around a framework of five system elements that states and nations that have improved education have strengthened: "Meaningful learning goals, supported by Knowledgeable and skillful educators, Integrated student supports, and High-quality early learning opportunities, all made possible with Adequate and equitably distributed school funding." The report argues policy changes in all five are possible in New Mexico and could bring significant improvement, and that inadequacies in each area were cited by the Martinez/Yazzie court.
requirements: Policy changes across all five elements, plus a thoughtful accountability system, since the report states the five elements alone are not enough to establish and sustain a high-quality education system
constraints: Framed for state-level system change in New Mexico's context of diversity, local control, and high poverty
target_learners: All New Mexico public school students, particularly at-risk students defined by the Martinez/Yazzie case
target_learning_goals: Meaningful 21st century learning across academic, cultural-linguistic, social-emotional, and college-and-career domains

article_title: Educator Learning to Enact the Science of Learning and Development
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., Flook, L., Schachner, A., & Wojcikiewicz, S. (with Cantor, P., & Osher, D.). (2021). Educator learning to enact the science of learning and development. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/859.776
title: Five key practices for educator preparation: grounding in human development, theory-practice integration, authentic practice with feedback, inquiry, and professional learning communities
description: The report enumerates key practices for educator preparation that "research has shown make a strong difference in the capacities of educators": anchoring candidate learning in the study of human development and learning; integrating theory and practice through clinical experiences and coursework; "providing opportunities for authentic practice, assessment, feedback, and reflection to accelerate learning"; engaging in inquiry and analysis strategies that guide reflection and application; and collaborating in professional learning communities offering mutual support and modeling.
requirements: These practices operate within program designs built on pedagogical alignment and clinical experiences tightly linked to coursework
constraints: The report characterizes the supporting research collectively without reporting specific effect sizes in the text provided
target_learning_goals: mastery of developmentally grounded teaching practices and adaptive expertise

article_title: Making Assessment Reports More Meaningful for Students & Families
citation: Levitan, S., & Munyan-Penney, N. (2024). Meaningful Assessment Reporting: Making Assessment Reports More Meaningful for Students & Families. EdTrust. https://edtrust.org/
title: Five best practices for designing meaningful individual score reports
description: The brief lays out "five essential best practices" for individual score report design: involving students and families in the design process, using asset-framing, clearly communicating the purpose of assessments, helping users make sense of the data, and providing actionable information. Reports should use a "bottom line up front" design that prominently highlights key takeaways, explain key terminology while minimizing jargon, include narrative explanations, high-quality translations, and guiding questions, and offer next steps such as a helpline and conversation starters. State examples include South Carolina's guiding questions, Texas's multilingual PDF walkthrough, Rhode Island's QR-code video, and Ohio's tailored recommendations.
requirements: A clear theory of action articulating the purpose of statewide assessments should inform draft reports used when engaging with families
Targeted consultation with students and families of color, low-income families, and multilingual families, with compensation and attention to time and meeting location
constraints: Space is limited on reports, so states must carefully decide which data needs additional explanation; including rich explanatory content can make reports text heavy, a trade-off states must balance
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of assessment results and use of results to support learning
examples: South Carolina's report includes guiding questions such as what the child's score means; Illinois' report includes questions and prompts for families to use with teachers and suggests actions by readiness level
key_sources: Levitan, S., & Munyan-Penney, N. (2024). Meaningful Assessment Reporting: Making Assessment Reports More Meaningful for Students & Families. EdTrust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED658190

article_title: How States Are Expanding Quality Summer Learning Opportunities
citation: Fitz, J., Woods, J., Duran, N., & McCombs, J. (2025). How states are expanding quality summer learning opportunities. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/910.329
title: Five categories of state action for supporting summer learning
description: The report organizes its case study findings into an explanatory framework of five categories of state action commonly observed across nine states: "1. Garnering support for summer learning investments, 2. Implementing state grant programs for summer learning, 3. Increasing access for priority groups, 4. Promoting high-quality programming, 5. Collecting and using data." Each category is elaborated with state examples and closing policy considerations. The framework is descriptive, derived from interviews and document analysis rather than from program outcome evaluation.
requirements: State-level actors including legislators, governor's offices, state agencies, and statewide networks engaged in each category of action
constraints: The study did not assess program quality; it attended to state practices promoting adoption of features associated with quality in the research literature
target_learners: K-12 students participating in voluntary summer learning programs
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in reading and math
social development and emotional well-being
career-related skills
examples: Case studies of Georgia, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Michigan, New Mexico, Oregon, Tennessee, Texas, and Vermont grant programs
key_sources: Fitz, J., Woods, J., Duran, N., & McCombs, J. (2025). How states are expanding quality summer learning opportunities. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/910.329

article_title: Advancing Integration and Equity through Magnet Schools
citation: George, J., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2021). Advancing integration and equity through magnet schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/magnet-schools
title: First door and second door components of diverse, effective magnet schools
description: The report organizes the shared features of diverse magnet schools that support positive social and academic outcomes into two categories. "First door" components bring students from different backgrounds to the school: integration embedded in school design and mission, intentional family outreach, inclusive enrollment practices, and free transportation. "Second door" components foster inclusive environments once students arrive: culturally responsive curriculum and instruction for all students, staff prepared for heterogeneous classrooms, ongoing professional development, and nondiscriminatory, restorative discipline practices. The report states these components "help to foster inclusive environments and promote shared success for students of color within diverse magnet schools, without tracking them into separate classes that depress their opportunities for success."
requirements: Magnet schools need support to effectively implement evidence-based components, per the report, including funding and policy support at federal, state, and district levels.
constraints: The report notes magnet schools vary significantly in theme, pedagogy, design, and implementation, making generalized conclusions about effectiveness difficult.
target_learners: white and more affluent students in diverse magnet schools
target_learning_goals: access to rigorous, culturally responsive curriculum for all students
inclusive school climates supporting achievement for students of all backgrounds
examples: The report lists first door components such as "intentional and ongoing family outreach and engagement" and "provision of free transportation," and second door components including "culturally responsive curriculum and instruction" and "nondiscriminatory, restorative discipline practices."
key_sources: George, J., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2021). Advancing integration and equity through magnet schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/magnet-schools

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Massachusetts
citation: Education Trust. (2020). Educator Diversity State Profile: Massachusetts. https://edtrust.org
title: Five-goal state policy framework for increasing educator workforce diversity
description: The brief organizes state policy conditions into five goals: making educator diversity data visible and actionable, setting clear state and district goals, supporting preparation programs to recruit and prepare teachers of color, targeting resources to recruit and hire a diverse workforce, and improving working conditions and growth opportunities for teachers of color. Each goal is scored on a three-level rating scale ("Meets Criteria, Partially Meets Criteria, Does Not Meet Criteria") with printed rating methodologies and exemplar states. The framework is used to profile Massachusetts and guide state-level advocacy.

examples: Massachusetts is rated against all five goals, earning greens on data dashboards, stakeholder engagement, Grow Your Own grants, and anti-bias training, and reds on completer data, retention data, scholarships, MSI investment, and residency pathways
key_sources: Education Trust. (2020). Educator Diversity State Profile: Massachusetts. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED622850

article_title: The 5P Reflection Model for Education in the Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) Era
citation: Rajan Kadel, Samar Shailendra, Islam Mohammad Tahidul, Urvashi Rahul Saxena, Aakanksha Sharma, and Sabitra Kaphle. (2026). The 5P Reflection Model for Education in the Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) Era. Pre-print submitted to IEEE Transactions on Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03413

description: The article organises the reflection literature into five families, each analysed for strengths, limitations in the GenAI era and application areas in Tables I-V: experiential (Kolb, Gibbs, DIEP), transformative (Mezirow and successors), reflective practitioner (Schön, Brookfield, CARL and others), emotional/affective (Boud and others), and self-regulated learning (Zimmerman, Pintrich, Winne and Hadwin, Boekaerts). The article states: "In this study, we classify reflection into five commonly recognised categories" spanning these traditions.

understanding of reflection model selection
examples: Tables I through V summarise each model's strengths, GenAI-era limitations and application areas, e.g. Gibbs' cycle for nursing and health sciences, Zimmerman's model for STEM education

article_title: Creating Safer Schools: A Case Study
citation: Duchesneau, N., & Zapata, M. (2023). Creating Safer Schools: A Case Study. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org
title: Five-type spectrum of school safety approaches, from school-to-prison pipeline schools to school-to-possibility pipeline schools
description: The report's authors categorize schools on a five-point spectrum of safety approaches. At one end, "School-to-prison pipeline schools" are "hardened schools with a high emphasis on physical security, no guardrails to prevent the harm that physical security can cause, and little to no attention on student well-being." Intermediate types add guardrails and scale up well-being practices while scaling down physical security. The ultimate goal, school-to-possibility pipeline schools, have fully adopted practices addressing root causes of violence and removed physical security. Leaders are advised to locate their schools on the spectrum and plan next steps toward the goal.
requirements: Leaders must first assess where their school or district currently stands on the spectrum in terms of current policies before planning next steps
constraints: The spectrum is a framework proposed by the report's authors based on this two-district case study and other research, not a validated measurement instrument
target_learners: students in urban districts serving majority Black, Latino, and/or low-income populations
target_learning_goals: creating safe, inclusive learning environments that support students' social, emotional, and academic development
examples: The report situates both case-study districts as retaining physical security while adopting well-being practices, placing them in intermediate spectrum categories rather than at the school-to-possibility end
key_sources: Duchesneau, N., & Zapata, M. (2023). Creating Safer Schools: A Case Study. The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED641760

citation: Rebeca Shackleford and Kristen Hengtgen. (2024). A Vision for Equitable Pathways: Enhancing Support and Innovation in College and Career Counseling. EdTrust/All4Ed. https://edtrust.org
title: Five elements of an ideal pathways system: clear choices, smart start, access for all, guided beginnings, final prep
description: The brief enumerates five essential elements an ideal pathways system ensures for students and families: "1. Clear choices: a clear understanding of all their options 2. A smart start: early outreach before entering high school 3. Access for all: information that is accessible and in multiple formats 4. Guided beginnings: regular touchpoints with a navigator 5. Final prep: dedicated and targeted support in high school." Each element is paired with promising state practices, such as Indiana's College Core planning tool, Connecticut's Student Success Plans, DCPS language access, Illinois' PaCE Framework, and Pinellas County college and career centers.

Federal investment at scale, since implementation varies across states and underfunded districts struggle to offer additional resources

target_learning_goals: Understanding and accessing college and career pathway options

article_title: Position: Adopting AI in Practice Does Not Guarantee the Productivity Boost
citation: Won Ik Cho, Seong-hun Kim, Geunhye Kim. (2026). Position: Adopting AI in Practice Does Not Guarantee the Productivity Boost. Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24688
title: Five-factor moderation framework extending the Gries-Naudé AI productivity model
description: The paper proposes that five human and environmental factors—human resource composition, baseline capability of individuals, learning curve of practitioners, incentives for fair use, and flexibility of objectives—moderate whether AI adoption translates into realized productivity gains. It formalizes these as an organizational effectiveness factor Ω = ωC·ωI, a capability-adjusted productivity term, a learning-curve factor λi(τ), and an endogenous automation threshold, revising the Gries-Naudé partial equilibrium model in which these were exogenous parameters. The authors state: "We identify five key moderating factors: human resource composition, baseline capability of individuals, learning curve of practitioners, incentives for fair use, and flexibility of objectives."
requirements: Requires treating human and environmental factors as endogenous organizational variables that practitioners actively manage, rather than exogenous technological parameters
constraints: The revised production function aggregates over a single organizational subunit such as a team or department, not an entire firm; the influence of each factor depends on the domain and organizational characteristics
target_learners: students and teachers in educational institutions
target_learning_goals: understanding conditions under which AI adoption yields realized productivity or learning gains
examples: The paper contrasts a flat AI task force where ωC approaches unity with a multi-layer hierarchy where ωC collapses despite high nominal expert availability
key_sources: Won Ik Cho, Seong-hun Kim, Geunhye Kim. (2026). Position: Adopting AI in Practice Does Not Guarantee the Productivity Boost. Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24688

It serves as the study's structured inventory of transition mechanisms available to curriculum designers and governance bodies.

Some classifications (Kazakhstan 2025/2026, Romania 2030) may already be in transition

article_title: Artificial intelligence in university physics education: a systematic review of empirical studies
citation: Malikova Z, Ualikhanova B, Turmambekov T, Rakhashev B and Berdaliyev D (2026). Artificial intelligence in university physics education: a systematic review of empirical studies. Front. Educ. 11:1964629. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1964629
title: Five-domain analytical synthesis of AI use in university physics education
description: The review organizes its cross-study synthesis of the 11 included studies into five analytical domains: "feedback and scaffolding; virtual tutoring and learning support; content generation and teacher preparation; collaborative learning and simulation/modeling; and AI literacy, trust, and critical evaluation." For each domain, Table 6 records patterns of AI use, contradictions across studies, and conditions identified as relevant to educational use, such as alignment between AI-supported activities and assessment tasks and support that guides reasoning rather than providing complete answers. Figure 2 provides a conceptual summary of the relationships among these patterns, conditions, contradictions, and outcomes.
requirements: Empirical studies of AI used for pedagogical purposes in university physics education with direct participation of university students, as defined by the review's PICOS criteria.
constraints: The review states the figure "should be interpreted as a conceptual synthesis of the reviewed evidence rather than as a causal model."
target_learning_goals: Physics conceptual understanding and problem solving
AI literacy and critical evaluation of AI outputs
examples: Table 6 maps each domain to patterns, contradictions, and conditions; e.g., in the feedback domain, benefits were stronger when homework and assessment content were closely aligned (Lu et al., 2025).

citation: Wen Liang, Li Siyan, Zackary Rackauckas, and Julia Hirschberg. (2026). A Survey of Automated Presentation Coaching: Systems, Methods, and Open Challenges. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27380
title: Five-dimensional task taxonomy for automated presentation coaching
description: The survey formalizes a taxonomy organizing presentation skills into five dimensions: segmental pronunciation, lexical stress, suprasegmental prosody, pacing, and content faithfulness. It states that "The taxonomy organizes presentation skills by the nature of the feedback they require and the methods available to assess them, providing a systematic framework for comparing existing systems and identifying coverage gaps." Each dimension is defined with its assessment methods and feedback type, and surveyed systems are mapped onto it (Table 1) to expose which dimensions are under-addressed.
requirements: Systems must be describable by their inputs (transcript, learner recording, slide-aligned scripts, reference slide content), outputs (per-phone flags, global scores, missing-keyword flags), and operating mode for the taxonomy to apply.
constraints: The survey notes its taxonomy and metrics "are derived from existing literature and may not capture all dimensions relevant to real-world coaching scenarios."

target_learning_goals: Pronunciation accuracy, lexical stress, prosody, pacing, and content coverage in oral presentations
examples: Figure 1 illustrates the taxonomy structure and Table 1 maps 15 surveyed systems onto the five dimensions.

article_title: Calibrating Trustworthiness: Co-Designing Metrics and Visualizations for Evaluating LLMs in Education
citation: Adam Coscia, Sujata Duwal, Langdon Holmes, Scott Crossley, and Alex Endert. (2026). Calibrating Trustworthiness: Co-Designing Metrics and Visualizations for Evaluating LLMs in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04006
title: Five trustworthiness metrics comprising 20 measures for evaluating LLM trustworthiness in education
description: The article co-constructed a set of five trustworthiness metrics comprising 20 quantitative measures tailored to pedagogical use. Metrics visible in the article include Misinformation, Sycophancy, Diplomacy, Disposition, Learning Method, and Response Quality, each defined by criteria such as "The LLM only generates true, substantiated factual claims" and "The LLM response follows established principles of learning." Measures were sourced from ML trustworthiness literature, education literature on pedagogical prompt patterns, and task-based response quality criteria, then refined through collaborative whiteboarding sessions with learning engineers.
requirements: Measures must automatically compute over every response
Measures must be grounded in the learning context including the textbook passage, learner summary, and preceding dialogue
constraints: Not every ML trustworthiness measure may be needed for education; some require re-contextualization to foreground the relevant pedagogical disruption
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students using LLM-powered digital textbooks
target_learning_goals: evaluating LLM responses for trustworthiness
detecting pedagogical disruptions in LLM-generated dialogue
examples: The Socratic measure aligns with Knowles' Principles of Adult Learning; the Scaffolding measure incorporates Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development; the SERT measure incorporates self-regulated learning principles

article_title: What Does the Credential Still Certify? Cognitive Stewardship for AI-Mediated Education
citation: Kai Yao. (2026). What Does the Credential Still Certify? Cognitive Stewardship for AI-Mediated Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19988
title: Five delegation types taxonomy
description: The framework uses five recurring delegation types: access support, feedback support, process support, substitution, and output-verification support. As the article states, "Access support enables participation, for example through translation, speech-to-text, or assistive scaffolding. Feedback support offers critique or suggestions while the learner retains judgment." Process support assists planning, drafting, debugging, or workflow; substitution occurs when AI performs the operation being assessed; output-verification support treats checking AI-mediated work as a capability to be taught and assessed. The categories describe the role of assistance in a task and are not moral or fixed tool labels.
requirements: The same use must be re-classified per task, since one use can be access support in one task and substitution in another
constraints: The categories are descriptive roles, not moral labels or fixed tool labels
target_learning_goals: classifying AI use relative to the certified learning claim
examples: The scenario stress test applied these five types plus a programming-workflow case to each audited policy package
key_sources: Kai Yao. (2026). What Does the Credential Still Certify? Cognitive Stewardship for AI-Mediated Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19988

article_title: The Tragedy of the Cognitive Commons: How AI Could Disrupt the Regeneration of Professional Expertise
citation: Lovett, N. (2026). The tragedy of the cognitive commons: How AI could disrupt the regeneration of professional expertise. Human Resource Development Review. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1177/15344843261470602
title: Five structural factors determining occupational commons vulnerability
description: The framework states that "The framework identifies five factors that determine an occupation's commons vulnerability": task substitutability (how far AI performs the tasks that historically provided novice developmental experience), regulatory intensity, safety criticality, professional association strength, and work modularization. Professions should show greater disruption where AI exposure is higher, where early-career development was concentrated organizationally rather than educationally, and where the three commons characteristics are most pronounced. The unit of analysis is the occupation, not the national economy, and countervailing dynamics (new AI-era developmental pathways, mixed aggregate labor-market evidence) establish that the depletion mechanism is not universal.
requirements: Vulnerability assessment requires occupation-level analysis of which specific cognitive tasks AI substitutes for
constraints: Applies only to professions meeting the three structural conditions; early empirical evidence is drawn from US, UK, and German labor markets, reflecting the research base rather than a theoretical limitation
target_learning_goals: Prioritizing expertise-regeneration interventions in high-vulnerability occupations
Generating testable predictions about differential commons disruption
examples: The paper places software engineering, financial analysis, and legal research in higher-vulnerability categories, and medicine and engineering in slower-degradation categories due to institutional counterpressures.
key_sources: Lovett, N. (2026). The tragedy of the cognitive commons: How AI could disrupt the regeneration of professional expertise. Human Resource Development Review. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1177/15344843261470602

article_title: Customizing AI for writing pedagogy: a systematic review of pedagogical goals, theoretical principles, and technical design
citation: Luo, Y. (2026). Customizing AI for writing pedagogy: a systematic review of pedagogical goals, theoretical principles, and technical design. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10697-w
title: Five-category taxonomy of pedagogical goals in customized AI writing instruction
description: The review derives five pedagogical goal categories through an iterative mixed inductive–deductive coding process across 23 studies: multi-dimensional feedback and scoring, writing process and metacognition, higher-order academic skills, alternative assessment models, and learner feedback literacy. The review reports that "multi-dimensional feedback and scoring dominated the literature (N = 9), followed by goals related to writing process and metacognition (N = 6) and higher-order academic skills (N = 6)", while alternative assessment models and learner feedback literacy were each represented by only one study, revealing a strong concentration on product- and performance-oriented outcomes.
requirements: Studies must pursue explicit pedagogical goals in customizing AI for writing instruction to be classifiable within the taxonomy
constraints: Derived from 23 empirical studies published between January 2020 and September 2025
target_learners: Higher education L2 academic writing learners
target_learning_goals: Writing competence development through AI-mediated feedback and process support
examples: The review coded studies reporting multiple goals under each applicable category, producing co-occurrence data visualized in Fig. 2

citation: Drummond, M., & Dale, G. (2026). Generating a Student-Informed Teaching and Learning Conceptual Framework for GenAI in Business Schools: A Case Study. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice. https://doi.org/10.53761/6jvtax83
title: AI-focused learning activities in the first-year undergraduate business curriculum
description: The instructional element evaluated in this case study is a set of newly implemented AI-focused learning activities introduced into the first-year undergraduate curriculum of a UK business school. The article states the school "introduced GenAI into its curriculum for first-year undergraduates" and that a mixed-methods survey of 149 students "gathered feedback on newly implemented AI-focused learning activities". Student feedback on these activities informed the resulting framework.
