article_title: ECNUClaw: A Learner-Profiled Intelligent Study Companion Framework for K-12 Personalized Education
citation: Yizhou Zhou, Jiayin Li, and Zhi Zhang. (2026). ECNUClaw: A Learner-Profiled Intelligent Study Companion Framework for K-12 Personalized Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08040
title: Five-dimension learner profile maintained across subject switches from dialogue signals
description: ECNUClaw constructs and maintains a learner profile across five dimensions—cognitive, behavioral, emotional, metacognitive, and contextual—stored as per-dimension JSON fields in a SQLite table. Signals are extracted at every turn via keyword dictionaries and turn counting: Bloom's taxonomy level from question patterns, weak knowledge points from error markers, mood and self-efficacy from sentiment keywords, and reflection and strategy preference from metacognitive markers. All subject companions share a single memory store, so the profile persists across subject switches.
requirements: Each dimension is updated after every interaction via update_profile_from_interaction, which processes accumulated user messages for signals
constraints: The keyword-based signal extraction is the most significant limitation: a student expressing frustration without predefined keywords will not have their profile updated, and Bloom's classification relies on surface-level question patterns rather than semantic understanding
target_learning_goals: Personalized guidance informed by cognitive, behavioral, emotional, metacognitive, and contextual learner state
examples: In the paper's example dialogue, a frustration marker triggers a self-efficacy decrement of 0.1 and adds 'fractions' as a weak topic, and the strategy engine steps back to basics with increased encouragement
key_sources: Yizhou Zhou, Jiayin Li, and Zhi Zhang. (2026). ECNUClaw: A Learner-Profiled Intelligent Study Companion Framework for K-12 Personalized Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08040

citation: Abdolali Faraji, Mohammadreza Molavi, Zohreh Rasoulkhani, Mohammadreza Tavakoli, and Gábor Kismihók. (2026). Cross-Dataset Bloom Question Classification: Supervised Models and Prompted LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13684
title: Cross-dataset Bloom classification benchmark corpus of five datasets totaling 4,179 questions
description: The study assembled five Bloom's taxonomy–annotated question datasets totaling 4,179 questions, mapped to the revised Bloom cognitive levels for comparability. Four are human-authored sets frequently used in Bloom classification research (Yahya et al. 2012: 600; Sangodiah et al. 2017: 415; Mohammed and Omar 2020: 126; Gani et al. 2023: 1,200 questions), plus an LLM-generated set from Scaria et al. 2024 (1,838 questions) included to reflect the growing prevalence of AI-generated educational content. Code, prompts, and datasets are available in the authors' GitLab repository.
requirements: All labels must be mapped to the revised Bloom taxonomy to ensure consistency across datasets
target_learners: researchers evaluating Bloom question classification methods
target_learning_goals: cross-dataset evaluation of Bloom-level question classification
examples: Each dataset served once as the training source in the cross-dataset evaluation, with the other four treated as unseen test sets

citation: Yongkyung Oh, Lynn Talton, Alex Bui. (2026). Engagement Intensity as a Learner-Modeling Signal for Adaptive AI Ethics Instruction. KDD 2026 AI for Education Day, at the ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD '26). https://kdd2026.kdd.org

Items are analyzed as distinct facets rather than pooled, alongside three intake features (usage frequency, familiarity, prior AI education).

citation: Chenguang Pan, Airui Meng, and Youmi Suk. (2026). Distilling Black-Box Machine Learning into a Small, Self-Explaining Language Model for Learning Analytics. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.21165
title: Fine-tuned Gemma E2B offline deployment with dashboard and conversational interfaces
description: The deployed artifact is the fine-tuned Gemma E2B model carrying a LoRA adapter that adds only 0.11 GB to the base weights. The authors built two interfaces, a dashboard for setting student characteristics directly and a conversational assistant accepting plain-language descriptions, and confirmed both run end-to-end on an Apple M-series MacBook Pro. At 16-bit precision the model occupies 10.3 GB on disk and inference peaks near 10.7 GB of memory, so "a single estimate and its explanation are produced in about ten seconds with no network access of any kind."

constraints: The tested configuration needs 32 GB of memory (the article's text is truncated at this point)
Estimates take about ten seconds each, so it is not a real-time batch system

target_learning_goals: Obtaining individualized, natural-language explanations of predicted educational intervention effects
examples: The article reports a dashboard and a conversational assistant, both confirmed to run end-to-end on an Apple M-series MacBook Pro with no network access

article_title: Generative AI in creative education: baseline-linked evidence on learning processes, artistic performance, and authorship
citation: Shen, N., Lee, L. S., and He, A. (2026). Generative AI in creative education: baseline-linked evidence on learning processes, artistic performance, and authorship. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1956939
title: Five-dimension creative-performance assessment rubric with blinded dual evaluation
description: Final artistic outcomes in the study were assessed with a standardized rubric across five 20-point dimensions — creativity, aesthetic quality, technique, authorship, and completion — summed to a 100-point total. The rubric defines authorship as "visible evidence of independent creative intention, decision-making, personal expression, and ownership in the ﬁnal artifact." Two doctoral-qualified instructors with more than 7 years of teaching experience evaluated all works blind to questionnaire responses and AI-use status, with a structured reconciliation protocol involving a third evaluator when score differences exceeded 5%.
requirements: Evaluators must receive only the submitted artworks and the standardized rubric, without access to AI-use information, to reduce scoring bias.
constraints: Artistic evaluation is subjective, which the article addresses through Cohen's kappa agreement checking and a reconciliation protocol rather than assuming objectivity.
target_learning_goals: multidimensional assessment of creative performance including authorship
examples: Authorship was scored on a 20-point ordered scale, and differences between the two evaluators exceeding 5% triggered an additional third-evaluator assessment.

article_title: Framing the 5% Problem: Teachers'' Perspectives on Persistence in Educational Technology
citation: Conrad Borchers. (2026). Framing the 5% Problem: Teachers’ Perspectives on Persistence in Educational Technology. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22294
title: Reframing the 5% problem as a situated instructional challenge requiring teacher-facing interpretive support
description: The article proposes that the 5% problem — only a small fraction of students engaging at levels sufficient for meaningful learning gains — should be understood not merely as a usage deficit but as a challenge of teacher interpretation. It argues that "the 5% problem extends beyond time-on-task and reflects challenges in interpreting meaningful student effort," and that teacher-facing systems should situate engagement patterns within broader instructional and contextual information rather than only detecting disengagement.
requirements: Teacher-facing systems would need to combine platform engagement data with instructional and contextual information to support teacher sensemaking about persistence.
constraints: Findings derive from an early needs-finding workshop with 12 volunteer teachers, one 90-minute session, one district, and one platform; transferability requires triangulation with observations, student interviews, or prototype trials.
target_learners: K-12 middle school mathematics students using adaptive learning platforms
target_learning_goals: Sustained student persistence and engagement in computer-assisted mathematics learning
examples: The workshop asked teachers for 'I wish I knew...' and 'I wish I could...' superpowers, such as knowing where students stall or reframing productive struggle.

article_title: From information providers to learning designers: heutagogical teaching practices in AI-enhanced education
citation: Hochberg N and Waitzman R (2026). From information providers to learning designers: heutagogical teaching practices in AI-enhanced education. Front. Educ. 11:1905833. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1905833
title: Five-dimensional typology of AI-enhanced heutagogical teaching practices
description: The article proposes a theory-informed typology in which AI-enhanced heutagogical teaching comprises five interconnected dimensions: designing for learner agency, self-regulated teaching and reflection, AI-supported learning design, designing for capability development, and critical AI literacy. The authors state that "The hybrid analysis generated five interconnected dimensions of AI-enhanced heutagogical teaching," with each dimension's analytic focus, illustrative reported practices, and boundary of inference summarized in Table 1. It functions as a formative design heuristic rather than a validated measurement scale.

constraints: Evidence concerns teacher reports and artifacts, not student outcomes; the typology is explicitly not a validated measurement scale

article_title: Who Am I? History-Aware Profiles for Student Simulation in Tutoring Dialogues
citation: Zhangqi Duan, Shuyan Huang, Alexander Scarlatos, Jaewook Lee, Simon Woodhead, Andrew Lan. (2026). Who Am I? History-Aware Profiles for Student Simulation in Tutoring Dialogues. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30051
title: Five-component structured student profile capturing knowledge and dialogue behavior
description: Each generated profile has a fixed structure with five sections: Knowledge State (estimated KC mastery as correct over total attempts), Knowledge Acquisition (how mastery changes over time), Misconception (recurring mathematical errors), Dialogue Behavior (tendencies and common dialogue acts), and Linguistic Style (verbosity, terminology use, fragment versus full explanations). "Each generated profile has a fixed structure with five components, which align with important aspects of student knowledge and behavior identified in (Scarlatos et al., 2026)." Profiles are initialized by prompting a proprietary reasoning LLM, then distilled into a trainable open-source generator.

constraints: The profile is a compact summary of a truncated history window, not the student's entire learning history

article_title: Generative AI Literacy Training Improves Intelligence Analysts’ Discrimination of Real and AI-Generated Images
citation: Negar Kamali, Candice Rockell Gerstner, Jessica Hullman, Matthew Groh. (2026). Generative AI Literacy Training Improves Intelligence Analysts' Discrimination of Real and AI-Generated Images. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28510
title: Five-category artifact taxonomy for evaluating AI-generated images
description: The article organizes visual inspection of AI-generated images around a taxonomy of five artifact categories drawn from a written guide on distinguishing AI-generated images from authentic photographs. The training "was structured around five categories of artifacts": anatomical implausibilities (hands, eyes, teeth, body structure, identity inconsistencies), stylistic artifacts (cinematization, plastic textures, hyper-real detail), functional implausibilities (dysfunctional objects, malformed text and logos), violations of physical constraints (inconsistent lighting, shadows, reflections, perspective), and sociocultural implausibilities (historically or culturally incongruent scenarios). Each category was taught with concise explanations paired with multiple visual examples, and the same taxonomy coded analysts' free-text reasoning in the qualitative analysis.
requirements: Explanations paired with multiple visual examples per category, with visual callouts highlighting regions of interest
Examples drawn from contemporary diffusion models so the taught cues match the artifacts current generators produce
constraints: The article cautions analysts against over-reliance on any single cue, since artifact visibility varies with scene complexity, pose, image resolution, and viewing time
Real photographs can contain non-generative artifacts such as compression and focus inconsistencies, so the presence of an artifact does not by itself imply an image is AI-generated
target_learners: professionals whose verification decisions carry operational weight, such as journalists and content moderators
target_learning_goals: distinguishing real photographs from AI-generated images
articulating detection reasoning using specific artifact categories
examples: The 30-minute training consisted of 32 slides with 50 AI-generated images and 7 real images, presenting concise explanations with visual examples for each artifact category
key_sources: Negar Kamali, Candice Rockell Gerstner, Jessica Hullman, Matthew Groh. (2026). Generative AI Literacy Training Improves Intelligence Analysts' Discrimination of Real and AI-Generated Images. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28510

article_title: Human Autonomy and Sense of Agency in Human-Robot Interaction: A Systematic Literature Review
citation: Glawe, F., Schmeckel, T., Brauner, P., & Ziefle, M. (2025). Human Autonomy and Sense of Agency in Human-Robot Interaction: A Systematic Literature Review. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22271
title: Five-cluster taxonomy of factors potentially influencing human autonomy and sense of agency in HRI
description: From a thematic synthesis of the 22 included studies, the review organises the factors examined as potentially influencing human autonomy or sense of agency in HRI into five broad clusters: robot adaptiveness, robot communication, robot anthropomorphism, robot exposure, and individual differences. The authors state these "clusters are broad but not exhaustive" and that every article was assigned to at least one cluster, with studies not isolating specific factors placed in an 'Other' category. The taxonomy serves as an initial map of the field's independent variables.
requirements: Applied to studies that measure human autonomy or sense of agency after, during, or for an imagined interaction with an autonomous robot or cobot
constraints: The clusters are described as broad but not exhaustive
target_learners: HRI researchers and designers studying human users of robots
target_learning_goals: Understanding and fostering human autonomy and sense of agency in human-robot interaction
examples: The review assigned each of the 22 included articles to at least one cluster, e.g., robotisation studies to robot exposure and individual differences.
key_sources: Glawe, F., Schmeckel, T., Brauner, P., & Ziefle, M. (2025). Human Autonomy and Sense of Agency in Human-Robot Interaction: A Systematic Literature Review. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22271

article_title: The Role of Instructional Guidance in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Empirical Evidence from Construction Engineering
citation: Xiaoyu Hou, Bo Xiao, Hexu Liu and Shane Mueller. (2026). The Role of Instructional Guidance in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Empirical Evidence from Construction Engineering Education.
title: Five-step prompting framework (Clarify, Organize, Integrate, Differentiate, Correct) operationalizing Generative Learning Theory in AI-supported review
description: The article introduces a five-step interaction framework that translates Generative Learning Theory's selecting, organizing, and integrating processes into observable student–AI interaction behaviors during review. "The framework guides students through a structured sequence consisting of Clarify, Organize, Integrate, Differentiate, and Correct." Each step has an instructional purpose and example prompt (e.g., asking for the 2–3 most important key points, a real-world example, a commonly confused concept, and the most important misconception). The sequence structures AI use as guided cognitive activity rather than open-ended querying.
requirements: A course-aligned generative AI platform with which learners can pose the structured prompts for each topic before proceeding to another
constraints: The structured sequence may not accommodate all individual learning preferences, and the study tested only this single prompting strategy without comparison to alternative designs
target_learners: undergraduate construction engineering students without prior construction management coursework
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding, organization, and integration of course content during self-directed review
examples: In the experiment, prompted participants applied the full five-step prompt sequence for each selected topic using the RAG-based course platform
key_sources: Xiaoyu Hou, Bo Xiao, Hexu Liu and Shane Mueller. (2026). The Role of Instructional Guidance in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Empirical Evidence from Construction Engineering Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05509

article_title: What do you mean by human-AI collaboration: Prerequisite functions and the affordances needed to achieve it
citation: Mutlu Cukurova. (2026). What do you mean by 'human–AI collaboration'? Prerequisite functions and the affordances needed to achieve it. Submitted to the Handbook of AI and the Future of Education. https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5843-4854
title: Five-level diagnostic taxonomy of human–AI teaming defined by observable affordances
description: The chapter proposes a diagnostic taxonomy of human–AI teaming with five levels: transactional, situational, operational, praxical, and synergistic. Each level 'introduces one additional affordance over the level beneath it', and 'the classification is functional and is intended to be coded from observable behaviour' such as whether the system surfaces state, accepts governance, revises durably from feedback, or co-reasons. Interaction types are querying, monitoring, governing, adapting, and co-reasoning; diagnosis proceeds top-down, classifying a system at the highest threshold it meets.
requirements: Coding from observable behaviour in deployment rather than unverifiable architectural claims
constraints: The levels are not strict supersets but minimum-affordance thresholds; mixed profiles are resolved by recording the highest threshold met
The taxonomy is a map of affordances, not a quality ranking; higher is not uniformly better
target_learners: teachers and learners using AI systems in education
target_learning_goals: distinguishing genuine collaboration from other human–AI interaction types
examples: A general-purpose chatbot used for one-shot lesson-plan drafting sits at the transactional level; real-time classroom dashboards with AI models are situational; configurable intelligent tutoring platforms are operational
key_sources: Mutlu Cukurova. (2026). What do you mean by 'human–AI collaboration'? Prerequisite functions and the affordances needed to achieve it. Submitted to the Handbook of AI and the Future of Education. https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5843-4854

article_title: What do you mean by human-AI collaboration: Prerequisite functions and the affordances needed to achieve it
citation: Mutlu Cukurova. (2026). What do you mean by 'human–AI collaboration'? Prerequisite functions and the affordances needed to achieve it. Submitted to the Handbook of AI and the Future of Education. https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5843-4854
title: Five requirements that characterise collaboration in a strong sense
description: Drawing on the socio-cognitive, socio-cultural, and shared-knowledge traditions, the chapter argues 'that at least five requirements characterise collaboration in a strong sense': a negotiated and partly symmetric situation, shared and negotiated goals, a low and shifting division of labour, interactivity with synchronicity and negotiability, and mutual modelling, grounding, and socially shared regulation. Collaboration is thereby 'a graded construct, not a binary one', present only when joint activity is sustained at a high level along several dimensions at once.
requirements: Situations in which asymmetry remains dynamic, negotiated, and mutually consequential rather than fixed at design time
constraints: Pure symmetry is rare and not strictly necessary; what matters is that asymmetry is negotiated and mutually consequential
target_learners: researchers, designers, and policymakers evaluating human–AI learning systems
target_learning_goals: defining and assessing collaborative learning conditions
examples: Dillenbourg's lost-keys thought experiment illustrates that coincident outcomes do not amount to shared intentions
key_sources: Mutlu Cukurova. (2026). What do you mean by 'human–AI collaboration'? Prerequisite functions and the affordances needed to achieve it. Submitted to the Handbook of AI and the Future of Education. https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5843-4854

article_title: Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children
citation: Kadharmoideen Fadurudeen. (2026). Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22377
title: Five-stage spoken learning loop with supplementary visual affordances
description: Kutti AI's interaction design is "a spoken conversation with five stages": welcome (a single large haptic-enabled control), spoken lesson delivery paced with natural pauses, voice response captured by a large microphone control or hands-free mode, adaptive response (encouragement, hint, or simplified question), and a spoken summary with an engagement score (0–100). Visual affordances—screen-reader compatibility, large touch targets, haptic confirmation, high-contrast scheme—are strictly supplementary for low-vision users and sighted caregivers.
requirements: Visual elements may exist for sighted caregivers but must never be required (R1)
target_learning_goals: completing an entire learning session through speech alone
examples: On completion the child hears an engagement score (0–100) and encouraging feedback, and the session is persisted for progress tracking
key_sources: Kadharmoideen Fadurudeen. (2026). Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22377

article_title: Incipit: Axiom-Grounded Scaffolding for Human-AI Literary Creation
citation: Qiang Liu and Chunyi Zhao. (2026). Literary Axioms: A Conceptual Framework for Literary Creation, Interpretation, and Evaluation. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25504
title: Five relational, multidimensional dimensions of literary evaluation
description: The framework organizes literary evaluation around five dimensions: interpretive coherence, contextual reach, distinctiveness, realization fidelity, and interpretive richness. The article states that "Coherence, contextual reach, distinctiveness, realization fidelity, and interpretive richness identify different achievements and failures." Each dimension is operationalized as a question (for example, whether competent readers can construct more than one grounded reconstruction), and the framework deliberately does not combine them into a scalar literary-quality measure.
requirements: Evaluation requires a stated comparison corpus and reader context
constraints: Broad contextual scope is not a proxy for quality; situated works may be important precisely because of their specificity
Distinctiveness is relational and time-dependent, and the dataset currently lacks the comparison corpus and attribution needed for a novelty estimate
target_learning_goals: literary evaluation
critique of literary works
examples: The article specifies operational questions for each dimension, such as whether textual choices repeatedly make the selected claims available rather than merely describing the author's topic
key_sources: Qiang Liu and Chunyi Zhao. (2026). Literary Axioms: A Conceptual Framework for Literary Creation, Interpretation, and Evaluation. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25504

article_title: What out-of-the-box LLMs can(t) do in law? A Turing test in Italian exams for lawyers, judges and notaries
citation: Germana Bertoli, Ilaria Amelia Caggiano, Francesca Lagioia, Riccardo Rovatti, Giovanni Sartor, Emiliano Troisi. (2025). What out-of-the-box LLMs can(t) do in law? A Turing test in Italian exams for lawyers, judges and notaries. https://github.com/SSIGPRO/LLMs-in-legal-professions
title: Five-category taxonomy of legal failures in LLM notarial drafting
description: A purpose-built classification of recurring LLM errors in notarial drafting, developed as a pilot analysis from expert evaluations. It jointly considers the requirements of notarial assignments and the soundness of the underlying legal reasoning, including consistency between proposed solutions, their justification, and theoretical discussion. "On this basis, we distinguish five main categories": legal-source failure, reasoning failure, pertinence failure, lexical failure, and formal failure. Even the best-performing model exhibited deficiencies across all categories in the inter vivos act.
requirements: Developed from expert evaluations of LLM-generated notarial deeds against the assignment's requirements and the soundness of the underlying legal reasoning
constraints: Presented as a pilot analysis based on a small number of exam papers and three expert evaluators
target_learning_goals: diagnosing recurring failure patterns in LLM legal drafting
examples: In the inter vivos act, even Gemini 2.5 Pro exhibited deficiencies across all categories, with a predominance of formal and reasoning failures; in the mortis causa assignment, ChatGPT-5 incurred reasoning failures and residual formal defects.
key_sources: Germana Bertoli, Ilaria Amelia Caggiano, Francesca Lagioia, Riccardo Rovatti, Giovanni Sartor, Emiliano Troisi. (2025). What out-of-the-box LLMs can(t) do in law? A Turing test in Italian exams for lawyers, judges and notaries. https://github.com/SSIGPRO/LLMs-in-legal-professions

article_title: LearnAI: Just-in-Time AI Co-Creation Across Disciplines at a University
citation: Weihao Qu, Ling Zheng, Chris Buzaid, and Daniel Crawford. 2026. LearnAI: Just-in-Time AI Co-Creation Across Disciplines at a University. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19164
title: 5-Stage Pedagogical Script for one-on-one AI co-creation sessions
description: A structured session protocol tutors follow to move clients from an "Oracle" mindset (expecting answers) to a "Process Partner" mindset (co-creating solutions). The article states "Sessions followed a structured protocol (Figure 2) designed to shift clients from an 'Oracle' mindset (expecting answers) to a 'Process Partner' mindset (co-creating solutions)," with stages: Problem Framing (5–10 min), Tool-Task Mapping (3–5 min), Iterative Co-Prompting (20–30 min), Deployment & Verification (10–15 min), and Ethical Reflection (3–5 min). Tutors adapt pacing and tool selection to individual clients, and each session ends with a facilitator-verified summary documenting tools used and next steps.
requirements: Tutors withhold tool suggestions until the problem is clearly scoped in Stage 1
Tutors calibrated by observing two sessions and co-facilitating two before leading independently
Ethical Reflection reframed as a required session-end checklist because it was the easiest stage to compress
constraints: Debugging or deployment sometimes consumed the final minutes, making Stage 5 the easiest to compress
Clients often arrived with vague goals requiring additional scoping time
target_learners: Mixed-ability clients: students, faculty, and staff with self-selected authentic tasks
target_learning_goals: Prompting as specification, requirement decomposition, output verification, and ethical reflection on AI use
examples: A senior tutor (30+ sessions facilitated) described following the script: "the first part is I try to figure out exactly what problem we're trying to solve today"; a nursing faculty member learned to reframe prompts as precise technical specifications and deployed a live newsletter platform with secure faculty login
key_sources: Weihao Qu, Ling Zheng, Chris Buzaid, and Daniel Crawford. 2026. LearnAI: Just-in-Time AI Co-Creation Across Disciplines at a University. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19164

article_title: LLM Pedagogical Behavior in AI Tutoring Interactions
citation: Suhyeon Lee, Juneha Baek, Jaehyeong Park, Donghyuk Shin. (2026). LLM Pedagogical Behavior in AI Tutoring Interactions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22993
title: Five-level scaffolding scale for measuring the directness of assistance in LLM tutoring responses
description: The article operationalizes scaffolding as a five-level ordinal scale characterizing LLM responses by the amount of assistance they provide: L0 Minimal, L1 Prompting, L2 Hinting, L3 Explaining, and L4 Solving, where "Higher levels provide more directly usable assistance and leave less of the task for the student to complete independently." The L3/L4 distinction is direct usability: L3 gives an approach the student must still apply, L4 a directly usable task-specific solution. Responses are classified with GPT-4o-mini at temperature 0 given the codebook and preceding context.
requirements: A codebook with level definitions and examples, preceding conversational context, and a classifier (or human annotators) applying the definitions to paired student–LLM turns
constraints: Automated classification is imperfect: most errors occur at the L3/L4 boundary, and low-assistance levels are rare, so fine-grained estimates for L0–L2 should be interpreted cautiously
target_learners: university students in an introductory AI course using an LLM for programming assignments
target_learning_goals: characterizing and evaluating the level of assistance LLM tutors provide during programming and problem-solving coursework
examples: Human validation on a stratified sample of 300 responses yielded human-human agreement of κ = .901 (95.0% raw agreement), and the classifier achieved 75.3% accuracy and weighted F1 of .751 on the held-out test split (n = 150)
key_sources: Suhyeon Lee, Juneha Baek, Jaehyeong Park, Donghyuk Shin. (2026). LLM Pedagogical Behavior in AI Tutoring Interactions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22993

article_title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: a systematic review of its impact on student engagement and the mediating role of teaching methods
citation: Long DY, Wang S, Md Rashid S and Lu XT. (2026). Artificial intelligence in higher education: a systematic review of its impact on student engagement and the mediating role of teaching methods. Front. Educ. 10:1648661. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2025.1648661
title: Five functional categories of AI in higher education applications
description: To organize the diverse AI applications found in the literature, the review proposes a classification of AIHE into five functional categories. The authors state: "we classify AIHE applications into five functional categories: (1) personalized learning systems, (2) real-time feedback and adaptive tutoring, (3) natural language processing (NLP) tools, (4) immersive learning environments, and (5) predictive analytics". This taxonomy is used to code included studies and to structure the RQ1 analysis of which AI types support which engagement dimensions.
requirements: Studies must be codable by the AI technology type they employ
constraints: Derived for higher education contexts reviewed between 2015 and 2025
target_learning_goals: personalized learning, feedback, interaction, immersion, and dropout/at-risk prediction
examples: Chatbots are categorized under NLP tools; Smart Sparrow under adaptive tutoring; i-Ntervene under predictive analytics
key_sources: Long DY, Wang S, Md Rashid S and Lu XT. (2026). Artificial intelligence in higher education: a systematic review of its impact on student engagement and the mediating role of teaching methods. Front. Educ. 10:1648661. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2025.1648661

article_title: When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution
citation: Kai Yao. (2026). When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28041
title: Five-capacity framework: end-setting, reason-giving, contestability, refusal/revision, and participation as a minimum functional set
description: The article proposes five capacities as the core of post-instrumental learning: "end-setting, reason-giving, contestability,refusal/revision, and participation. They form a proposed minimum functional set, not a complete theory of education." End-setting keeps purposes open to judgment; reason-giving connects outputs to inspectable considerations; contestability supplies routes to challenge; refusal/revision makes exit and redesign possible; participation sustains the shared practices in which the others are learned. Table 1 translates each capacity into an institutional design question and a failure mode, for example that without contestability "Affected people encounter decisions as settled facts". The capacities are interdependent but not interchangeable and should be distributed across affected people, intermediaries, and communities.
requirements: Distribution across affected people, institutional intermediaries, and public or professional communities, so delegation remains accountable rather than private dependence on expertise
constraints: The claim is normative and functional rather than psychometric; the capacities may overlap and are not an empirically validated scale
target_learners: intermediaries such as teachers, clinicians, caseworkers, lawyers, engineers, and public officials
target_learning_goals: setting ends, giving reasons, contesting decisions, refusing and revising dependence, and participating in shared practices
key_sources: Kai Yao. (2026). When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28041

article_title: Dynamic Learning Solutions: A System for Personalized Educational Video Generation
citation: Siddhanth Sridhar, Shreya Chaurasia, Baddela Sai Yaswantha Reddy, Deepak Parmar, and Dr. Shylaja S S. (2026). Dynamic Learning Solutions: A System for Personalized Educational Video Generation. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14408
title: Figure-aware document extraction for NCERT diagram references in RAG indexing
description: A preprocessing component that detects standardized figure references such as "Fig 8.1" using regular expressions and extracts surrounding caption text into dedicated figure-related documents. These are "indexed alongside normal text chunks within the vector database, enabling the retriever to surface relevant diagram explanations when queries reference figures." It complements regex-based cleaning that removes structural noise like page headers and summary sections before chunking.
requirements: Source PDFs that reference figures with standardized patterns such as "Fig 8.1" or "Fig. 5.2"
Regular-expression pattern matching over extracted PDF text before embedding
constraints: Designed for the formatting and pedagogical style of NCERT textbooks; generic pipelines treating all extracted text uniformly do not gain this structure
target_learners: school students querying NCERT science textbooks
target_learning_goals: answering textbook-style questions that reference diagrams and figures
examples: Figure descriptions are converted into separate document entries and indexed alongside normal text chunks in the Chroma vector database

article_title: From Sentiment Classification to Actionable and Responsible Feedback: A Scoping Review and Evidence Map of NLP in Student Evaluation of Teaching, 2015–2026
citation: Eicher, J., & da Silva, R. (2026). From Sentiment Classification to Actionable and Responsible Feedback: A Scoping Review and Evidence Map of NLP in Student Evaluation of Teaching, 2015–2026. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27939
title: Five-axis evidence map framework: a technical axis (RQ1) read against four value dimensions (analytical depth, methodological validation and reporting, actionability, responsible use)
description: The review's organizing framework separates technical sophistication (RQ1: tasks, methods, technological families, contexts) from four analytically separate value dimensions (RQ2–RQ5). The review states it "distinguishes technical sophistication (RQ1) from four related but analytically separate value dimensions (RQ2–RQ5)" covering depth, validation and reporting, actionability, and responsible use. Its core argument is that "Technical complexity should therefore not be used as a proxy for analytical depth, methodological robustness, educational usefulness, or responsible use." The framework is operationalized through seven extraction domains and versioned coding rules (D1–D5 depth, A0–A5 actionability, M1–M11 reporting indicators) applied to 421 studies.
requirements: Requires verbatim-evidence extraction with adjudication so that composite constructs (D1–D5, A0–A5) are derived by explicit, versioned coding rules rather than assigned directly by LLM judges
constraints: The review states all proportions and cross-tabulations are descriptive of the 421 mapped studies, not causal effects or population estimates, because the corpus was built without probability sampling
target_learners: higher education instructors and institutions using student evaluation of teaching
target_learning_goals: actionable and responsible use of NLP analysis of open-ended teaching-evaluation comments
examples: The review maps 421 studies along the five axes and identifies the A2+ to A3+ actionability cliff as the map's sharpest quantified gap

article_title: Teacher Involvement in Developing Sustainable Education Materials for AI Integration in Green Energy Education
citation: Riandi Riandi, Ismail Ismail, Ida Kaniawati, Wahyu Sopandi, Diana Ayu Rostikawati, Defrizal Hamka & Suhendar Suhendar. (2026). Teacher involvement in developing sustainable education materials for AI integration in green energy education. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-34422-4
title: Five-construct dichotomous questionnaire measuring teacher AI readiness in green energy education
description: A structured questionnaire measuring five constructs aligned with TPACK domains: Knowledge of AI, Use of AI in Green Education, Development of ESD-Based Teaching Materials, Attitudes Toward AI, and Ability to Use AI. "Each construct was represented by five dichotomous items (Y es = 1, No = 0)." The binary format was chosen to accommodate varying technological familiarity and reduce respondent burden. The instrument was content-validated by three experts in science education and learning technology and distributed online via Google Forms between August and September 2024.
requirements: Content validation by subject-matter and learning-technology experts; PLS-SEM-compatible binary indicators handled via dummy-variable standardisation
constraints: The dichotomous 0/1 scale limited response variability and sensitivity, which the authors identify as likely weakening detection of knowledge and attitude effects
target_learners: in-service teachers without formal AI training
target_learning_goals: self-assessment of AI-related knowledge, attitudes, use, and integration ability in sustainability education
examples: Sample indicator: "I actively develop teaching modules with sustainability (ESD) principles."

article_title: Retrieval-Augmented Tutoring for Algorithm Tracing and Problem-Solving in AI Education
citation: Mragisha Jain, Tirth Bhatt, Griffin Pitts, Aum Pandya, Peter Brusilovsky, Narges Norouzi, Arto Hellas, Juho Leinonen, Bita Akram. (2026). Retrieval-Augmented Tutoring for Algorithm Tracing and Problem-Solving in AI Education. Proceedings of the 21st Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2026), co-located with ACL 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12988
title: Five-intent classification routing tutoring responses to intent-specific pedagogical strategies
description: KITE does not use a single response strategy for all student questions; instead, "Each incoming query is classified into one of five pedagogical intents using a keyword and pattern-matching classifier." The five intents are Direct Question, Conceptual Questions, Algorithm Validation, Debugging, and Algorithm Tracing, plus a dedicated answer evaluation mode that bypasses classification. The classified intent determines which response generation strategy is invoked, distinguishing factual explanation from scaffolded support for procedural, debugging, validation, and tracing requests. This pattern pairs retrieval grounding with differentiated pedagogical delivery matched to the form of help-seeking.
requirements: A keyword and pattern-matching intent classifier and course materials to ground the intent-specific responses
constraints: Intent classification uses keyword and pattern matching rather than a learned model, per the article's description
target_learning_goals: algorithmic problem-solving
debugging
algorithm tracing
examples: Debugging responses follow a structured hint progression and include a learning point connecting the bug to the underlying conceptual principle

article_title: Framing human-AI dynamics: An epistemological perspective on generative AI practices
citation: Strydom, S. (2026). Framing human-AI dynamics: An epistemological perspective on generative AI practices. Journal of Applied Learning and Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2026.9.2.11
title: Five epistemological dimensions as a lens on human-GAI engagement
description: Drawing on Schommer (1994) and Schommer-Aikins and Easter (2008)'s multidimensional model, the article differentiates five dimensions of personal epistemological beliefs: "the source of knowledge, certainty of knowledge, organisation of knowledge, control of knowledge acquisition and speed of knowledge acquisition". The author contends these dimensions "offer an understanding of human-GAI engagement", serving as the analytical axes against which the seven paradigms are examined.
requirements: Adopts the multidimensional model of Schommer (1994) and Schommer-Aikins and Easter (2008) as its theoretical basis
target_learning_goals: interpreting learners' and educators' beliefs about knowledge in AI-mediated learning
examples: Each of the seven paradigms is examined against the five epistemological dimensions

article_title: Quality-Conditioned Agreement in Automated Short Answer Scoring: Mid-Range Degradation and the Impact of Task-Specific Adaptation
citation: Abigail Victoria Gurin Schleifer, Moriah Ariely, Beata Beigman Klebanov, Asaf Salman, Giora Alexandron. (2026). Quality-Conditioned Agreement in Automated Short Answer Scoring: Mid-Range Degradation and the Impact of Task-Specific Adaptation. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07647v2
title: Deploy automated scoring as a first pass that auto-handles extreme-quality responses and routes predicted mid-range responses to a human rater
description: The article recommends staged deployment of ASAS: "automated scoring as a first pass can identify these responses and handle them without human intervention, while responses predicted to be in the middle range would be routed to the human rater for scoring". As human-scored data accumulates and fine-tuning becomes feasible, the scoring can be automated more fully.
requirements: human rater capacity to score responses predicted to fall in the mid-range of quality
accumulation of human-scored data before fine-tuning-based fuller automation becomes feasible
constraints: the article warns that few-shot-only scoring may be inequitable, with substantially inaccurate scores concentrating on partially incorrect responses
target_learning_goals: reliable scoring of open-ended science explanations
appropriate learning support triggered by accurate knowledge-state detection
examples: on the test set, GPT few-shot models in all scenarios showed average distance of less than one category on score 9-10 responses, supporting extreme-band automation

article_title: 'It''s OK Because...": The Wild West of Student Rationalization of AI Use in Academic Writing'
citation: Kim, Jiyoon; Toyama, Kentaro; Kim, Sangmi; Carroll, John. (2026). "It's OK Because...": The Wild West of Student Rationalization of AI Use in Academic Writing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29090
title: Five-sites framework of AI-use expectations in a course
description: The article proposes that for any given course, concepts of appropriate AI use for academic writing are housed in five distinct sites: faculty intention, formal policy, student interpretation, student self-policy, and student practice. These sites, whether explicit or implicit, formal or informal, often differ from one another, and the divergences create openings for re-interpretation of ethically questionable AI use. The framework explains how instructor expectations are translated, interpreted, personalized, and enacted, with the boundary of acceptable use softening at each site.
requirements: Analysis of a course requires access to both syllabi or formal policy documents and student accounts of their interpretation and practice, as the article obtained through interviews, syllabi, chat logs, and submissions.
constraints: Faculty intention was not measured directly; the article states it was inferred from syllabi and participant interviews because faculty were not interviewed.
target_learning_goals: understanding and negotiating course AI policies in academic writing
examples: The article illustrates site mismatches with a student who copied AI text believing idea-generation permission covered it, students who misremembered or mixed up policies across courses, and students who violated their own stated norms in practice.
key_sources: Kim, Jiyoon; Toyama, Kentaro; Kim, Sangmi; Carroll, John. (2026). "It's OK Because...": The Wild West of Student Rationalization of AI Use in Academic Writing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29090

article_title: Teacher feedback vs. AI-assisted peer feedback in L2 writing: A quasi-experimental study in a Chinese university
citation: Tang J, Li P, Luo R (2026) Teacher feedback VS AI-assisted peer feedback in L2 writing: A quasi-experimental study in a Chinese University. PLoS One 21(6): e0345976. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0345976
title: Five-dimensional feedback checklist for structuring teacher and AI-assisted peer feedback
description: A standardized checklist adapted from Yang's (2022) Feedback Checklist and Orit Zeevy Solovey's (2022) Error Categories, covering "organizational structure, content and argumentation, grammar, vocabulary, and technical details". It guided both feedback modes in the study, providing "a structured operational framework for both scaffolding modes". Content validity was rated by three experts (CVI = 0.92), and pilot evaluation on 10 non-experimental essays yielded Cronbach's alpha coefficients from 0.78 to 0.86 across the five dimensions.
requirements: Expert content-validity review and pilot reliability testing before formal use
Unified training on the collaborative feedback procedure for students using it in AI-assisted peer review
target_learners: Second-language writing learners in higher education
target_learning_goals: Systematic coverage of organizational, content, grammar, vocabulary, and technical dimensions in writing feedback
examples: Both the control class teacher and the experimental class peer pairs applied the same checklist when generating feedback on argumentative drafts submitted via iWrite 2.0
key_sources: Tang J, Li P, Luo R (2026) Teacher feedback VS AI-assisted peer feedback in L2 writing: A quasi-experimental study in a Chinese University. PLoS One 21(6): e0345976. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0345976

article_title: Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem
citation: Jaidka K and Cai M. (2026). Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem. Front. Psychol. 17:1935527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935527
title: Five interpretability affordance strategies: source transparency, rationale generation, uncertainty expression, interactive scrutiny, and progressive disclosure
description: The article proposes that "interpretability can be built into the interaction through five strategies," each serving three goals: protecting the user's ability to judge, making the system contestable, and preserving usability. The strategies are source transparency (inline citations, RAG, confidence-calibrated hyperlinks), rationale generation paired with source attribution, uncertainty expression, interactive scrutiny tools, and progressive disclosure with layered explanations. Each has a boundary located by the user typology.
requirements: Rationales must be paired with source attribution and presented as a useful account, not a faithful report of internal processing
constraints: Every strategy waits for the user to act, so these affordances serve motivated profiles well and barely touch unmotivated ones
target_learners: Motivated chatbot users across ability levels
target_learning_goals: Making evaluation of chatbot outputs possible
examples: Cai et al. (2019) found clinicians worked more effectively with layered explanations than with either full technical detail or no explanation
key_sources: Jaidka K and Cai M. (2026). Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem. Front. Psychol. 17:1935527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935527

article_title: Towards Synergistic Teacher-AI Interactions with Generative Artificial Intelligence
citation: Mutlu Cukurova, Wannapon Suraworachet, Qi Zhou, and Sahan Bulathwela. (2025). Towards Synergistic Teacher-AI Interactions with Generative Artificial Intelligence. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19580
title: Five levels of teacher-AI teaming: transactional, situational, operational, praxical and synergistic
description: The chapter proposes an orthogonal conceptual framework of teacher-AI teaming focused on information flows, decisions and actions shared between teacher and AI, grounded in distributed cognition. The authors state: "we propose (1) transactional, (2) situational, (3) operational, (4) praxical and (5) synergistic levels of teaming, as shown in Fig. 8.1." Levels run from minimal request-response interactions to mutual co-adaptation, and the framework is validated against a systematic review of teacher-facing AI studies. The authors caution the levels "need not always follow a progressive ordered hierarchy" and that improving teaming level does not guarantee improving teaching performance.
requirements: Systems must be positioned within the framework by analysing current interaction affordances before improvement directions can be identified
constraints: The levels need not follow a progressive ordered hierarchy; higher teaming levels do not guarantee better teaching performance; educational contexts are fuzzy and require context-sensitive teaming rather than aiming for synergy in every interaction
target_learners: teachers using AI tools in educational contexts
target_learning_goals: teacher competence development through AI interaction
design of pedagogically aligned GenAI systems
examples: The chapter illustrates each level with a teacher support application example, such as a teacher requesting AI to translate text (transactional) and iterative PCA co-design with simulated students (praxical)
key_sources: Mutlu Cukurova, Wannapon Suraworachet, Qi Zhou, and Sahan Bulathwela. (2025). Towards Synergistic Teacher-AI Interactions with Generative Artificial Intelligence. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19580

article_title: A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI
citation: Larry Engelhardt. (2026). A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15518
title: Five-pillar tool-invariant framework for competent use of any computational method
description: The article organizes what a learner must know to use any computational method—pencil, calculator, library, or agentic AI—into five pillars: inputs and outputs, conceptual understanding of the method, terminology, sensemaking, and operating the tool. The author states that "competent use of any computational method, at any scale, with any tool, requires five things," and argues the pillars' content changes little across tool eras while their curricular weight shifts; under agentic AI, sensemaking becomes load-bearing. Table I maps the pillars to antecedent constructs in the computational-thinking literature, with the re-weighting offered as the new element.
requirements: The framework is offered as a structure for practitioner adaptation, not an empirically tested conclusion; the article notes the field lacks controlled studies of students learning computational physics through agentic AI.
constraints: The five pillars largely repackage constructs already in the computational-thinking literature; what the article claims as new is the re-weighting under agentic mediation, validation authority, and the assessment consequence.
target_learners: undergraduate physics students, from introductory through senior-level computational courses
target_learning_goals: competent, verifiable use of computational methods including agent-orchestrated simulation
examples: The article illustrates the pillars at two rungs: a child adding 2 + 3 and a senior directing an AI agent to build a molecular dynamics simulation.
key_sources: Larry Engelhardt. (2026). A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15518

article_title: Teaching Reinforcement Learning and Humanoid Robotics to High-School Students: An Expert-Validated Curriculum Design on a Low-Cost Open Platform
citation: Yuanzhe Dong, Jie Cao, Shuman Wang. (2026). Teaching Reinforcement Learning and Humanoid Robotics to High-School Students: An Expert-Validated Curriculum Design on a Low-Cost Open Platform. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25674
title: Five design principles: one artifact, dependency sequencing, progressive sim-hardware integration, scaffolded bounded choice, and paired collaboration with individual evidence
description: The article states five principles (P1-P5) describing the framework: coordinate disciplines through one artifact; sequence by technical dependencies with observable gates; integrate simulation and hardware progressively; combine scaffolded checkpoints with bounded choice; and pair collaboration with individual evidence. As the article puts it, "Progress from a worked example to a controlled modification and an independent decision." Teachers elicit cross-disciplinary explanations explicitly.
requirements: Observable gates such as safety induction, power-on, standing, and walking
Instructor-set limits on customization choices
Rotation of operating and checking roles with separately recorded individual reasoning
constraints: Independent algorithm implementation is positioned as an extension, not a core requirement
target_learning_goals: Explaining robot behavior across disciplines
Distinguishing equipment faults, simulation errors, and learning failures
examples: Students explain a failed standing attempt using both balance and control concepts; a supplied policy checks robot operation before a student-trained policy is introduced
key_sources: Yuanzhe Dong, Jie Cao, Shuman Wang. (2026). Teaching Reinforcement Learning and Humanoid Robotics to High-School Students: An Expert-Validated Curriculum Design on a Low-Cost Open Platform. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25674

article_title: Potential for Enhanced Learning in Machine Learning Classes by Using Wiki LLM Indexing
citation: Brian Wright. (2026). Potential for Enhanced Learning in Machine Learning Classes by Using Wiki LLM Indexing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25303
title: Five-part question taxonomy with multi-endpoint metrics for evaluating course-grounded AI tutors
description: The article extends a prior 30-question generic/specific set into a five-part taxonomy of classroom question types: "(a) single fact lookup, (b) multi hop concept linking, (c) thematic explanation and synthesis, (d) contradictionandambiguityhandling(Houetal.2024),and (e) curriculum update questions probing sensitivity to revisedmaterials." Questions were human-generated with reference answers and word limits and balanced across course topics, yielding 59 retained questions (45 topic-page, 14 cross-page). The taxonomy is paired with a multi-endpoint metric suite — RAGAS core metrics plus claim-citation alignment, blinded LLM-judge synthesis quality, robustness under knowledge shift, and cost — scored separately to avoid winner-take-all conclusions.
requirements: Questions must be human-generated with reference answers and word limits, balanced across course topics, and judged against the full corpus with arm labels hidden for synthesis and preference endpoints.
constraints: Scoring used a single LLM judge rating and a binary groundedness flag rather than the full RAGAS context recall/faithfulness/factual correctness triad, and each arm was answered and graded only once per question.
target_learning_goals: evaluating whether AI tutor answers align with course content across recall, cross-unit linking, synthesis, contradiction handling, and curriculum currency
examples: The 59 retained questions were labeled factual (n=18), conceptual (n=18), and synthesis (n=18), with the 45 topic-page questions balanced evenly across the ml-bias, knn, and decision-trees pages.
key_sources: Brian Wright. (2026). Potential for Enhanced Learning in Machine Learning Classes by Using Wiki LLM Indexing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25303

article_title: Adaptivity Makes Feedback Effective: Evidence From AI-Generated Feedback on Children's Plans
citation: Sukjaitham, S., Schaaf, M., Brod, G., & Breitwieser, J. (2026). Adaptivity Makes Feedback Effective: Evidence From AI-Generated Feedback on Children's Plans. Preprint. https://osf.io/4w6rz/overview?view_only=dd3ec8d2878243579a463ccd0d77d723
title: Refined five-criterion plan quality rubric for children's if-then plans
description: The study adapted the Schaaf et al. (2025) plan quality rubric into a five-category binary checklist assessing the situational cue of children's implementation intentions: specificity, externality, salience, appropriateness, and temporal precision, yielding total scores from 0 to 5. The refinement separated characteristics that the original category-based rubric had treated jointly, which had "thereby limiting diagnostic precision". Inter-rater reliability ranged from κ = .63 to κ = .95 across dimensions.
requirements: Raters need the scoring checklist, scoring guidelines, and example/justification guide for consistent coding
constraints: Remains primarily suited for assessing action initiation plans in children's everyday activities, not adults or other plan types
target_learners: children aged 10-13 in fifth and sixth grade
target_learning_goals: formulating high-quality if-then implementation intentions for everyday activities
examples: Plans were scored dichotomously on all five dimensions; a second rater independently coded a randomly selected subset of 20% of plans
key_sources: Sukjaitham, S., Schaaf, M., Brod, G., & Breitwieser, J. (2026). Adaptivity Makes Feedback Effective: Evidence From AI-Generated Feedback on Children's Plans. Preprint. https://osf.io/4w6rz/overview?view_only=dd3ec8d2878243579a463ccd0d77d723

article_title: Faculty Readiness for AI-Supported Teaching and Scalable Online Program Delivery in Higher Education: The EPIQ-AI Framework for Epistemic Integrity
citation: Sangwa, S., Ndahayo, C., Dusengumuremyi, F., & Mutabazi, P. (2025). Faculty Readiness for AI-Supported Teaching and Scalable Online Program Delivery in Higher Education: The EPIQ-AI Framework for Epistemic Integrity. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/kj4vt_v1
title: Five institutional supports recur as readiness enablers for AI-supported teaching
description: Across the evidence sources the synthesis identifies a recurring set of institutional conditions that enable faculty readiness for AI-supported teaching. These are: "(1) access to appropriate AI tools and resources; (2) AI literacy and skills training; (3) curated best practices and use cases; (4) clear guidelines for AI in teaching; and (5) an environment that encourages innovation and tolerates failure". The pattern is used to organize capacity-building priorities, with the inverse signal that 80% of faculty do not find institutional AI guidelines comprehensive marking policy ambiguity as a readiness inhibitor.
requirements: Institutional investment in guidelines, training, curated best practices, tool access, and an innovation-tolerant environment
constraints: Sector surveys are not uniformly comparable across countries and roles, per the article's methodological limitations
target_learning_goals: Effective and epistemically sound integration of GenAI into teaching and assessment
examples: The Digital Education Council survey's top enablers: access to tools (65%), AI literacy training (64%), best-practice collections (60%), and clear guidelines (50%)
key_sources: Sangwa, S., Ndahayo, C., Dusengumuremyi, F., & Mutabazi, P. (2025). Faculty Readiness for AI-Supported Teaching and Scalable Online Program Delivery in Higher Education: The EPIQ-AI Framework for Epistemic Integrity. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/kj4vt_v1

article_title: AI Literacy in Secondary Education: Framework, Assessment, and Professional Development in the Ukrainian Context
citation: Marienko, M. V., Markova, O. M., & Semerikov, S. O. (2026). AI literacy in secondary education: framework, assessment, and professional development in the Ukrainian context. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, 10, 100605. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100605
title: Five-level AI literacy competency framework integrated with three paradigms of AI in education
description: The article proposes a conceptual five-level AI literacy competency model for secondary educators — Awareness, Application, Evaluation, Creation, Ethics — visualized as a developmental pyramid. The framework is "a conceptual five-level AI literacy competency model integrated with the three paradigms of AI in education" (AI-directed, AI-supported, AI-empowered), mapping competency levels to each paradigm's demands. Levels 1-4 align with Ng et al.'s categories while ethics is separated as a distinct highest level reflecting ethical reasoning as a sophisticated capability requiring deliberate development.
requirements: Future research should subject the framework to psychometric validation through confirmatory factor analysis, as the article states
constraints: The article presents it as a conceptual framework synthesizing existing literature and empirical observations, not yet psychometrically validated
target_learning_goals: AI literacy competency development across awareness, application, evaluation, creation, and ethical reasoning
examples: The article maps digital storytelling with AI as addressing all five levels simultaneously, from awareness of AI capabilities to ethical considerations of authorship and authenticity
key_sources: Marienko, M. V., Markova, O. M., & Semerikov, S. O. (2026). AI literacy in secondary education: framework, assessment, and professional development in the Ukrainian context. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, 10, 100605. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100605

article_title: A Systematic Review of Emerging Technology Applications for Teaching English as a Foreign Language Across Different Educational Levels
citation: Mengjia Liu, Harwati Hashim, Nur Ainil Sulaiman. (2026). A systematic review of emerging technology applications for teaching English as a foreign language across different educational levels. Educational Research Review 52 (2026) 100795. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2026.100795
title: Five effective pedagogical practices for integrating emerging technologies into EFL curricula: personalization, authentic contexts, collaborative learning, multimodal integration, and cultural responsiveness
description: The review's thematic synthesis, using a hybrid deductive–inductive coding procedure in NVivo 14, identified "five key areas of effective practice for integrating emerging technologies into EFL curricula." The five parent themes were derived deductively from SLA-grounded affordances literature, while fifteen sub-themes (e.g., "self-regulated pacing," "anxiety-reducing low-stakes practice," "cultural identity preservation") were refined or generated inductively from the 33 studies (inter-coder reliability κ = 0.81). The review presents this as "an empirically grounded framework for technology implementation decisions" and stresses that effective integration is fundamentally pedagogical rather than technological.
requirements: Technologies must be embedded within purposeful, learner-centered instructional designs aligned with SLA principles rather than deployed as tools alone
constraints: Cultural responsiveness was less frequently documented in the corpus, representing a gap the review notes warrants further investigation
target_learners: EFL learners at primary, secondary, and tertiary educational levels
target_learning_goals: English language proficiency across speaking, writing, reading, listening, vocabulary, and grammar
engagement and motivation in technology-mediated language learning
examples: Personalization spanned AI speech recognition for primary phonics (Hu, 2021), self-regulated mobile grammar systems (Wang et al., 2021), and AWE feedback at tertiary level (Yildiz & Kuru Gonen, 2024)
VR provided authentic simulated real-world scenarios for tertiary oral communication (Feng & Ng, 2023; Ma, 2021; Xie et al., 2022)
key_sources: Mengjia Liu, Harwati Hashim, Nur Ainil Sulaiman. (2026). A systematic review of emerging technology applications for teaching English as a foreign language across different educational levels. Educational Research Review 52 (2026) 100795. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2026.100795

article_title: Theoretical Perspectives on Teaching with Robots: From Interdisciplinary Prerequisites and Necessities in Today’s Classrooms to Five Different Types of Robots
citation: Christ, O., Riedl, R., Schmid, J., Zürcher, P., & Thilo, F. (2026). Theoretical Perspectives on Teaching with Robots: From Interdisciplinary Prerequisites and Necessities in Today's Classrooms to Five Different Types of Robots. AI Educ. 2, 28. https://doi.org/10.3390/aieduc2030028
title: Five-type typology of pedagogical social robots for classroom support
description: Developed through five two-hour design-thinking workshops with a team of seven experts, the typology distinguishes five functionally distinct pedagogical roles: 'non-interactive demonstration, haptic interaction, one-on-one empathic dialogue, externally guided performative agents, and situated behavioural reflection'. Earlier iterations produced seven categories, merged during a consensus process. The types are defined by key characteristics, relevant situations, added value, and weaknesses, and are illustrated in Figure 1a–e.
requirements: An impactful use of robots in classrooms requires both a concrete pedagogical setting and a situated design of the robots
constraints: The typology is not intended as an empirically validated classification, but as a heuristic design framework; it is not exhaustive
target_learners: pupils between the ages of eight and fifteen
target_learning_goals: emotional learning
social competence
conflict mediation skills
examples: Robot type a enacts a generic conflict scenario to illustrate generalisable dynamics, whereas type e re-enacts a specific, previously observed classroom situation for situated reflection
key_sources: Christ, O., Riedl, R., Schmid, J., Zürcher, P., & Thilo, F. (2026). Theoretical Perspectives on Teaching with Robots: From Interdisciplinary Prerequisites and Necessities in Today's Classrooms to Five Different Types of Robots. AI Educ. 2, 28. https://doi.org/10.3390/aieduc2030028

article_title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later
citation: Sweller, J., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Paas, F. (2019). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 261–292. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09465-5
title: Five biologically primary principles of natural information processing systems underlie cognitive load theory
description: The review describes human cognition as a natural information processing system mimicking biological evolution, characterised by five principles: information store, borrowing and reorganising, randomness as genesis, narrow limits of change, and environmental organising and linking. The article states these "can be described by five basic, biologically primary principles. These principles provide the cognitive architecture that underlies the instructional procedures of cognitive load theory." They explain why explicit instruction reduces working memory load compared with random generate-and-test discovery.
requirements: Instruction should accord with the architecture: explicit, organised to reduce working memory load
constraints: The narrow limits of change principle's fixed-capacity assumption must be modified to allow working memory depletion after effort and recovery after rest, per Chen et al. as cited
target_learning_goals: constructing and storing knowledge in long-term memory to govern appropriate action
examples: Borrowing information from others reduces working memory load compared with generating it via random generate and test during problem solving
key_sources: Sweller, J., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Paas, F. (2019). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 261–292. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09465-5

article_title: Gender Inequality in Deliberative Participation
citation: Christopher F. Karpowitz, Tali Mendelberg, and Lee Shaker. (2012). Gender Inequality in Deliberative Participation. American Political Science Review, Volume 106, Issue 3, pp. 533-547. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055412000329
title: Fit deliberative procedure to the social context to avoid gender inequality
description: The article's design recommendation is that deliberative settings can be arranged to avoid gender inequality by matching institutional procedure to the situation's social context. As the authors state, "Deliberative design can avoid inequality by fitting institutional procedure to the social context of the situation." In practice this means choosing decision rules in light of the group's gender composition, per the interaction finding.
requirements: Designers must know or control the group's gender composition and choose a decision rule deliberately
constraints: The article's supporting evidence comes from experimental deliberation groups; the available text reports the finding at the level of rule-by-composition combinations
target_learning_goals: equal voice and authority in deliberation
examples: The article reports the gap disappears under unanimous rule and few women, or under majority rule and many women.
key_sources: Christopher F. Karpowitz, Tali Mendelberg, and Lee Shaker. (2012). Gender Inequality in Deliberative Participation. American Political Science Review, Volume 106, Issue 3, pp. 533-547. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055412000329

article_title: Continued Progress: Promising Evidence on Personalized Learning
citation: John F. Pane, Elizabeth D. Steiner, Matthew D. Baird, Laura S. Hamilton. (2015). Continued Progress: Promising Evidence on Personalized Learning. RAND Corporation. https://www.rand.org/t/RR1365z2
title: Five-strategy framework of personalized learning: learner profiles, personal learning paths, competency-based progression, flexible learning environments, and college and career readiness
description: The report organizes school design features around five strategies identified by funders and leaders in the personalized learning space. Each "strategy encompasses a set of tools and features of the personalized learning environment"; some, like flexible pathways, are "central to a personalized approach," while others such as technology are enablers. The framework structures the report's implementation analysis of the 32 NGLC schools.
requirements: Schools adopting the framework implement learner profiles, personal learning paths, competency-based progression, flexible learning environments, and an emphasis on college and career readiness
constraints: There is not yet one shared definition of personalized learning; schools showed considerable diversity in instructional model details
target_learners: K-12 students in charter and district schools implementing personalized learning
target_learning_goals: Tailoring instruction to individual needs, skills, and interests; college and career readiness; student ownership of learning
examples: The 32 NGLC schools' implementation of each of the five strategies was assessed via administrator interviews, teacher and student surveys, teacher logs, and site visits
key_sources: John F. Pane, Elizabeth D. Steiner, Matthew D. Baird, Laura S. Hamilton. (2015). Continued Progress: Promising Evidence on Personalized Learning. RAND Corporation. https://www.rand.org/t/RR1365z2

article_title: Affect and willingness to communicate in digital game-based learning
citation: Hayo Reinders and Sorada Wattana. (2015). Affect and willingness to communicate in digital game-based learning. ReCALL, Volume 27, Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0958344014000226
title: Fifteen-week digital game-based language learning program at a Thai university
description: The studied intervention was a fifteen-week digital game-based learning program at a university in Thailand, in which five students participated. The program served as the setting for investigating how learners "actually experience the use of games" and how gameplay affected their affect and willingness to communicate in English. Its effects were traced through six interviews per participant, for a total of 30 interviews.
requirements: Sustained gameplay over a fifteen-week period with student participation sufficient to support repeated interviews.
constraints: Studied with only five participants at a single Thai university.
target_learners: University students learning English as a foreign language
target_learning_goals: L2 interaction and willingness to communicate in English
examples: Five students completed the program and were interviewed six times each, yielding 30 interviews.

article_title: Student Diversity Representation and Reporting in Universal School-Based Social and Emotional Learning Programs: Implications for Generalizability
citation: Rowe, H. L., & Trickett, E. J. (2018). Student Diversity Representation and Reporting in Universal School-Based Social and Emotional Learning Programs: Implications for Generalizability. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9425-3
title: Five-characteristic framework of student diversity for evaluating universal SEL interventions
description: The review operationalizes student diversity for evaluating universal SEL interventions in terms of five demographic characteristics: "gender, race/ethnicity, SES, disability status, and sexual orientation/gender identity." It uses this framework to assess how and when demographic characteristics were reported, whether they were analyzed as moderators of program outcomes, and how differential effects entered generalizability discussions. The framework organizes the review's content analysis of published evaluations.
requirements: Demographic information must be reported at the same level as the level of analysis; the review excluded district-level SES when the intervention was administered at grade level
constraints: The review excluded moderation tests of three-way interactions because each moderator's unique effects could not be teased apart
target_learners: children and adolescents in universal school-based SEL programs
target_learning_goals: social and emotional learning outcomes
examples: The review coded published SEL evaluations against these five diversity characteristics to assess reporting, moderation testing, and generalizability discussion
key_sources: Rowe, H. L., & Trickett, E. J. (2018). Student Diversity Representation and Reporting in Universal School-Based Social and Emotional Learning Programs: Implications for Generalizability. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9425-3

article_title: Comparing the quality of human and ChatGPT feedback of students’ writing
citation: Steiss, Jacob; Tate, Tamara; Graham, Steve; Cruz, Jazmin; Hebert, Michael; Wang, Jiali; Moon, Youngsun; Tseng, Waverly; Warschauer, Mark. (2023). Comparing the Quality of Human and ChatGPT Feedback on Students' Writing. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Comparing+the+Quality+of+Human+and+ChatGPT+Feedback+on+Students+Writing
title: Five-component framework of quality formative feedback on writing
description: The study operationalizes quality formative feedback on writing using five deductively coded components: the degree to which feedback "was criteria-based, provided clear directions for improvement, was accurate, prioritized essential features, and used a supportive tone." Each component is scored 1-5 with anchored rubric descriptors (e.g., criteria-based ranges from all feedback generic to consistently explicit genre criteria; supportive tone ranges from directive, unaffirming language to suggestive, affirming language). The framework, derived from a literature review and expert consultation, grounds the Writer(s)-Within-Community model's reconceptualization process, where quality feedback helps students compare their writing to genre ideals and identify specific improvement steps.
requirements: Raters or systems must be able to reference genre-specific criteria for source-based argumentative writing
Feedback must be scored against anchored rubric descriptors for each component
constraints: Timeliness was deliberately excluded as an evaluation criterion in this study
The framework was developed for source-based argument writing in secondary history
target_learners: secondary students (Grades 6-12) writing source-based argument essays
target_learning_goals: improving source-based argumentative writing through formative feedback and revision
examples: Raters double-coded 15% of the sample (n = 60), achieving exact agreement of 68-87% and Cohen's Kappa of .71 to .84 across the five components
