key_sources: Steiss, Jacob; Tate, Tamara; Graham, Steve; Cruz, Jazmin; Hebert, Michael; Wang, Jiali; Moon, Youngsun; Tseng, Waverly; Warschauer, Mark. (2023). Comparing the Quality of Human and ChatGPT Feedback on Students' Writing. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Comparing+the+Quality+of+Human+and+ChatGPT+Feedback+on+Students+Writing

article_title: Can Online Peer Assessment be Trusted?
citation: Bouzidi, L., & Jaillet, A. (2009). Can Online Peer Assessment be Trusted?. Educational Technology & Society, 12(4), 257-268. https://www.ifets.info/
title: Five-hypothesis validation process for online peer assessment
description: The article proposes a validation procedure in which peer assessment may only be judged valid after five prior conditions are confirmed: teacher reliability, correct test items, internal consistency of the test, reliability of the observation and marking tools, and clear, coherent marking instructions and scale schemes. The authors state that "a method which requires that five hypotheses must be confirmed before checking the validity of peer assessment" was used, operationalised through expert comparison, item analysis (difficulty and discrimination indexes), Cronbach's alpha, tool checks, and marking-scheme coherence checks before a final teacher-peer agreement analysis.
requirements: A teacher deemed a reliable expert assessor, correctly set test items, internally consistent items, reliable computer-assisted marking tools, and clear coherent marking instructions and scale schemes
constraints: The GEE-2007 exam failed the internal-consistency hypothesis and had to be excluded, showing the process can block validity verification for unreliable tests
target_learners: second- and third-year engineering students in exact science courses
target_learning_goals: valid summative and formative assessment of calculations, mathematical reasoning, short algorithms and short texts
examples: The process was applied to three classroom exams (CA-2006, CA-2007, GEE-2007), screening out Q7 of CA-2007 and the whole GEE-2007 exam before the final t-test and correlation analysis
key_sources: Bouzidi, L., & Jaillet, A. (2009). Can Online Peer Assessment be Trusted?. Educational Technology & Society, 12(4), 257-268. https://www.ifets.info/

article_title: Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context
citation: Olivia Brown, Nicola Power, and Julie Gore. (2024). Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context. Organizational Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.1177/10944281241271216
title: Five key questions for determining whether CTA methods fit a research study
description: The article provides an enumerated set of five considerations for judging whether CTA is appropriate: whether the study concerns a complex workplace environment characterized by uncertainty, whether the research focuses on cognition that is hard to articulate, whether relevant experts can be accessed, whether onto-epistemological assumptions have been considered, and whether findings have potential to impact practice. These are printed as question prompts in Table 1, guiding researchers on when CTA fits versus when alternatives such as the Critical Incident Technique are more appropriate.
requirements: Research questions targeting complex cognition rather than task attributes alone
Access to genuine expert participants
constraints: If the research question focuses primarily on identifying task characteristics, the Critical Incident Technique is likely more appropriate
target_learners: Management and organization researchers designing cognition studies
target_learning_goals: Selecting appropriate knowledge-elicitation methods for studying expert cognition
examples: Table 1 pairs each question with prompts, e.g. asking whether the context can be characterized by uncertainty
key_sources: Olivia Brown, Nicola Power, and Julie Gore. (2024). Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context. Organizational Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.1177/10944281241271216

article_title: Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics
citation: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3
title: Record game telemetry at the finest usable grain size with sufficient context to reconstruct events
description: The chapter defines "ﬁnest usable grain size" as "a data element that has a clear deﬁnition associated with it"; a bare click is unusable, whereas a qualified datum such as clicking the reset button is usable. It recommends that "game telemetry should contain sufﬁcient information to describe the context in which the event occurred" in enough detail to link data to a specific school, teacher, period, player, game level, and game state, illustrated by an index-card reconstruction test.
requirements: Each logged data element must have a clear definition, e.g., an attempted addition logged with information about the denominators
Unique player ID, game level, time, and game state information sufficient to reconstruct the record sequence
constraints: Logging at too coarse a grain (e.g., a generic attempted addition) merges events with different explanations, such as same- versus different-denominator additions
target_learners: researchers and analysts using game log data from school-based studies
target_learning_goals: interpreting in-game actions as evidence of domain understanding
examples: In the fractions game, telemetry included the player ID, level, time, the fraction being added, the fraction it was added to, and other game state information
key_sources: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3

article_title: Collaborative learning through augmented reality role playing
citation: Klopfer, E., Perry, J., Squire, K., & Jan, M.-F. (2004). Collaborative Learning through Augmented Reality Role Playing. https://education.mit.edu
title: Five criteria for designing collaborative learning challenges
description: The article adopts, from Johnson et al. (1994), a framework of five criteria that collaborative learning challenges should require: positive interdependence, promotive interaction, individual accountability, interpersonal and small group skills, and group processing. Positive interdependence means "one cannot succeed unless everyone succeeds"; promotive interaction means students promote each other's success; individual accountability means each student's performance is assessed and fed back. The authors use these criteria as design lenses in tables mapping game components to collaborative mechanisms in both game generations.
requirements: Game challenges must be designed so that each of the five criteria — positive interdependence, promotive interaction, individual accountability, interpersonal and small group skills, and group processing — is supported
target_learning_goals: collaboration
scientific investigation practices
examples: Tables in the article map Environmental Detectives components and the redesigned engine's role-based components onto each of the five criteria
key_sources: Klopfer, E., Perry, J., Squire, K., & Jan, M.-F. (2004). Collaborative Learning through Augmented Reality Role Playing. https://doi.org/10.3115/1149293.1149333

article_title: Tenacious Assessments: Using In-Game Behaviors to Measure Student Persistence and Challenge Navigation
citation: Malkiewich, L. J., Lee, A., Slater, S., & Chase, C. C. (2016). Tenacious Assessments: Using In-Game Behaviors to Measure Student Persistence and Challenge Navigation. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Tenacious+Assessments+Using+In-Game+Behaviors
title: Measure motivation in games with fine-grained behavioral indicators of willingness to attempt difficult strategies, not just total persistence times
description: The article recommends that game researchers "be more varied in the ways they define, operationalize, and measure student motivation", using log data to capture whether students attempt effortful strategies on hard problems rather than only total persistence times. These fine-grained measures "provide more fine-grained data than traditional assessments of motivation" and related to both a classic persistence measure and learning in this study.
requirements: A game environment that logs code complexity, level difficulty, attempts, and timing around failures so that percent-occurrence and time-based behavioral measures can be computed
constraints: The authors were "limited in this study by our small sample size and the fact that students only played one game"; measures may need adaptation for games with different structures, e.g. without gating
target_learners: fifth-grade students learning computer programming in an after-school program
target_learning_goals: measuring student persistence and challenge navigation as motivational behaviors during learning
examples: The study correlated eleven log-derived measures with challenge time and posttest scores, finding complex-code challenge-approach measures most predictive while traditional level-choice measures were not
key_sources: Malkiewich, L. J., Lee, A., Slater, S., & Chase, C. C. (2016). Tenacious Assessments: Using In-Game Behaviors to Measure Student Persistence and Challenge Navigation. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Tenacious+Assessments+Using+In-Game+Behaviors

article_title: Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach
citation: Mayer, Richard E. (2014). Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach. The MIT Press. http://direct.mit.edu/books/monograph/4028/bookpreview-pdf/2362507
title: Five defining characteristics of games mapped to game elements
description: The book defines games by five characteristics: "games are interactive, simulated systems that are rule based, responsive, challenging, cumulative, and inviting." Rule-based means events occur within a causal system based on knowable rules; responsive means the environment responds promptly and saliently to player actions; challenging means opportunities to succeed on difficult tasks; cumulative means the current state reflects previous actions; inviting means the environment is interesting and fun. Each characteristic maps to game elements such as feedback, replay, goals, levels, time, reward structure, aesthetics, and storytelling.
requirements: To be called a game, a learning environment must possess all five defining characteristics
constraints: The book treats the line between simulation game and computer game as fuzzy and includes simulations and games in the same category
target_learning_goals: designing educational activities that qualify as games for learning
examples: Table 1.1 maps the responsive characteristic to the game elements of feedback and replay, and the inviting characteristic to aesthetics, curve of interest, and storytelling
key_sources: Mayer, Richard E. (2014). Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach. The MIT Press. http://direct.mit.edu/books/monograph/4028/bookpreview-pdf/2362507

article_title: Evidence-Based Strategies for Reading Instruction of Older Students with Learning Disabilities
citation: Roberts, G., Torgesen, J. K., Boardman, A., & Scammacca, N. (2008). Evidence-Based Strategies for Reading Instruction of Older Students with Learning Disabilities. Learning Disabilities Research & Practice, 23(2), 63–69. http://www.centeroninstruction.org/
title: Five adjusted essential areas of reading instruction for older struggling readers
description: The article adapts the National Reading Panel's five essential areas of early reading instruction for older struggling readers, replacing phonemic awareness and phonics with word study and adding motivation. As printed: "for older readers, we would adjust the ﬁve essential areas in the NRP' s report to include these ﬁve areas: (1) word study, (2) ﬂuency, (3) vocabulary, (4) comprehension, and (5) motivation." Each area is then described with features of effective instruction for students in late elementary, middle, and high school.
requirements: Diagnostic testing and analysis to differentiate whether students need advanced word study or continued phonics-level instruction
constraints: Intended for students who continue to struggle with reading in late elementary, middle, and high school, many identified as having LD
target_learners: Older struggling readers with learning disabilities in upper elementary, middle, and high school
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Word reading
Reading motivation
examples: The article organizes its instructional recommendations section by section under these five headings, summarizing meta-analytic evidence for each
key_sources: Roberts, G., Torgesen, J. K., Boardman, A., & Scammacca, N. (2008). Evidence-Based Strategies for Reading Instruction of Older Students with Learning Disabilities. Learning Disabilities Research & Practice, 23(2), 63–69. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5826.2008.00264.x

article_title: Lexical Processing of Nouns and Verbs at 36 Months of Age Predicts Concurrent and Later Vocabulary and School Readiness
citation: Koenig Ashley, Arunachalam Sudha, Saudino Kimberly J. (2020). Lexical processing of nouns and verbs at 36 months of age predicts concurrent and later vocabulary and school readiness. Journal of cognition and development : official journal of the Cognitive Development Society. https://doi.org/10.1080/15248372.2020.1802277
title: Fixation-star lexical processing task with noun and verb trials
description: A variant of Fernald et al.'s (1998) lexical processing task in which, during the Response phase, 'the two images or videos disappeared, and a centrally positioned yellow star appeared, during which children heard the test query'. The two scenes then reappeared with a 'ding' sound to facilitate coding. The task included 13 trials with 7 nouns and 6 verbs, with noun referents shown as static images and verb referents as dynamic videos of people performing everyday actions. Latency was coded manually from video at 30 frames per second as the time from the onset of the 'ding' to the first look to the target scene. Because children look at the center at word onset, latency can be measured on all trials.
requirements: Children must be able to view the two scenes side-by-side and hear the auditory test query; the design requires that children are looking at the center of the screen at word onset so latency of the first saccade toward the target can be measured on all trials.
constraints: Latencies are measured from the onset of when the scenes reappear after word onset rather than from word onset, so they are 'not directly comparable to those in other studies'.
target_learning_goals: receptive vocabulary and lexical processing speed for nouns and verbs
examples: In this study the task used 13 trials with target words such as airplane, corn, crab, goldfish, hamburger, rocketship, and squirrel (nouns) and lift, march, rip, roll, shake, and stretch (verbs), with target side counterbalanced across trials.
key_sources: Koenig Ashley, Arunachalam Sudha, Saudino Kimberly J. (2020). Lexical processing of nouns and verbs at 36 months of age predicts concurrent and later vocabulary and school readiness. Journal of cognition and development : official journal of the Cognitive Development Society. https://doi.org/10.1080/15248372.2020.1802277

article_title: From scribbles to scrabble: preschool children’s developing knowledge of written language
citation: Puranik, Cynthia S., Lonigan, Christopher J. (2011). From Scribbles to Scrabble: Preschool Children's Developing Knowledge of Written Language. Reading and Writing. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-009-9220-8
title: Five-task emergent writing assessment protocol with feature-based scoring system
description: The study developed an assessment protocol of five writing tasks: Write Letters, Write Name, Write CVC Words, Picture Description, and Sentence Retell. A detailed scoring system quantified features such as linearity, segmentation, and left-to-right orientation, scored present or absent, with CVC spelling scored on a 7-point invented-spelling scale. The authors note "there is no gold standard for scoring emergent writing" and that no previous study had attempted to quantify features in children's writing. Internal consistencies were high (αs = .92-.96).
requirements: Trained scorers; the feature set scored should be tailored to the task, as the features providing highest cohesion varied with the task being scored
constraints: The spontaneous writing task initially included was dropped because most children could not attempt it; some 3-year-olds showed floor effects on complex tasks
target_learning_goals: emergent writing and written language knowledge
examples: The protocol was pilot-tested with 20 children; inter-rater reliability on ~30% of samples (n = 77) ranged from 93 to 100%
key_sources: Puranik, Cynthia S., Lonigan, Christopher J. (2011). From Scribbles to Scrabble: Preschool Children's Developing Knowledge of Written Language. Reading and Writing. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-009-9220-8

article_title: Effectiveness of Universal Self-regulation–Based Interventions in Children and Adolescents
citation: Pandey A, Hale D, Das S, Goddings A-L, Blakemore S-J, Viner RM. (2018). Effectiveness of Universal Self-regulation–Based Interventions in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Pediatrics. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6059379/
title: Five-category taxonomy of universal self-regulation interventions: curriculum-based, mindfulness and yoga, family-based, exercise-based, and social and personal skills.
description: The review organizes the 50 included interventions into five categories: "curriculum based, mindfulness and yoga, family based, exercise based, and other social and personal skills–based intervention strategies/delivery methods." These classifications were based on discussion between the review team members. Curriculum-based interventions (21 of 50, 42%) combine teacher professional training with classroom activities; mindfulness and yoga interventions (8 studies) are short-duration school-based programs with qualified instructors; family-based interventions (9 studies) involve parents and/or siblings; exercise-based interventions (6 studies) use physical activity; and social and personal skills interventions (6 studies) use small-group training with frameworks of personal responsibility, model behavior, and conflict resolution.
requirements: Classification was based on discussion between the review team members (A.P., D.H., and S.D.) rather than a pre-specified coding scheme
constraints: The review notes no advantage of 1 type of intervention over another with regards to effect on distal outcomes
target_learners: Children and adolescents aged 0 to 19 years in universal (non-targeted) settings
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation: controlling emotions, positive interactions with others, avoiding inappropriate or aggressive actions, and self-directed learning
key_sources: Pandey A, Hale D, Das S, Goddings A-L, Blakemore S-J, Viner RM. (2018). Effectiveness of Universal Self-regulation–Based Interventions in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Pediatrics. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6059379/

article_title: The effect of fine motor skills on handwriting legibility in preschool age children
citation: Seo S-M. (2018). The effect of fine motor skills on handwriting legibility in preschool age children. J. Phys. Ther. Sci. 30: 324–327. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/
title: During handwriting instruction and treatment for preschool children, provide activities that develop fine motor precision and in-hand manipulation skills
description: The article recommends that occupational therapists embed fine-motor development activities into handwriting instruction and treatment for preschool-age children. Because fine motor precision and in-hand manipulation were the factors that affected legibility, "occupational therapists can provide activities that aid the development of fine motor precision and in-hand manipulation skills for children during the instruction and treatment of handwriting".
requirements: Children must first have sufficient handwriting readiness skills, since children without sufficient development of such readiness skills are at risk of bad handwriting habits
constraints: The supporting evidence is correlational and limited to normally developing children sampled from one region
target_learners: preschool age children of normal growth and development
target_learning_goals: handwriting legibility
examples: The study measured fine motor precision, manual dexterity, and Functional Dexterity Test performance in 52 preschool children and found these skills predicted handwriting legibility
key_sources: Seo S-M. (2018). The effect of fine motor skills on handwriting legibility in preschool age children. J. Phys. Ther. Sci. 30: 324–327. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/

article_title: Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction
citation: van de Kamp, M.-T., Admiraal, W., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2016). Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction. Instructional Science, 44, 543–566. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9384-y
title: A five-phase lesson structure for metacognitive strategy instruction on divergent thinking
description: The intervention lesson followed a structured sequence of five phases: (1) orientation on metacognitive knowledge activating prior conceptions of creativity, (2) metacognitive strategy instruction exemplifying divergent thinking with visual examples, (3) divergent thinking strategy instruction explaining and exercising the twelve strategies, (4) application through independent use of strategies, and (5) evaluation through reflection and prediction. The authors state that "the specific order of lesson phases was based on studies about the structuring of instructional-learning episodes," grounding the sequence in instructional design theory.
requirements: Each phase builds on the previous one; explicit instruction and teacher modeling are central to phases 2 and 3
Whole-class discussion and peer feedback are used to integrate and evaluate new knowledge
constraints: Designed and tested as a 50-minute lesson within a secondary visual arts curriculum
target_learners: Grade-11 secondary school students in visual arts education
target_learning_goals: Build metacognitive knowledge and skills for regulating divergent thinking strategies to generate original ideas
examples: In phase 3, twelve divergent thinking strategies were explained and exemplified through direct instruction and teacher modeling, then applied in an alternative uses test in phase 4
key_sources: van de Kamp, M.-T., Admiraal, W., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2016). Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction. Instructional Science, 44, 543–566. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9384-y

article_title: Breaking Bad Behaviors: A New Tool for Learning Classroom Management Using Virtual Reality
citation: Lugrin J-L, Latoschik ME, Habel M, Roth D, Seufert C and Grafe S (2016) Breaking Bad Behaviors: A New Tool for Learning Classroom Management Using Virtual Reality. Front. ICT 3:26. https://doi.org/10.3389/fict.2016.00026
title: Five-level bad behavior classification for virtual students, adopted and extended from Borich's typology
description: The system classifies virtual student behaviors into five intensity levels of perceived disruption — null, low, mid, high, and extreme — with null corresponding to normal behaviors such as a quiet listening student and extreme including behaviors like fighting and screaming. The classification was "adopted and extended" from Borich's (2011) typology, which provides a single dimension with mild, moderate, and severe levels. It provides "a convenient way to systematically control a large set of virtual students to easily raise or lower the level of stress perceived by a teacher", and each level maps to associated animations of the virtual students.
requirements: New character models or animations require only a reference to their name and associated bad behavior categories to be included in the system
constraints: During the evaluation, some animations were not directly controllable by the instructor
target_learners: Trainee teachers practicing responses to disruptive behavior
target_learning_goals: Managing disruptive student behavior at graded intensity levels
examples: Table 1 lists behaviors per level, e.g., whispering at low, talking-neighbors at mid, receiving-phone-call at high, and screaming at extreme
key_sources: Lugrin J-L, Latoschik ME, Habel M, Roth D, Seufert C and Grafe S (2016) Breaking Bad Behaviors: A New Tool for Learning Classroom Management Using Virtual Reality. Front. ICT 3:26. https://doi.org/10.3389/fict.2016.00026

article_title: Material syntonicity: Examining computational performance and its materiality through weaving and sewing crafts
citation: Anna Keune (2022). Material syntonicity: Examining computational performance and its materiality through weaving and sewing crafts. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2022.2100704
title: Fiber crafts course with weaving and fabric manipulation units in a school design studio
description: A fiber crafts course facilitated within a weekly design studio at a K-8 public charter school, in which 16 middle school students aged 11-14 self-selected into units on weaving and fabric manipulation. Students wove personal designs on backstrap, rigid heddle, and tabletop looms, and sewed 3D shapes using a laser-cut template of a checkered matrix. Students planned designs on grid paper before implementing them, a tool drawn from the crafting community, and were not introduced to computing concepts in relation to crafts during the study.
requirements: Looms warped before sessions and a checkered matrix template for tracing dots onto fabric, so students could engage the matrix structures of both crafts.
constraints: The course consisted of three units of two sessions apiece (1 h 10 min/session); this article focuses on the first two units, and students knew the research concerned fiber crafts and computing.
target_learners: middle school students aged 11-14 in a K-8 public charter school
target_learning_goals: performing computational concepts through personally meaningful craft projects
examples: Students wove an average of 18 rows of plain weave before their first pattern variation, and all students sewed four twisted square units as their first fabric manipulation project.
key_sources: Anna Keune (2022). Material syntonicity: Examining computational performance and its materiality through weaving and sewing crafts. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2022.2100704

article_title: The new information literate: Open collaboration and information production in schools
citation: Andrea Forte. (2015). The new information literate: Open collaboration and information production in schools. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. 10:35–51. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9210-6
title: First- and second-order information assessment strategies
description: The article proposes a shallow taxonomy of information assessment strategies developed via grounded theory coding of student interviews. First-order strategies involve "adopting known heuristics for assessing sources", while second-order strategies involve "reflective construction of standards based on students' understanding of how information is produced" and the tasks at hand. The constructs are linked to Scardamalia and Bereiter's first- and second-order learning environments and used to explain how production experience supports reflection on novel publication models.
requirements: Applied to learners engaging with participatory information sources in a perpetually changing information landscape
constraints: Developed through interpretive grounded theory in two high school settings; products of interpretive research are framed as empirically driven hypotheses, not causal proof
target_learners: High school students (juniors and seniors) in science classes
target_learning_goals: Information literacy: finding, assessing, and using information sources
examples: Coding of 57 interviews yielded categories such as "criteria for citing a source", refined via axial coding into the taxonomy
key_sources: Andrea Forte. (2015). The new information literate: Open collaboration and information production in schools. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. 10:35–51. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9210-6

article_title: Coordinating modalities of mathematical collaboration in shared VR environments
citation: Wen Huang, Candace Walkington, Mitchell J. Nathan. (2023). Coordinating modalities of mathematical collaboration in shared VR environments. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09397-x
title: Five emergent multimodality interaction themes characterize collaborative problem-solving across stages
description: The multimodal analysis surfaced five emergent interaction themes showing participants' collaborative patterns in different problem-solving stages and their different strategies. These themes capture how learners orchestrate actions on virtual objects, gestures, body movements, and speech together — for example, action on objects first followed by reasoning through language. The themes are derived from the systematic coding and episode-building of the recorded VR sessions.
requirements: Multimodal video-coding at micro (low-level episode) and macro (high-level episode) levels to extract the themes
target_learning_goals: collaborative geometric reasoning
orchestration of embodied multimodal resources
key_sources: Wen Huang, Candace Walkington, Mitchell J. Nathan. (2023). Coordinating modalities of mathematical collaboration in shared VR environments. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09397-x

article_title: Learning within fiber-crafted algorithms: Posthumanist perspectives for capturing human-material collaboration
citation: Anna Keune. (2024). Learning within fiber-crafted algorithms: Posthumanist perspectives for capturing human-material collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09412-1
title: Fiber crafts course (weaving and fabric manipulation) as a context for computational learning with middle school youth
description: A 6-session fiber crafts course, facilitated twice at a K-8 charter school, offered weaving with three loom types and fabric manipulation with a laser-cut matrix template as contexts for performing computational concepts. "The participants of the course were 16 middle school students between 11 and 14 years old," self-selected via an interest survey. The crafts were chosen because they are matrix-based, connected historically to computing, and require routine movements that perform algorithms such as loops and conditional pairings.
requirements: Pre-warped looms and prepared materials (laser-cut grid template, threads, needles) so sessions could focus on production
Facilitators familiar with the crafts and with the study's purpose regarding computing-crafting connections
constraints: Facilitators did not ask students to recognize the crafting tools and materials as co-actors
Soft-robotic actuator animation sessions were excluded from this analysis
target_learners: seventh- and eighth-grade students in a maker-centered school program
target_learning_goals: performing computational concepts (loops, variables, conditionals) through physical crafting
examples: Projects included plain weave and gap patterns on backstrap, rigid heddle, and tabletop looms, and twisted-square stitched designs on cotton fabric
key_sources: Anna Keune. (2024). Learning within fiber-crafted algorithms: Posthumanist perspectives for capturing human-material collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09412-1

article_title: Bridging communities and schools in Urban development: community and citizen science
citation: Rikke Magnussen, Yotam Hod. (2023). Bridging communities and schools in Urban development: community and citizen science. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09641-9
title: Five-phase design-thinking process bridging students as residents and as students in CCS urban development projects
description: The educational design used a design-thinking process comprising five phases: "discovery, definition, ideation, experimentation and model construction, and testing and presentation." In discovery, professionals present the problem and students learn the urban-developer perspective through the What Is a Place? module, interview residents, and photograph good, bad, and developable places. Definition develops problem scoping and empathy with local community members; ideation generates many ideas; model construction uses LEGO, miniature and outdoor models, and digital tools such as Minecraft; and presentation elicits feedback from urban developers and architects. The process ran over two weeks per class.
requirements: Local urban developers who set authentic challenges connected to students' local environments and participate in feedback
Teachers and researchers introducing the needs of both students and other citizen groups during discovery and evaluation
constraints: Interventions lasted one to two weeks per class; in the second iteration some classes were reduced to one week due to COVID-19 lockdown
target_learners: Students aged 11–15 in grades 5–9 in vulnerable residential areas of Copenhagen
target_learning_goals: Strengthening design-thinking skills and the ability to take part in solving complex, authentic problems derived from local expertise
examples: Students built models out of LEGO, made miniature models indoors, built large models outside, and made digital models in Minecraft before presenting to a panel of urban developers and architects
key_sources: Rikke Magnussen, Yotam Hod. (2023). Bridging communities and schools in Urban development: community and citizen science. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09641-9

article_title: Do we need teachers as designers of technology enhanced learning?
citation: Kirschner, P. A. (2015). Do we need teachers as designers of technology enhanced learning? Instructional Science, 43, 309–322. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-015-9346-9
title: Five-competency professional cycle applied to teaching
description: Kirschner applies van Merriënboer and Kirschner's account of professional competence to teaching: a competency is a "combination of complex cognitive and higher-order skills, highly integrated knowledge structures, interpersonal and social skills, and attitudes and values". Professionals work through five competencies, often cyclically: gathering background/situational information, analyzing it and diagnosing, determining what steps to take, carrying out the actions, and evaluating whether results matched expectations, re-entering the cycle if not. He argues the expert teacher-designer follows the same cycle as doctors or chefs, and that the underlying competencies persist over decades while the enabling knowledge, skills, attitudes and tools change.
requirements: Teachers must be able to apply the competencies across varied situations and over an unlimited time span, as transfer and lifelong learning
constraints: The article presents this as a conceptual argument, not a tested result
target_learning_goals: professional design competence for learning experiences, including technology enhanced learning
examples: The article likens the teacher's cycle to a doctor taking a history, diagnosing, determining therapy, carrying it out and evaluating results, and to an expert chef using a broad palette of tools, techniques and ingredients
key_sources: Kirschner, P. A. (2015). Do we need teachers as designers of technology enhanced learning? Instructional Science, 43, 309–322. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-015-9346-9

article_title: Integrating dispositions in instructional design: an exploratory study in higher education
citation: Jafar Tavakoli, Marisa Exter, Ankita Kotangale. (2025). Integrating dispositions in instructional design: an exploratory study in higher education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09762-3
title: Fink's Integrated Course Design framework for aligning learning goals, teaching activities, and feedback and assessment
description: The study's organizing framework is Fink's (2013) Integrated Course Design, which "revolves around three primary components: Learning Goals, Teaching and Learning Activities, and Feedback and Assessment". The framework emphasizes creating significant learning experiences beyond simple content delivery, and holds that these three elements must be integrated and support each other; Fink warns that a course lacking this connection is a "broken course" that cannot work effectively because it is not integrated. The authors use it to structure their analysis of how dispositions are integrated across course design components.
requirements: The three components must be integrated and aligned with each other and with the desired outcomes for the course to work effectively
constraints: The article applies the framework to higher education course design and to dispositions as learning goals
target_learning_goals: dispositions such as attitudes, beliefs, and values alongside knowledge and skills
examples: The study analyzed instructional designers' integration of dispositions through the framework's components of learning goals, teaching and learning activities, and feedback and assessment
key_sources: Jafar Tavakoli, Marisa Exter, Ankita Kotangale. (2025). Integrating dispositions in instructional design: an exploratory study in higher education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09762-3

article_title: Keeping worlds apart to put them back together: VET teachers’ instructional patterns in simulation-based training
citation: Giulia Messina Dahlberg · Susanne Gustavsson. (2025). Keeping worlds apart to put them back together: VET teachers' instructional patterns in simulation-based training. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09714-x
title: Fidelity and authenticity as interactionally accomplished, emergent properties of simulated activity rather than fixed design features.
description: Drawing on Hontvedt and Øvergård (2020), the article advocates conceptualizing fidelity as a verb rather than a noun, something that "goes beyond its connection to the simulator as a tool and the resemblance to the real work environment". Fidelity and authenticity are described as "double-edged swords" that create coherence but also confusion and stress, and as emergent processes requiring individuals' engagement rather than elements related to a task solely by design. The article applies this framework to analyze how VET teachers and students accomplish fidelity and authenticity in the moment-by-moment interaction of simulator-based training.
requirements: Analysis must attend to moment-by-moment interaction among student, teacher, and simulator rather than to the simulator's technical specifications alone.
constraints: The article notes an intrinsic conflict between the simulator and its referent regarding what knowledge is and whether it is something that is, or something that is done in interaction.
target_learners: Upper-secondary VET students (ages 16-19) in the Natural Resource Program
target_learning_goals: Vocational knowledge and skills for operating forestry and agricultural machinery
examples: The article analyzes how a student identifies the artificial dimensions of a simulated environment designed to simplify and remove complex aspects of an authentic environment.
key_sources: Giulia Messina Dahlberg · Susanne Gustavsson. (2025). Keeping worlds apart to put them back together: VET teachers' instructional patterns in simulation-based training. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09714-x

article_title: Simulation-based training in professional education: learning, participation, and instructional design
citation: Charlott Sellberg & Oskar Lindwall. (2025). Simulation-based training in professional education: learning, participation, and instructional design. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09763-2
title: Fidelity as an interactional and instructional achievement rather than a fixed property of simulation technology
description: The editorial reconceptualises simulation fidelity, commonly defined as the extent to which a simulation reproduces physical, procedural, or functional features of a work setting, as something accomplished in practice. It argues that "fidelity emerges through participants' coordination, mutual orientation, and instructional framing, rather than from the simulator's realism alone". The educational value of a simulator depends on how it is embedded in instructional work and made relevant to learners' ongoing activity, as illustrated by forestry teachers' orchestration of simulator tasks.
requirements: Simulators must be embedded in instructional work and made relevant to learners' ongoing activity for their educational value to be realised
constraints: Applies to simulation-based education settings where participants, tools, and tasks are coordinated in instructional settings
target_learners: novices in professional education domains such as healthcare, aviation, maritime, forestry, and military training
target_learning_goals: professional skills and competencies developed through simulation-based training
examples: Messina Dahlberg and Gustavsson (2025) show fidelity in forestry-driving simulators emerges through teachers' orchestration of tasks, guidance, and links to outdoor practice
key_sources: Charlott Sellberg & Oskar Lindwall. (2025). Simulation-based training in professional education: learning, participation, and instructional design. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09763-2

article_title: Modelling evidence-based practice in initial teacher training: effects on teachers’ skills, knowledge and self-efficacy
citation: Sam Sims, Harry Fletcher-Wood, Thomas Godfrey-Faussett, Peps Mccrea, Stefanie Meliss. (2026). Modelling evidence-based practice in initial teacher training: effects on teachers’ skills, knowledge and self-efficacy. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09779-2
title: Evidence-based instructional summary of five principles for questioning for retrieval
description: A written summary document given to all participants before the first simulator attempt, which “provides the basis for both our video models and the way in which we measure teacher skills within the simulator”. It sets out five evidence-based principles: signalling any student could be called on, waiting three seconds or more, framing incorrect answers as learning opportunities, telling students an answer is incorrect with elaborative feedback, and giving partial hints after ‘I don’t know’ answers. The article states: “For space reasons, we limit ourselves here to highlighting the five principles for questioning for retrieval contained in the summary”.
requirements: Trainees must read the document before practising; the simulator coding framework awards credit against these same five principles
constraints: The knowledge test covered only content included in both the summary and the annotated video, to equalise exposure across arms
target_learning_goals: evidence-based questioning for retrieval practice
examples: The restudy arm re-read this document for 4.5 minutes as an active control, equating training duration across arms
key_sources: Sam Sims, Harry Fletcher-Wood, Thomas Godfrey-Faussett, Peps Mccrea, Stefanie Meliss. (2026). Modelling evidence-based practice in initial teacher training: effects on teachers’ skills, knowledge and self-efficacy. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09779-2

article_title: Effect of metaconceptual processes on 7th-grade students’ understanding of the concepts of republic, democracy, and the state of law
citation: Osman Sabancı, Nejla Yürük. (2026). Effect of metaconceptual processes on 7th-grade students’ understanding of the concepts of republic, democracy, and the state of law. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09805-3
title: Cyclical sequence of five metaconceptual activities externalising, monitoring, and evaluating civic concepts
description: The intervention organized instruction as a non-linear, cyclical sequence of five activities: analyzing concepts and their features, extracting hidden concepts from Atatürk's sayings via group posters, concept mapping with a law-making simulation, concept cartoons with concept cards, and interviews with family members. The article states: "Metaconceptual teaching activities such as poster preparation, journaling, concept maps, concept cartoons, and cards were used." Each activity was paired with group and class discussions and journal writing, and the tools were used "sequentially and cyclically to ensure continuous metacognitive engagement." Activities were mapped onto the three metaconceptual processes, e.g., cartoons maximising evaluation through cognitive conflict and role-based discussion.
requirements: Same teacher across branches; consultation with language, subject, and education specialists and the class teacher during design and implementation
constraints: "The activities were limited to the time periods specified in the curriculum (four weeks)"
target_learners: 7th-grade students in a public school in Ankara, Türkiye
target_learning_goals: Understanding republic, democracy, and the state of law
Activating metaconceptual awareness, monitoring, and evaluation
examples: In the poster activity groups of five to six students defined a concept, presented posters, voted on the best, justified revisions, and documented metacognitive processes in journals
key_sources: Osman Sabancı, Nejla Yürük. (2026). Effect of metaconceptual processes on 7th-grade students’ understanding of the concepts of republic, democracy, and the state of law. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09805-3

article_title: Scaffolding students’ use of metacognitive activities using discipline- and topic-specific reflective prompts
citation: Sijmkens, E., De Cock, M., & De Laet, T. (2024). Scaffolding Students' Use of Metacognitive Activities Using Discipline- and Topic-Specific Reflective Prompts. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72353-1_2
title: Five problem-solving dimensions structuring reflective prompts
description: The DLC's reflection questions are structured according to five problem-solving dimensions: (1) Strategy plan, (2) Concepts, (3) Mathematical model, (4) Computations, and (5) Interpretation. These align with established problem-solving models such as the logical problem-solving model of the University of Minnesota. Each dimension targets specific metacognitive activities — planning, monitoring, and evaluating — and expands students' metacognitive knowledge about strategies through tailored feedback.
requirements: Reflection questions must be crafted to align with common student difficulties for the specific problem
target_learners: first-year university science and engineering students
target_learning_goals: strategic problem solving
metacognitive planning and monitoring
self-evaluation of solutions
examples: The first reflection question asks students to recognise essential steps in their strategy plan; the final question triggers thinking about how to evaluate the validity of their own solution
key_sources: Sijmkens, E., De Cock, M., & De Laet, T. (2024). Scaffolding Students' Use of Metacognitive Activities Using Discipline- and Topic-Specific Reflective Prompts. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09363-w

article_title: Scaffolding students’ use of metacognitive activities using discipline- and topic-specific reflective prompts
citation: Sijmkens, E., De Cock, M., & De Laet, T. (2024). Scaffolding Students' Use of Metacognitive Activities Using Discipline- and Topic-Specific Reflective Prompts. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72353-1_2
title: Five characteristics of metacognitive prompt interventions
description: The article organises interventions for scaffolding metacognition around five characteristics: embedding (embedded vs non-embedded), specificity (task-specific vs generic), customisation (hard/generalised vs soft/personalised scaffolds), directness (direct instruction vs indirect guidance), and broadness (comprehensive vs narrow subset of metacognitive activities). The article reviews evidence for each: embedded prompts are more effective than non-embedded; specific prompts have a significantly larger impact than generic ones; personalised scaffolds are more effective for self-regulated skills; directness should be adapted to expertise level; and comprehensive support systems are needed for students with limited prior knowledge.
requirements: Interventions must be designed considering all five characteristics to effectively scaffold metacognition
constraints: Reflective prompts are only effective if students have a clear understanding of the task they are reflecting upon, per Kauffman et al. (2008)
target_learning_goals: metacognitive abilities
self-regulated learning
transfer of knowledge to new problems
examples: The DLC is characterised as discipline-/topic-specific, non-embedded (but embedded within modules), indirect (questions) with direct (feedback suggestions), hard scaffold, and broad in scope
key_sources: Sijmkens, E., De Cock, M., & De Laet, T. (2024). Scaffolding Students' Use of Metacognitive Activities Using Discipline- and Topic-Specific Reflective Prompts. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09363-w

article_title: The impact of retrieval processes, age, general achievement level, and test scoring scheme for children’s metacognitive monitoring and controlling
citation: Krebs, S.S., Roebers, C.M. (2012). The impact of retrieval processes, age, general achievement level, and test scoring scheme for children's metacognitive monitoring and controlling. Metacognition and Learning 7, 75–90. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9079-3
title: Film-plus-cloze metacognitive assessment paradigm with confidence judgments and answer withdrawal
description: A multi-phase assessment paradigm for children's metacognitive monitoring and control. Children "watched an educational film and predicted their test performance," then "solved a cloze test regarding the film content including answerable and unanswerable items and gave confidence judgments to every answer." Finally, "children withdrew answers that they believed to be incorrect," allowing monitoring accuracy and control behavior to be measured before and during test taking across answerable and unanswerable items.
requirements: An educational film establishing the content to be tested
A cloze test containing both answerable and unanswerable items
Confidence judgments collected for every answer
target_learners: Primary school children aged 9/10 and 11/12 years
target_learning_goals: Assessment of metacognitive monitoring and control processes during test taking
examples: Applied with N = 150 high and low achievers who watched an educational film, predicted performance, took the cloze test, and withdrew answers they believed incorrect.
key_sources: Krebs, S.S., Roebers, C.M. (2012). The impact of retrieval processes, age, general achievement level, and test scoring scheme for children's metacognitive monitoring and controlling. Metacognition and Learning 7, 75–90. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9079-3

article_title: Confounded or Controlled? A Systematic Review of Media Comparison Studies Involving Immersive Virtual Reality for STEM Education
citation: Lawson, A. P., Martella, A. M., LaBonte, K., Delgado, C. Y., Zhao, F., Gluck, J. A., Munns, M. E., LeRoy, A. W., & Mayer, R. E. (2024). Confounded or Controlled? A Systematic Review of Media Comparison Studies Involving Immersive Virtual Reality for STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09908-8
title: Five control criteria framework for judging degree of control in media comparison studies
description: The review proposes that a media comparison is adequately controlled when five criteria are met: matched activities, matched non-IVR activities, matched practice with the dependent measure, matched time spent learning (within 20% difference), and matched content. The article states "To determine the degree to which the IVR and conventional conditions were controlled on instructional method and content in each article, five control criteria were assessed." Comparisons are then graded from fully controlled to fully not controlled, with a second approach flagging comparisons whose control is difficult to determine due to missing information.
requirements: Each condition must be operationally defined well enough for coders to judge whether activities, practice, time, and content were matched between conditions.
constraints: When information for any criterion is missing, the comparison's degree of control is labeled difficult to determine rather than counted as met.
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students in STEM courses
target_learning_goals: STEM content learning outcomes such as retention and transfer
examples: The review applied the criteria to 50 comparisons, e.g., coding a comparison as confounded when the IVR condition received a paper-based worksheet the conventional condition did not.
key_sources: Lawson, A. P., Martella, A. M., LaBonte, K., Delgado, C. Y., Zhao, F., Gluck, J. A., Munns, M. E., LeRoy, A. W., & Mayer, R. E. (2024). Confounded or Controlled? A Systematic Review of Media Comparison Studies Involving Immersive Virtual Reality for STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09908-8

article_title: Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach
citation: Kalyuga, S. (2023). Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09812-7
title: Five principles of natural information processing systems underpinning the evolutionary approach in cognitive load theory
description: The evolutionary approach in cognitive load theory describes human cognitive architecture as a natural information processing system analogous to biological evolution by natural selection, characterized by five principles: randomness as genesis, borrowing and reorganizing, narrow limits of change, information store, and environmental organizing and linking. The paper states these principles explain "the operation of these two natural information processing systems", with the first two relating to acquisition of information, the next two to processing and storing, and the last to using stored information. Working memory is analogous to the epigenetic system and long-term memory to the genetic system.
requirements: The analogy was established to substantiate the main characteristics of human cognitive architecture relevant to cognitive load theory
target_learners: learners acquiring biologically secondary knowledge in formal education
target_learning_goals: acquisition of domain-specific knowledge in educational institutions
examples: The paper maps random mutations to trial-and-error problem solving, genome to long-term memory, and the epigenetic system to working memory
key_sources: Kalyuga, S. (2023). Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09812-7

article_title: The Transfer of Teacher Training to Inclusive Classroom Practice: A Meta-Analytic SEM Approach
citation: Donath, J. L., Lüke, T., Tran, U. S., Botes, E., & Goetz, T. (2025). The Transfer of Teacher Training to Inclusive Classroom Practice: A Meta-Analytic SEM Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10081-9
title: Five competing models of learning transfer from teacher training to classroom practice
description: The article synthesizes overlapping theories of teachers' learning in in-service training into five models of the transfer process: Knowledge-to-Practice, Knowledge-Skills-Beliefs, Reaction-to-Training, Practice-to-Belief, and Willingness-to-Change. Each model specifies a different central aspect and sequence — for example, Knowledge-to-Practice "assumes a serial succession from knowledge acquisition to improved classroom practices and student outcomes", while Willingness-to-Change models "assume that teacher training can enhance teachers’ willingness to change and professional knowledge by provoking ‘aha’ moments". The taxonomy served as the framework tested against pooled empirical data in the MASEM analyses.
requirements: Testing a model requires primary studies reporting correlations among at least two of the seven transfer variables (knowledge, skills, practices, beliefs, willingness to change, satisfaction, student outcomes).
constraints: The models were tested in the context of teacher training for inclusive education, with influencing factors such as training design and school context deliberately omitted to focus on the steps of the transfer process.
target_learners: in-service teachers participating in professional development on inclusive education
target_learning_goals: transfer of training content to inclusive classroom practice and improved student outcomes
examples: The article illustrates each model with a vignette, e.g. a teacher whose provocative training questions prompted willingness to try a new classroom-management approach
key_sources: Donath, J. L., Lüke, T., Tran, U. S., Botes, E., & Goetz, T. (2025). The Transfer of Teacher Training to Inclusive Classroom Practice: A Meta-Analytic SEM Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10081-9

article_title: Stimulating Elementary School Students’ Self-Regulated Learning Through High-Quality Interactions and Relationships: A Narrative Review
citation: Niels J. de Ruig, Peter F. de Jong, Marjolein Zee. (2023). Stimulating Elementary School Students' Self-Regulated Learning Through High-Quality Interactions and Relationships: A Narrative Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09795-5
title: Five-component model of self-regulated learning embedded in a cyclic process
description: The review conceptualizes SRL as a process in which students "systematically attempt to monitor, regulate, and control" five components: cognition, metacognition, motivation, emotions, and behaviors. It draws primarily on social-cognitive models (Pintrich, Boekaerts) and organizes the components within a preparatory, performance, and appraisal phase cycle. The review uses this five-component structure as its outcome taxonomy, coding each included study's SRL measures against it (Table 1), and structures its results sections by component rather than by phase because the phases may occur dynamically rather than sequentially.
requirements: Measurement instruments must distinguish the SRL components being targeted; the review notes most self-report instruments capture only a narrow subset of components
constraints: The review notes theoretical debate about whether the phases are clearly distinguishable, so it structures its synthesis by component rather than phase
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning across cognitive, metacognitive, motivational, emotional, and behavioral components
examples: The review's Table 1 maps subcomponents such as target goal setting, planning, monitoring, help-seeking, and emotion regulation strategies onto the three phases
key_sources: Niels J. de Ruig, Peter F. de Jong, Marjolein Zee. (2023). Stimulating Elementary School Students' Self-Regulated Learning Through High-Quality Interactions and Relationships: A Narrative Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09795-5

article_title: Situational Motivation in Academic Learning: A Systematic Review
citation: Törmänen, T., Ketonen, E., Lehtoaho, E., Turunen, M., Zabolotna, K., Shubina, T., & Järvenoja, H. (2025). Situational Motivation in Academic Learning: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10036-0
title: Five major motivation theories as a comprehensive framework for situational motivation
description: The review organizes situational motivation research through five theories — attributional theory, expectancy-value theory (including its situated extension SEVT), social cognitive theory, achievement goal theory, and self-determination theory. The authors state these "provide a comprehensive framework to understand the multifaceted nature of motivation," collectively covering constructs such as intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, goal orientations, and attributions, and each explicitly considering situational and contextual factors in different ways. The framework structures which constructs were measured situationally and how studies approach situatedness theoretically and methodologically.
requirements: Each included study must measure at least one construct from the five theories or another situational motivational construct as defined by the study authors
constraints: The review notes evidence on a situational level is still limited for theories other than SDT, EVT, and SCT's self-efficacy construct
target_learners: Learners across all ages and educational levels in academic contexts
target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting students' situational motivation during academic learning
examples: The review coded all 80 included studies by motivation theory (SDT, EVT, SCT, AGT, ATT, or other) and summarized measured constructs and instruments for each wave
key_sources: Törmänen, T., Ketonen, E., Lehtoaho, E., Turunen, M., Zabolotna, K., Shubina, T., & Järvenoja, H. (2025). Situational Motivation in Academic Learning: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10036-0

article_title: School-based teaching for democracy: A systematic review of teaching methods in quantitative intervention studies
citation: Teegelbeckers, J.Y., Nieuwelink, H., & Oostdam, R.J. (2023). School-based teaching for democracy: A systematic review of teaching methods in quantitative intervention studies. Educational Research Review, 39, 100511. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100511
title: Five-type taxonomy of teaching methods for democracy: instruction, small-group work, assignments, projects, and democratic decision-making
description: The review organizes democratic-schooling interventions into five types of teaching methods. As the article states, "We categorized these interventions into five types of teaching methods: instruction, small-group work, assignments, projects, and democratic decision-making." This taxonomy is the review's primary organizing axis for comparing which interventions were effective for which democratic competences, and it structures the analysis of educational characteristics across the 54 included interventions.
requirements: Quantitative intervention studies of school-based teaching for democracy that can be classified into one of the five method types
constraints: Derived from 51 quantitative effect studies written between 2010 and 2020; the review notes there is still much to be gained in the description of teaching methods
target_learners: School students in quantitative intervention studies of democratic education
target_learning_goals: Democratic competences (knowledge, attitude, skill, behavior)
examples: The review classified 54 interventions from 51 studies into the five method types and analyzed their effectiveness by democratic competence
key_sources: Teegelbeckers, J.Y., Nieuwelink, H., & Oostdam, R.J. (2023). School-based teaching for democracy: A systematic review of teaching methods in quantitative intervention studies. Educational Research Review, 39, 100511. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100511

article_title: Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models
citation: Peng Wang, Fred Paas. (2026). Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10195-8
title: Five educational-psychology lenses for interpreting AI training: curriculum design, scaffolding, social learning, assessment validity, and ethical alignment
description: The article organizes AI training analysis around five educational-psychology domains, mapping each construct onto a concrete AI analogue and validity risk. It states that its reflection "focuses on five interrelated domains where the analogy between AI training and human education is especially illuminating": curriculum design, instructional scaffolding, social learning via feedback, assessment and construct validity, and ethical alignment. Table 1 pairs each lens with practical design checks, such as planning fading tests for scaffolds and auditing teacher signals for feedback.
requirements: The framework is used as a design heuristic for interpreting training interventions, not as a claim of shared mechanisms between human and machine learning
constraints: The article states the mapping "is not a claim that human learning and model optimization share underlying mechanisms"
target_learners: AI researchers and developers acting as trainers of models
educational psychologists evaluating AI capability claims
target_learning_goals: Evaluating whether AI training gains reflect robust competence rather than support dependence or proxy optimization
examples: Table 1 maps constructs such as hints and worked examples to prompting supports, and formative versus summative assessment to benchmarks and reward functions
key_sources: Peng Wang, Fred Paas. (2026). Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10195-8

article_title: The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects
citation: Pekrun, R. (2019). The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 905–914. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09512-1
title: Five options for defining contested psychological concepts, from dropping terms to listing variants
description: The article enumerates five strategies for reducing gaps between research traditions' definitions: dropping terms, definition by common core, definition by components and causes, definition by prototype, and definition by listing variants. It recommends the common core approach for curiosity and interest, since dropping terms is not viable for communication, and component definitions must assemble elements in nonarbitrary ways based on structural and functional covariation.
requirements: Component-based definitions should be assembled in nonarbitrary ways so their usefulness can be empirically scrutinized
constraints: Definitions cannot be discovered by empirical investigation; they must be constructed and are subject to theoretical preferences
target_learning_goals: conceptual clarity and consistent measurement in motivation research
examples: The article illustrates the common core principle with the definition of personality as characteristics that vary between persons and are relatively stable over time
key_sources: Pekrun, R. (2019). The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 905–914. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09512-1

article_title: Promoting Argumentation Competence: Extending from First- to Second-Order Scaffolding Through Adaptive Fading
citation: Noroozi, O., Kirschner, P. A., Biemans, H. J. A., & Mulder, M. (2018). Promoting Argumentation Competence: Extending from First- to Second-Order Scaffolding Through Adaptive Fading. Educational Psychol Rev, 30, 153–176. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9400-z
title: Distinction between first-order scaffolding (task performance) and second-order scaffolding (self-directed learning)
description: Drawing on Van Merriënboer and Kirschner's Ten Steps to Complex Learning, the article distinguishes two scaffold types: "first-order (i.e., regular) scaffolding refers to providing support and guidance for the acquisition and performance of domain-specific complex skills, second-order scaffolding provides support and guid- ance for self-directed learning". Applied to argumentation, first-order scaffolding supports desirable argumentation within a task, while second-order scaffolding aims at argumentation competence transferable to similar tasks once support is removed.
requirements: Second-order scaffolding requires taking learners' internal scripts into account
Argumentation competence includes knowledge, skill, and attitude/willingness to apply it
constraints: Transfer is framed as within the same discipline, not across disciplines or areas, because disciplines differ in argumentation rules, goals, and epistemology
target_learners: students dealing with complex, ill-defined, controversial issues, e.g., in the natural sciences
target_learning_goals: transferable argumentation competence
self-directed learning
examples: The article argues second-order scaffolding should be prioritized in class situations where students frequently deal with complex authentic problems
key_sources: Noroozi, O., Kirschner, P. A., Biemans, H. J. A., & Mulder, M. (2018). Promoting Argumentation Competence: Extending from First- to Second-Order Scaffolding Through Adaptive Fading. Educational Psychol Rev, 30, 153–176. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9400-z

article_title: A Systematic Review of Peer Assessment Design Elements
citation: Alqassab, M., Strijbos, J.-W., Panadero, E., Fernández Ruiz, J., Warrens, M., & To, J. (2023). A Systematic Review of Peer Assessment Design Elements. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09723-7
title: Five prototypical peer assessment design patterns from latent class analysis
description: The review's LCA of 891 cases yielded a five-class solution describing latent patterns of peer assessment designs. Class 1 is "Online asynchronous formative anonymous random-matched bi-direc tional intragroup (individually assessed) peer assessment via written comments [with revision]"; Class 2 is the summative scoring counterpart without revision; Class 3 is face-to-face synchronous formative non-anonymous self-selection matched with oral and written comments and revision; Class 4 is online asynchronous formative intergroup scoring plus written comments with revision; Class 5 is online asynchronous summative non-anonymous domain-matched intra- and intergroup scoring without revision. Classes 1, 2, and 3 were large (32.8%, 25.7%, 21.6%); Classes 4 and 5 small (13.1%, 6.8%).
requirements: Design elements must be reported in sufficient detail for coding; the review notes vagueness of design descriptions in most published articles limited reliable coding
constraints: Patterns derive from studies published 2011–October 2018 in peer-reviewed journals, excluding grey literature and workplace settings
target_learning_goals: domain-specific knowledge or skills
social skills
examples: Class 1 (32.8% of sample): formative, written comments, revision, intragroup, anonymous, online asynchronous, random matching
Class 3 (21.6%): face-to-face synchronous, formative, non-anonymous, self-select matching, oral and written comments, with revision
key_sources: Alqassab, M., Strijbos, J.-W., Panadero, E., Fernández Ruiz, J., Warrens, M., & To, J. (2023). A Systematic Review of Peer Assessment Design Elements. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09723-7

article_title: Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches
citation: Chrysi Rapanta & Mark K. Felton. (2022). Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09637-2
title: Five-level taxonomy of argument quality for coding reasoning gains
description: The review codes argumentative reasoning gains on five levels combining structural and functional elements: main (claims/reasons), elaborated (evidence, questions, TAP structure), complex (internal relationships and quality of evidence/justification), dialogic (transactivity, critique, rebuttal), and dialectic (revision or integration of alternative theories, quality of counterarguments, critical questions). The authors state: "we had previously identified five types or levels of arguments, comprising both structural and functional elements, namely: main, elaborated, complex, dialogic, and dialectic". Table 1 details the codes per level, e.g., level 4 codes T, CAR, CAR/E for dialogic argument.
requirements: Coding requires identifying presence or combination of elements such as claims, reasons, evidence, TAP structure, transactive moves, counterarguments, and revisions
constraints: The authors note that asserting specific argument elements are effective may require additional pragmatic criteria such as conceptual complexity, coherence, and relevance
target_learning_goals: Argumentative reasoning gains as products of dialogue
examples: Pattern 2 studies were mostly coded at the elaborated level (TAP-structure arguments) while Pattern 4 studies were mostly coded at the dialectic level
key_sources: Chrysi Rapanta & Mark K. Felton. (2022). Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09637-2

article_title: Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead
citation: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2
title: Five-group organizing framework for motivation–personality integration in educational psychology
description: The article proposes an organizing framework that maps five groups of theories offering pathways toward integrating motivation and personality: theories from personality psychology that include motivational elements, motivational theories that implicitly or explicitly incorporate personality, cognitive-domain theories, construct-specific integrative theories, and process-oriented theories of learning. The authors state their aim to combine "motivation" primarily in terms of motivational constructs commonly examined in educational psychology (e.g., subject- or domain-specific expectancies, values, interests, and goals) with a Big Five personality focus, noting the work is "intentionally asymmetrical". Integration is said to operate at multiple levels, including dynamic state-level interplay, long-term trait development, compensatory mechanisms, and principles of sustainable and self-regulated learning.
requirements: Integration combines education-relevant motivational constructs with broad Big Five personality aspects, requiring researchers to work across disciplinary borders
constraints: The article states it is not intended as a comprehensive review; it is meant to encourage deeper reflection on integration
target_learning_goals: understanding learning behaviors, engagement, performance, and educational choices
key_sources: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2

article_title: How Are Curiosity and Interest Different? Naïve Bayes Classification of People’s Beliefs
citation: Donnellan, E., Aslan, S., Fastrich, G. M., & Murayama, K. (2021). How Are Curiosity and Interest Different? Naïve Bayes Classification of People's Beliefs. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09622-9
title: Five proposed state-level distinctions between curiosity and interest: triggers, information-seeking character, knowledge states, affect, and incentive salience
description: The article's theoretical review organises proposed distinctions between state curiosity and situational interest into five facets. As printed: "In this section, we outline five distinctions between state-level interest and curiosity proposed by researchers who maintain that the concepts are meaningfully separable." These are (1) triggers — curiosity requires collative variables inducing information gaps while interest has broader, possibly subjective triggers; (2) character of information seeking — curiosity ceases on closing a specific gap whereas interest lacks stopping rules and can last longer; (3) knowledge states — curiosity follows an inverted U-shaped function of perceived knowledge, interest does not; (4) affect — curiosity is initially aversive then pleasant, interest pleasant from triggering; (5) incentive salience — D-type curiosity involves higher initial "wanting" distinct from "liking".
requirements: Distinguishing state-level forms is required because trait-level distinctions depend on whether traits are tendencies to experience corresponding states
constraints: The article notes lines demarcating one dimension may not demarcate others, and situational interest and state curiosity may be indistinguishable under some accounts
target_learners: educational researchers designing curiosity- or interest-based interventions
target_learning_goals: understanding how curiosity and interest differ as motivations for information seeking and learning
examples: The review cites Litman's I/D-type framework, Loewenstein's information-gap theory, and the four-phase model of interest development as the frameworks from which the distinctions derive
key_sources: Donnellan, E., Aslan, S., Fastrich, G. M., & Murayama, K. (2021). How Are Curiosity and Interest Different? Naïve Bayes Classification of People's Beliefs. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09622-9

article_title: A developmental perspective on feedback: How corrective feedback influences children’s literacy, mathematics, and problem solving
citation: Fyfe Emily R., Borriello Giulia, Merrick Megan. (2023). A developmental perspective on feedback: How corrective feedback influences children's literacy, mathematics, and problem solving. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2022.2108426
title: Five-Stage Model of feedback processing
description: The review adopts the Bangert-Drowns et al.
