(1991) Five-Stage Model, a cycle of learner mental states: initial state, retrieval, response with confidence, evaluation of the feedback message, and adjustment of knowledge, goals, and interests that feed back into the initial state. The authors use it as a springboard for developmental questions, noting it "highlights the multistep nature of the feedback process, the mindfulness of the learner, and the mutual influence between the learner and the environment."
requirements: Learners must notice feedback, be able to interpret its form, and view it as credible for Stage 4 evaluation to occur
constraints: The authors do not test the model directly; they use it as a springboard for identifying open questions about feedback in childhood
target_learners: preschool and elementary school children ages 3-11
target_learning_goals: learning from task-level corrective feedback in literacy, mathematics, and problem solving
examples: The review proposes feedback alerts may constitute a new pre-task stage, and that Stage 4 should be broken into notice, decode, evaluate, and act-upon steps
key_sources: Fyfe Emily R., Borriello Giulia, Merrick Megan. (2023). A developmental perspective on feedback: How corrective feedback influences children's literacy, mathematics, and problem solving. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2022.2108426

article_title: Improving norms in research culture to incentivize transparency and rigor
citation: Mellor, D. (2021). Improving norms in research culture to incentivize transparency and rigor. Educational Psychologist, 56(2). https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3125-5888
title: Five-stage diffusion-of-innovations roadmap for changing research culture
description: The article adapts Rogers' diffusion of innovations into a strategy for normalizing open science practices in educational psychology. Adoption proceeds through adopter groups, each needing a different condition: "Innovators only need a new practice to be possible in order to pick it up", early adopters need practices designed to be easy, the early majority needs a community of practice, the late majority needs specific rewards, and laggards come on board only when practices are required. Stakeholders supply the matching opportunity at each stage.
requirements: Each adopter group must be offered the opportunity or incentive matching its stage: possibility, ease, community of practice, rewards, or requirements
constraints: The article states the recommendations are "by no means exhaustive" and that making practices required is appropriate only once they are widely possible, easy, normal, and rewarded
target_learners: academic policy makers at journals, funders, and universities
target_learning_goals: adopting open science practices such as data sharing and preregistration
shifting community norms toward transparency and rigor
examples: The article maps each stage to concrete mechanisms: digital repositories make practices possible, the OSF makes them easy, Open Science Badges and unconferences make them normative, Registered Reports and hiring criteria make them rewarding, and the TOP Guidelines and funder policies make them required
key_sources: Mellor, D. (2021). Improving norms in research culture to incentivize transparency and rigor. Educational Psychologist, 56(2). https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3125-5888

article_title: Spatial skills in early childhood education
citation: Bobrowicz, Katarzyna; Mendes, Angélica. (2026). Spatial skills in early childhood education. Learning and Instruction, 103, 102308. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102308
title: Five-theme, sixteen-indicator framework for coding spatial skills in early childhood curricula
description: The study coded curricular documents with a deductive six-phase latent thematic analysis in which "Five themes with a total of sixteen indicators were identified based on previous literature." The framework organizes the curricular representation of spatial skills — abilities underpinning processing of shapes, locations, and inter-relations among entities and frames of reference — into themes whose indicator occurrences were compared across country-specific curricula. It serves as a reusable coding scheme for analyzing how curricula represent spatial skills.
requirements: Curricular-guideline documents pertaining to early childhood education to code
Previous literature from which the themes and indicators are deductively derived
constraints: Developed and applied to early childhood curricular guidelines; the available text does not print the names of the five themes or sixteen indicators
target_learning_goals: spatial skills such as processing shapes, locations, and inter-relations among entities and frames of reference
examples: Applied to 81 documents with curricular guidelines from fifty-two countries across six continents, with proportions of indicator occurrences compared using descriptive statistics and Kruskal-Wallis tests
key_sources: Bobrowicz, Katarzyna; Mendes, Angélica. (2026). Spatial skills in early childhood education. Learning and Instruction, 103, 102308. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102308

article_title: Preliminary investigation of skimming in reading.
citation: Whipple, G. M., & Curtis, J. N. (1914). Preliminary Investigation of Skimming in Reading. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=preliminary+investigation+of+skimming+in+reading
title: Five modes of rapid reading and skimming
description: The article proposes that skimming is not one process but embraces at least five varieties: (a) fast reading in which every word is read, (b) trailing, perceiving without apperceiving, (c) covering, like trailing but possibly vertical as well as horizontal, (d) omitting logically, and (e) omitting arbitrarily. Different observers used different combinations of these modes, and their skimming devices differed so much across readers as to preclude summarizing.
requirements: Readers must have mastered ordinary careful word-by-word reading before skimming modes develop
constraints: The taxonomy derives from introspective reports of six adult observers and is described as tentative
The article states the devices adopted in skimming differ so much between readers as to preclude summarizing
target_learning_goals: efficient extraction of gist from prose texts
adaptive reading rate for different purposes
examples: B used trailing and logical omitting; Fr used arbitrary jumps of a fixed size; Gou read topic sentences then skimmed down the page center
key_sources: Whipple, G. M., & Curtis, J. N. (1914). Preliminary Investigation of Skimming in Reading. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=preliminary+investigation+of+skimming+in+reading

article_title: A group scale of intelligence for use in the first three grades.
citation: Pressey, L. W. (1919). A Group Scale of Intelligence for Use in the First Three Grades. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Five special requirements for group testing young children
description: A framework of five problems in building group tests for first-grade children that do not arise for older children: literacy, fatigue, directions, integration, and motivation. The summary states that (b) "fatigue must be reduced to a minimum, (c) the directions must be such that the children can take an active part in them, (d) the tests of the scale must be care- fully integrated, and (e) the work must be motivated and main- tained by interest rather than by disciplinary control." The first requirement is that all elements of school training must be avoided, since no reading or writing can be involved for young children.
requirements: No reading or writing, even of letters or numbers, in the test material
Directions that let children take an active part
Careful integration of the tests in the scale
Motivation from interest rather than disciplinary control
constraints: The author states these difficulties do not appear, or barely appear, in making tests for older children
target_learners: Children in the first three grades of elementary school
target_learning_goals: Measurement of general intelligence for school entry screening and ability grouping
examples: The scale avoids literacy: two only of the hundred items involve any school acquirement; all four tests use one cross-out response; directions use a question-answer method; interest is sustained by picture and block materials and game-like participation
key_sources: Pressey, L. W. (1919). A Group Scale of Intelligence for Use in the First Three Grades. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0072897

article_title: A Book Describing An Elementary School Curriculum Based on Year-Long Series of Projects.
citation: Rugg, E. U. (1921). New Publications. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Journal+of+Educational+Psychology
title: The American Public School (Finney), a survey history of American public education for beginning teachers
description: A Macmillan textbook covering the Colonial period through the Recent Period (1890-1920), with chapters on Rousseau, Pestalozzi, Herbart, and Froebel, designed for normal school students. The reviewer calls it "a brief survey, made concrete by the inclusion of numerous pictures, charts and diagrams" that should help make beginning teachers intelligent about public education's historical development.
requirements: Would have been helped by references and suggestive problems at the end of chapters, which the reviewer notes are absent
constraints: The reviewer says it is encyclopedic, discussing many important movements in a paragraph, and gives too little space to the English Poor Laws and the Apprenticeship system
target_learners: normal school students preparing to be beginning teachers
target_learning_goals: historical development of public education in the United States
European educational influences
examples: The recent period section discusses educational reorganization, enrichment of the curriculum, and educational theory and practice
key_sources: Rugg, E. U. (1921). New Publications. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Journal+of+Educational+Psychology

article_title: Profiles of teachers’ striving and wellbeing: Evolution and relations with context factors, retention, and professional engagement.
citation: De Clercq, Mikaël, Helen Watt, & Paul Richardson. (2021). Profiles of Teachers’ Striving and Wellbeing: Evolution and relations with context factors, retention and professional engagement. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000702
title: Five-profile typology of teachers' striving and wellbeing
description: The study applies and empirically grounds an existing typology of teacher striving and wellbeing, identifying "Five profiles ... (Sparing, Good health, Ambitious, Burnout and Wornout)" among a longitudinal sample of Australian teachers. The profiles combine dimensions of striving (ambition, effort) and wellbeing (health, burnout), and are used as the states between which teachers transition over career stages.
requirements: Longitudinal measurement of teachers' striving and wellbeing indicators to assign profiles and track transitions
constraints: Profiles were identified among Australian secondary and primary teachers from early to mid-career
target_learners: teachers in early to mid-career stages
target_learning_goals: understanding and supporting teacher wellbeing, striving and professional development
key_sources: De Clercq, Mikaël, Helen Watt, & Paul Richardson. (2021). Profiles of Teachers’ Striving and Wellbeing: Evolution and relations with context factors, retention and professional engagement. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000702

article_title: Research in public schools.
citation: Research in Public Schools. (1914). The Journal of Educational Psychology, 5(2). https://eric.ed.gov
title: Five-group classification of exceptional children via teacher questionnaire census
description: A preliminary census of exceptional children was taken by questionnaire to teachers, after which "the children were roughly classified into five groups": feeble-minded or insane, backward, exceptionally gifted, incorrigible, and children of good intelligence suffering physical defects. This classification organized the department's subsequent intensive case studies.
requirements: a preliminary census of exceptional children taken by means of a questionnaire to the teachers
constraints: the classification is described as rough, based on teacher questionnaire data
target_learning_goals: identifying children needing special treatment or placement
examples: Group E covered children of apparently good intelligence suffering from defective vision, hearing, or speech, crippled children, and epileptics
key_sources: Research in Public Schools. (1914). The Journal of Educational Psychology, 5(2). https://doi.org/10.1037/h0075864

article_title: Constructivist developmental theory is needed in developmental neuroscience
citation: Arsalidou, M. & Pascual-Leone, J. (2016). Constructivist developmental theory is needed in developmental neuroscience. npj Science of Learning 1, 16016. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.16
title: Five categorical modes of processing proposed as a more comprehensive alternative to dual-process theories
description: The article argues dual-process (type 1/type 2) theories are descriptively valid but neither comprehensive enough nor formulated from within the person's processing, and lack developmental data. It proposes distinguishing five categorical modes of processing: (1) the intuitive meaning-bearing experiential mode, (2) affective-motivational schemes and processes, (3) the explicit logical and linguistic mode, (4) sociocultural and sociomotivational processes, and (5) the brain's hidden operators and executive control processes. Each mode is claimed to be explicitly expressed in the brain, and distinguishing them should permit comprehensive neuroscientific interpretation.
requirements: Distinguishing the categorial modes of processing to permit comprehensive neuroscientific interpretations
constraints: Dual-process theories lack developmental data and are not organismic in a comprehensive way, discussing only two of many dimensions of variation
target_learners: children and adults whose processing is interpreted in neuroscience studies
target_learning_goals: interpreting relations between cognition, brain processes and development
examples: The article maps type-2 processing to the experiential mode and type-1 to automatised explicit linguistic processing, and links gist-versus-verbatim fuzzy-trace processing to scheme-based overdetermination
key_sources: Arsalidou, M. & Pascual-Leone, J. (2016). Constructivist developmental theory is needed in developmental neuroscience. npj Science of Learning 1, 16016. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.16

article_title: Interleaved practice enhances memory and problem-solving ability in undergraduate physics
citation: Joshua Samani and Steven C. Pan. (2021). Interleaved practice enhances memory and problem-solving ability in undergraduate physics. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00110-x
title: Five candidate mechanisms for the interleaving benefit in physics problem-solving
description: The article proposes five non-mutually-exclusive explanatory accounts for the observed interleaving benefits, adapted from the interleaving literature to physics problem-solving: inductive learning of confusable problem categories, distributed practice via study-phase retrieval, reduced lag-to-test, relational processing of non-isomorphic problem types (described as material-appropriate processing), and practice in strategy selection. The authors state these accounts "are not necessarily mutually exclusive" and that the study was not designed to adjudicate between them.
requirements: The accounts are drawn from the interleaving literature with adaptations to problem-solving in introductory physics and remain candidates rather than tested mechanisms
constraints: The article states none of the accounts are mutually exclusive and the study did not adjudicate between them; inductive learning of problem categories alone might not be sufficient to explain the results because criterial tests also required memory retrieval of formulas
target_learning_goals: recall and application of physics formulas and principles
problem-solving with novel, multi-topic problems
examples: The article notes interleaved homework sets provided more opportunities to compare non-isomorphic problem categories than blocked sets, and that blocked assignments allowed students to bypass memory retrieval by reusing solutions held in working memory
key_sources: Joshua Samani and Steven C. Pan. (2021). Interleaved practice enhances memory and problem-solving ability in undergraduate physics. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00110-x

article_title: Commentary for the International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education Special Issue on K-12 AI Education
citation: H. Chad Lane. (2023). Commentary for the International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education Special Issue on K-12 AI Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00359-w
title: The Five Big Ideas of AI framework organizes K-12 AI instruction around five ideas with grade-band progressions
description: The AI4K12 initiative's Five Big Ideas framework structures what should be taught in K-12 AI education. As the commentary describes, "The Big Five Ideas (perception, representation and reasoning, learning, natural interaction, and societal impact) act as the basis for their approach," with grade band progressions split as K-2, 3-5, 6-8, and 9-12. The commentary endorses the framework as intuitive and influential across the special issue, while stressing that classroom testing is needed to validate the developmental appropriateness of the grade bands.
requirements: Classroom testing is needed; the commentary calls to "conduct testing in classrooms" to confirm vocabulary appropriateness across grade bands
constraints: The commentary notes AI lacks convergence on agreed foundational ideas compared with older fields like mathematics and physics
target_learners: K-12 students across grade bands K-2, 3-5, 6-8, and 9-12
target_learning_goals: AI awareness, knowledge, skills, and ethics
examples: A deep dive into machine learning (Big Idea 3) demonstrates grade-band-relevant instruction, carving ML into sub-concepts such as training a model, neural networks, and reasoning
key_sources: H. Chad Lane. (2023). Commentary for the International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education Special Issue on K-12 AI Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00359-w

article_title: Fully Individualized Curriculum with Decaying Knowledge, a New Hard Problem: Investigation and Recommendations
citation: Lebis, A., Humeau, J., Fleury, A., Lucas, F., & Vermeulen, M. (2024). Fully Individualized Curriculum with Decaying Knowledge, a New Hard Problem: Investigation and Recommendations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00376-9
title: FIC/DK-P: a formal framework modeling fully individualized curricula with decaying knowledge
description: FIC/DK-P models the problem of selecting, for a student, a sequence of courses such that the student becomes qualified for a stated objective while mastery values decay over time. It represents mastery continuously in [0;1], courses as macro entities with prerequisites, credits and temporal availability, and student profiles with per-knowledge decay functions, so that "it becomes essential to predict and mitigate this decay effect to determine the optimal sequence of courses."
requirements: Institutions must catalog courses with the knowledge taught, prerequisites, credit values and temporal availability; a knowledge decomposition into the [0;1] mastery interval must be agreed upon.
constraints: The study makes four stated hypotheses: no logistical constraints, a complete course catalog, courses confined to a single academic term, and perfect learning (no probabilistic learning models).
target_learners: university and engineering school students building individualized curricula toward professional objectives
target_learning_goals: sequencing courses so prerequisites and objective requisites remain satisfied despite knowledge decay
examples: Instantiated with an Ebbinghaus-inspired decay function on simulated datasets from a French engineering school master's program (catalog size C between 300 and 500 courses, K between 200 and 600 knowledge).
key_sources: Lebis, A., Humeau, J., Fleury, A., Lucas, F., & Vermeulen, M. (2024). Fully Individualized Curriculum with Decaying Knowledge, a New Hard Problem: Investigation and Recommendations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00376-9

article_title: ML4STEM Professional Development Program: Enriching K-12 STEM Teaching with Machine Learning
citation: Jingwan Tang, Xiaofei Zhou, Xiaoyu Wan, Michael Daley, Zhen Bai. (2023). ML4STEM Professional Development Program: Enriching K-12 STEM Teaching with Machine Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00292-4
title: Ground ML teacher professional development in five principles of effective learning activities to mitigate technological and pedagogical barriers
description: ML4STEM adopts five pedagogical principles drawn from the technology-integration PD literature. The article states that it "adopted five principles of effective learning activities to mitigate identified technological and pedagogical learning barriers: learning by design, hands-on experience with technology, modeling of technology use, collaborative participation, and reflection". These principles are realized as concrete activities: tutorial-video modeling, hands-on engagement with pre-designed ML activities, group discussion and journal reflection, and collaborative lesson-plan design with peers and researchers.
requirements: Learning activities must connect technology, subject matter, and pedagogy, e.g., exemplars co-designed with a science educator
constraints: The article notes professional learning does not occur as a one-time effort, so sufficient duration and progressive sequencing are needed
target_learners: K-12 in-service STEM teachers learning to integrate new technologies
target_learning_goals: TPACK knowledge development for ML integration
Positive attitudes toward technology integration
examples: TaL session combined modeling, hands-on activity, and reflection; TaD session combined learning by design, collaborative participation, and reflection journals
key_sources: Jingwan Tang, Xiaofei Zhou, Xiaoyu Wan, Michael Daley, Zhen Bai. (2023). ML4STEM Professional Development Program: Enriching K-12 STEM Teaching with Machine Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00292-4

article_title: Adapting Progress Feedback and Emotional Support to Learner Personality
citation: Matt Dennis, Judith Masthoff, Chris Mellish. (2016). Adapting Progress Feedback and Emotional Support to Learner Personality. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0059-7
title: Five Factor Model of personality as an axis for adapting learning feedback
description: The Five Factor Model (Big 5) describes personality via five traits: Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Emotional Stability (vs neuroticism), and Openness to Experience, with nomenclature and definitions adopted from John and Srivastava (1999). The authors adopt it because it "is considered robust by most psychologists", trait levels remain relatively stable over time, and validated questionnaires measure it with as few as 10 to 300 items. It serves as the organising framework for the paper's five feedback-adaptation experiments.
requirements: Validated questionnaires (e.g. IPIP-NEO, Mini-Markers) to identify or convey an individual's trait levels
constraints: Psychologists agree on five traits but not on their names
In this paper the model is used via polarised trait-level stories rather than measured trait scores
target_learners: learners in digital educational systems whose personality can be represented via the five traits
target_learning_goals: adapting progress feedback and emotional support to learner personality and performance
examples: Each experiment addressed one trait, using validated high/low stories and six possible scores (10% to 90%) on a mock test
key_sources: Matt Dennis, Judith Masthoff, Chris Mellish. (2016). Adapting Progress Feedback and Emotional Support to Learner Personality. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0059-7

article_title: Utilizing a Pretrained Language Model (BERT) to Classify Preservice Physics Teachers’ Written Reflections
citation: Wulff, P., Mientus, L., Nowak, A., & Borowski, A. (2023). Utilizing a Pretrained Language Model (BERT) to Classify Preservice Physics Teachers' Written Reflections. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 33, 439–466. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00290-6
title: Reflection-supporting model with five elements (circumstances, description, evaluation, alternatives, consequences) for structuring preservice teachers' written reflections
description: The article uses a reflection-supporting model developed by Nowak et al. (2019), based on the ALACT-model by Korthagen and Kessels (1999), which "defines a reflection to include the elements: circumstances of the teaching situation, description of the teaching situation, evaluation of students' and teacher actions, devising of alternatives, and derivation of consequences." Preservice teachers were instructed to produce written reflections following this five-element scaffold during teaching placements. The authors state "the simplicity of the model makes it accessible to teachers at various degrees of expertise."
requirements: Preservice teachers receive explicit instruction on what is expected in each element of the reflection
constraints: The model was employed with preservice physics teachers at two mid-sized German universities
target_learning_goals: reflective thinking about teaching experiences
professional development through structured written reflection
examples: Preservice teachers wrote reflections on self-taught lessons or on lessons observed in a 16-minute video vignette
key_sources: Wulff, P., Mientus, L., Nowak, A., & Borowski, A. (2023). Utilizing a Pretrained Language Model (BERT) to Classify Preservice Physics Teachers' Written Reflections. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 33, 439–466. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00290-6

article_title: An Intelligent Support System to Help Teachers Plan Field Trips
citation: Noemi Mauro, Liliana Ardissono, Federica Cena, Livio Scarpinati, Gianluca Torta. (2024). An Intelligent Support System to Help Teachers Plan Field Trips. Int J Artif Intell Educ 34, 793–824. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00366-x
title: FieldTripOrganizer web application for teacher-led field trip planning
description: FieldTripOrganizer is a web-based, mobile-accessible application that helps teachers design custom field trips by filtering Points of Interest and activities by geographical area, domain of interest, school level, and type, and by incrementally building an itinerary. The article proposes "a field trip planner based on the mixed-initiative approach aimed at increasing teachers' autonomy and motivation in designing educational tours". While the user designs the trip, the application keeps the spare time visible, invokes the VROOM solver to re-estimate the optimal schedule after each addition or removal, and graphically annotates items with a green or red semaphore indicating whether they fit the time constraints. It was instantiated on science field trips in the Ivrea area of Piedmont, Italy, and evaluated with 18 science teachers.
requirements: Domain experts must populate the external data source (Omeka-S CMS) with places and activities at setup time
constraints: Budget constraints are not handled; administrative aspects such as paying services are out of scope
target_learners: Student classes from preschool to high school visiting cultural and natural sites
target_learning_goals: Out-of-school learning through science field trips complementing in-class work
examples: In the user study, participants organized a science field trip for a class of students in two geographical areas (Ivrea City and Alice Lake), once per application
key_sources: Noemi Mauro, Liliana Ardissono, Federica Cena, Livio Scarpinati, Gianluca Torta. (2024). An Intelligent Support System to Help Teachers Plan Field Trips. Int J Artif Intell Educ 34, 793–824. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00366-x

article_title: An Intelligent Support System to Help Teachers Plan Field Trips
citation: Noemi Mauro, Liliana Ardissono, Federica Cena, Livio Scarpinati, Gianluca Torta. (2024). An Intelligent Support System to Help Teachers Plan Field Trips. Int J Artif Intell Educ 34, 793–824. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00366-x
title: Generic ontology-based domain data model for places, activities, and objects
description: FieldTripOrganizer's domain knowledge is expressed as an OWL ontology (Fig. 1) stored in the Omeka-S content management system, which domain experts populate at setup time. The model defines "Items" representing places (PoIs), activities, or objects, related through is-a, use_in, and is_in relations, so that a PoI can aggregate one or more activities — unlike the atomic elements of typical tourist applications. Activities carry attributes for school levels (difficulty), type (laboratory or outdoors), and setup time (10 minutes by default). The generic data model abstracts from entity details and specifies only "Domains of interest", making the application suitable for tours on different topics such as science and arts.
requirements: Domain experts must author and revise the domain information in the CMS, which offers a user-friendly interface suitable for non-technical people
constraints: The school-level difficulty classification is currently coarse-grained (for all students, from kindergarten, from primary school, and so forth)
target_learners: Student classes across school levels visiting PoIs in the project's target areas
target_learning_goals: Filtering places and activities by domain of interest and required school level to match didactic objectives
examples: The displacement matrix TD was instantiated with constant walking-time values retrieved from Google Maps
key_sources: Noemi Mauro, Liliana Ardissono, Federica Cena, Livio Scarpinati, Gianluca Torta. (2024). An Intelligent Support System to Help Teachers Plan Field Trips. Int J Artif Intell Educ 34, 793–824. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00366-x

article_title: Embracing discomfort in active learning and technology-rich higher education settings: sensemaking through reflexive inquiry
citation: McLay, K. F., Thomasse, L., & Reyes, V. C., Jr. (2023). Embracing discomfort in active learning and technology-rich higher education settings: sensemaking through reflexive inquiry. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10192-6
title: Five design principles for a technology-rich active-learning teacher education course
description: The redesigned educational technology course followed five design principles embedding active-learning strategies across curriculum, pedagogy and assessment: flipped learning via short (under ten minutes) online videos; course staff as "critical friends" and co-explorers rather than experts; "cyclical tutorials linked to assessment" following a three-wave 'Sandpit–Synergy–Showcase' structure; group assessment with a shared mark in three of four tasks; and formal critical reflection. Together these scaffolded four target competencies: curation, collaboration, creation and critical reflection.
requirements: Tutors willing to act as co-explorers rather than digital-tool experts
Assessment tasks aligned with the Sandpit–Synergy–Showcase tutorial cycle
constraints: The authors report the course evoked student resistance, anxiety and polarised evaluations, so the pattern does not guarantee satisfaction
target_learning_goals: Twenty-first century skills: curation, collaboration, creation, critical reflection
examples: Approximately 270 (2017) and 300 (2018) students experienced the redesigned course in tutorials of about 20 students
key_sources: McLay, K. F., Thomasse, L., & Reyes, V. C., Jr. (2023). Embracing discomfort in active learning and technology-rich higher education settings: sensemaking through reflexive inquiry. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10192-6

article_title: Metacognition research in education: topic modeling and bibliometrics
citation: Xieling Chen, Xinyue Li, Di Zou, Haoran Xie, & Fu Lee Wang. (2025). Metacognition research in education: topic modeling and bibliometrics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10451-8
title: Five correlation-based thematic groups organizing the 19 metacognition research topics
description: Using STM's assumption that documents are mixtures of correlated topics, the article estimated and visualized topic correlations with the "huge" package, plotting a graph where nodes represent topics and shorter connected lines indicate higher positive correlation. The analysis discovered five groups (G1–G5): G1 pairs "self-regulated learning" with "statistical analysis of gender differences"; G2 links collaborative learning/CSCL, digital and online learning, assessment and feedback, healthcare education, and metacognitive models; G3 links epistemic belief revision, scientific inquiry, reflective pedagogy, and teacher education; G4 pairs special/early childhood education with problem-solving; G5 links second language writing with listening/speaking and reading comprehension. The article states these correlations "reveal potential interdisciplinary thematic areas or emerging subfields where further research might be fruitful".
requirements: Topic correlation estimation requires the document–topic proportion distributions from the fitted STM
constraints: Positive correlations (> 0) suggest likelihood of co-occurrence in one article; negatively correlated topics show no connections
target_learning_goals: identifying interdisciplinary thematic areas for future metacognition research
examples: The article suggests metacognition instruction for developing language skills as one direction, evidenced by the close connections among reading and language comprehension, L2 writing and motivation, and listening and speaking
key_sources: Xieling Chen, Xinyue Li, Di Zou, Haoran Xie, & Fu Lee Wang. (2025). Metacognition research in education: topic modeling and bibliometrics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10451-8

article_title: Using social media affordances to support Ill-structured problem-solving skills: considering possibilities and challenges
citation: Adrie A. Koehler, Daniela Rezende Vilarinho-Pereira. (2023). Using social media affordances to support Ill-structured problem-solving skills: considering possibilities and challenges. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10060-1
title: Five prominent educational affordances of social media: association, visibility, persistence, searchability, and identity creation
description: The article synthesizes prior affordance frameworks (e.g., Treem and Leonardi; Boyd; Xue and Churchill) and identifies the affordances named at least three times across articles. It states: "we identified five prominent affordances: association, visibility, persistence, searchability, and identity creation." Affordances are treated as relations between agent abilities and environment features rather than tool properties, and the article maps how each affordance is embodied differently across applications (wikis, blogs, Instagram, Snapchat, Facebook) and how each can support problem finding and solution generation in problem-centered learning.
requirements: Affordances exist only in relation to a user's abilities and a specific context, so tool selection must connect to the context and audience
constraints: Social media applications are constantly being created, updated, and discontinued, so affordance-based analysis rather than tool-specific analysis is needed
target_learners: K-12, undergraduate, and graduate learners in problem-centered learning
target_learning_goals: Ill-structured problem-solving skills, including problem finding and solution generation
examples: Table 4 compares how wiki, blog, Instagram, Snapchat, and Facebook embody association, visibility, persistence and searchability, and identity
key_sources: Adrie A. Koehler, Daniela Rezende Vilarinho-Pereira. (2023). Using social media affordances to support Ill-structured problem-solving skills: considering possibilities and challenges. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10060-1

article_title: Systematic design of a learning environment for domain-specific and domain-general critical thinking skills
citation: Tiruneh, D. T., Weldeslassie, A. G., Kassa, A., Tefera, Z., De Cock, M., & Elen, J. (2016). Systematic design of a learning environment for domain-specific and domain-general critical thinking skills. Education Tech Research Dev, 64, 481–505. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-015-9417-2
title: First Principles of Instruction model as a framework for designing CT-embedded subject matter instruction
description: The article draws on Merrill's First Principles of Instruction model, which "abstracted five interrelated prescriptive instructional design principles: activation, demonstration, application, integration and problem-centeredness". The model holds that learning is promoted when learners acquire knowledge and skills in the context of real-world problems, and that instruction designed on these principles can result in effective, efficient and engaging learning. The authors used it as the design framework for the experimental E&M learning environment, translating each principle into concrete classroom activities: whole-task problems, prior-knowledge activation, instructor modelling, coached application, and peer presentation and defence of solutions.
requirements: Design requires identifying desired CT outcomes and splitting them into sub-skills before designing instruction
Instructors need training and involvement in the design process to implement lessons as designed
constraints: No previous study, to the authors' knowledge, had tested the efficacy of this model in designing interventions targeting CT skill development
target_learning_goals: domain-specific critical thinking skills in electricity and magnetism
domain-general critical thinking skills
examples: The experimental learning environment gave students whole-task problems such as explaining why lightning-strike charge stays on the exterior of an aircraft, before instruction on the chapter began.
key_sources: Tiruneh, D. T., Weldeslassie, A. G., Kassa, A., Tefera, Z., De Cock, M., & Elen, J. (2016). Systematic design of a learning environment for domain-specific and domain-general critical thinking skills. Education Tech Research Dev, 64, 481–505. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-015-9417-2

article_title: Design, development, and evaluation of an individual digital study assistant for higher education students
citation: Karrenbauer, C., Brauner, T., König, C. M., & Breitner, M. H. (2023). Design, development, and evaluation of an individual digital study assistant for higher education students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10255-8
title: Five quality domains from the literature as the theoretical framework underlying IDSA requirements
description: The literature review provided the theoretical framework for the requirements and the basis for prototype development. The article states that "Five domains were identified: (a) user satisfaction, (b) pedagogical domain, (c) service quality, (d) perceived information quality, and (e) perceived system quality." The pedagogical domain was grounded in the ICAP framework, whose criteria are "specifically adapted to online teaching and learning", while the technological domains cover service quality, information quality, and system quality variables mapped onto the derived requirements.
requirements: Requirements must be mapped onto the five domains, with net-benefit variables such as content completeness, knowledge acquisition, and performance improvement assigned to the pedagogical domain
constraints: The framework was derived from a literature review of information-systems success research rather than tested directly in this study
target_learners: Higher education students using digital study support systems
target_learning_goals: User acceptance and effective use of digital study support for self-regulated learning
key_sources: Karrenbauer, C., Brauner, T., König, C. M., & Breitner, M. H. (2023). Design, development, and evaluation of an individual digital study assistant for higher education students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10255-8

article_title: Ideas for supporting student-centered stem learning through remote labs: a response
citation: West, R.E., Sansom, R., Nielson, J., Wright, G., Turley, R.S., Jensen, J., & Johnson, M. (2021). Ideas for supporting student-centered stem learning through remote labs: a response. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09905-y
title: Five-phase inquiry framework for online labs: orientation, conceptualization, investigation, conclusion, and discussion
description: The article organizes guidance for virtual and remote labs around de Jong and Lazonder's framework of five inquiry phases for online labs. As the authors state, they "adopt the same inquiry framework as Zacharia et al. (2015)" covering "orientation, conceptualization, investigation, conclusion, and discussion." The framework structures how guidance tools and strategies are mapped onto stages of student inquiry in computer-supported inquiry learning environments.
requirements: The framework is applied to online lab-based inquiry learning, where each phase of student inquiry can be supported with distinct guidance tools and strategies
constraints: The article applies it specifically to virtual student lab-based learning during COVID-19 emergency remote teaching
target_learners: STEM students in higher education using virtual and remote labs
target_learning_goals: Scientific inquiry skills across the phases of orientation, conceptualization, investigation, conclusion, and discussion
examples: The authors used the framework to organize strategies learned from STEM faculty about supporting virtual lab-based learning during the COVID-19 shutdown
key_sources: West, R.E., Sansom, R., Nielson, J., Wright, G., Turley, R.S., Jensen, J., & Johnson, M. (2021). Ideas for supporting student-centered stem learning through remote labs: a response. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09905-y

article_title: Improving workplace-based assessment and feedback by an E-portfolio enhanced with learning analytics
citation: van der Schaaf, M., Donkers, J., Slof, B., Moonen-van Loon, J., van Tartwijk, J., Driessen, E., Badii, A., Serban, O., Ten Cate, O. (2016). Improving workplace-based assessment and feedback by an E-portfolio enhanced with learning analytics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-016-9496-8
title: Five-phased iterative, user-centred design approach for learning-analytics-enhanced assessment tools
description: The article develops the enhanced E-portfolio through "An iterative design approach with a central role for the user" matching the information system development life cycle. "Our approach consists of five iterative phases": making pedagogical knowledge about workplace learning explicit (phase 1, Delphi studies and seven focus groups with 78 participants), translating it into probabilistic student models (phase 2), developing personalized feedback and visualization (phase 3), implementing the prototype in professional education (phase 4), and evaluating perceived usefulness (phase 5), with findings fed back to preceding phases.
requirements: Design must be an integral part of implementation with detailed decision making at each stage and involvement of end users such as students and supervisors
The student model must be aligned with a substantive learning theory, operationalized in descriptions of workplace tasks
constraints: The design is only successful when developed and implemented through the eyes of the users; feedback quality improves only if the environment remains responsive to learners', supervisors' and experts' requirements
target_learners: students and supervisors in professional education programs
target_learning_goals: workplace-based assessment and personalized feedback supporting professional competency development
examples: A four-staged prototyping strategy moved from a mock-up model, to an expert-based prototype student model, to a complete curriculum-wide model tuned with institutional data, to integration with the JIT and VIZ modules
key_sources: van der Schaaf, M., Donkers, J., Slof, B., Moonen-van Loon, J., van Tartwijk, J., Driessen, E., Badii, A., Serban, O., Ten Cate, O. (2016). Improving workplace-based assessment and feedback by an E-portfolio enhanced with learning analytics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-016-9496-8

article_title: Teachers’ experiences of teaching online during COVID-19: implications for postpandemic professional development
citation: Carlos González, Daniel Ponce, Violeta Fernández. (2023). Teachers' experiences of teaching online during COVID-19: implications for postpandemic professional development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10200-9
title: Five-dimension framework of higher education teachers' digital competencies for post-GOT online and blended teaching
description: The article organizes teachers' digital competencies around the four dimensions proposed by Esteve-Mon et al. (2020)—basic digital skills, the pedagogical application of digital technologies, the use of technology to support continuous professional development, and the ability to further the digital competencies of higher education students—extended with Villarroel and Bruna's (2017) transversal competencies. The authors state: "We organized our results around these five dimensions to converge the analysis of teachers' experiences with teachers' digital competency development needs for post-GOT online and blended teaching." The framework structures both the interview analysis and the professional development recommendations.
requirements: The framework was applied to higher education teachers teaching undergraduate courses online due to COVID restrictions in Chile
constraints: The article notes existing competency frameworks were not initially developed for use in higher education
target_learning_goals: digital competencies for online and blended teaching
examples: The results section presents themes under each of the five dimensions, with interview excerpts from 151 teachers and full excerpt tables in an appendix
key_sources: Carlos González, Daniel Ponce, Violeta Fernández. (2023). Teachers' experiences of teaching online during COVID-19: implications for postpandemic professional development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10200-9

article_title: Expanding conceptual evidence-building with the science of learning: integrating evidence weights, alignment estimates and iterative updates for educational innovations
citation: Natalia Kucirkova, Phil Vahey, David Patterson, David Dockterman. (2026). Expanding conceptual evidence-building with the science of learning: integrating evidence weights, alignment estimates and iterative updates for educational innovations. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10732-w
title: A five-step systematic methodology for building the conceptual evidence base of educational innovations
description: The article introduces a structured methodology for evaluating educational innovations' conceptual foundations, developed through practice at the International Centre for EdTech Impact. It proceeds from evidence identification to interpretation and application: "We followed five systematic steps. First, we conducted a rapid literature review, guided by the principle of methodological plurality. Second, we evaluated the identified studies using the criterion of weight of evidence." The sequence was designed to reduce the risk of retrospectively selecting evidence to justify existing product features, and culminates in a theory of change shared with the company to inform its research roadmap.
requirements: A rapid literature review guided by the innovation's learning goals and instructional approach, with predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria
Weight-of-evidence appraisal of identified studies across multiple disciplines
Alignment analysis relating evidence to the innovation's specific features and assumptions
Discussion of findings with representatives of the organization that designed the innovation
Development of a theory of change integrating the literature with a logic model
constraints: The authors describe it as "a conceptually grounded, practice-informed methodological proposal and not an application of grounded theory in the strict methodological sense"
Rapid reviews "may not provide the same depth as a full systematic review"
target_learners: developers and researchers of educational innovations
school districts and procurement teams evaluating educational tools
target_learning_goals: evaluating and strengthening the conceptual research foundations of educational innovations
examples: The methodology was applied to two case studies: the I Can Read early childhood literacy product from Asia and the entirely digital SplashLearn math and reading platform from the USA
key_sources: Natalia Kucirkova, Phil Vahey, David Patterson, David Dockterman. (2026). Expanding conceptual evidence-building with the science of learning: integrating evidence weights, alignment estimates and iterative updates for educational innovations. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10732-w

article_title: Differences in personalized learning practice and technology use in high- and low-performing learner-centered schools in the United States
citation: Dabae Lee, Yeol Huh, Chun-Yi Lin, Charles M. Reigeluth, Eunbae Lee. (2021). Differences in personalized learning practice and technology use in high- and low-performing learner-centered schools in the United States. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09937-y
title: Five essential features of personalized learning in learner-centered schools
description: The study organizes personalized learning practice in K-12 learner-centered schools around five features: "personalized learning plan, competency-based student progress, criterion-referenced assessment, project- or problem-based learning, and multi-year mentoring". These features served as the constructs compared between high- and low-performing learner-centered schools in the national survey of ELA teachers, operationalized in a survey instrument whose constructs and operational definitions are given in the article's appendix.
requirements: Schools must be identified as learner-centered for the feature comparison to apply, as in the national survey of ELA teachers in identified learner-centered schools
constraints: The features were compared against standardized test results as the performance criterion, under annual standardized testing pressure the article notes
target_learning_goals: personalized learning implementation across plans, progress, assessment, projects, and mentoring
examples: The national survey of ELA teachers measured each of the five features and compared high- and low-performing learner-centered schools on them
key_sources: Dabae Lee, Yeol Huh, Chun-Yi Lin, Charles M. Reigeluth, Eunbae Lee. (2021). Differences in personalized learning practice and technology use in high- and low-performing learner-centered schools in the United States. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09937-y

article_title: Dual empowerment in VR-based technical training: longitudinal evidence of developmental dynamics in learning outcomes and skill transfer
citation: Min Jou, Yungwei Hao. (2026). Dual empowerment in VR-based technical training: longitudinal evidence of developmental dynamics in learning outcomes and skill transfer. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10654-7
title: Five-stage dual-empowerment blended learning sequence alternating VR and physical empowerment
description: The instructional sequence is a staged progression in which "The instructional sequence followed a five-stage progression aligned with experiential and spiral learning principles", with each stage systematically integrating VR and physical empowerment. Stage 1 introduces concepts and safety; Stage 2 familiarizes basic flat-welding skills with real-time parameter display and short hands-on sessions; Stage 3 applies horizontal welding with seam inspection against VR metrics; Stage 4 adds high-difficulty vertical tasks under authentic constraints; Stage 5 reviews longitudinal skill charts and conducts final real-condition performance tests that operationalize the transfer criterion.
requirements: Task complexity increases across stages while psychological regulation is maintained through feedback continuity between VR and physical practice
constraints: Developed and evaluated for welding training in a semester-long vocational course; transferability to other skill-intensive domains is proposed by the authors but not tested in this study
target_learners: vocational students without prior welding certification in a semester-long welding course
target_learning_goals: progressive welding skill acquisition across flat, horizontal, and vertical butt-joint tasks, culminating in transfer validation under real welding conditions
examples: Stage 5 compared longitudinal simulation data with real-world performance to assess consistency, closing the feedback loop between LO and STR
key_sources: Min Jou, Yungwei Hao. (2026). Dual empowerment in VR-based technical training: longitudinal evidence of developmental dynamics in learning outcomes and skill transfer. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10654-7

article_title: Metacognition design framework to aid metacognitive skill development in university students supported by the virtual learning environment
citation: O'Neill, E. J., Fulton, C., Matthews, J., & Hensey, C. (2026). Metacognition design framework to aid metacognitive skill development in university students supported by the virtual learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10574-y
title: Five evidence-based metacognitive themes form the core of the framework, adapted from the EEF guidance report
description: The framework's core is five evidence-based metacognitive themes adapted from the Education Endowment Foundation guidance report (Quigley et al., 2018): "The EEF report detailed seven evidence-based recommendations to support the teaching of metacognitive skills in secondary-level education." The authors focused on five teaching-centered recommendations: explicit teaching of metacognitive strategies, modelling metacognitive thinking, setting the appropriate level of challenge, promoting metacognitive dialogue, and explicitly teaching management and organization of learning. Table 1 lists example learning approaches for each theme, such as structured reflection, chunking to avoid overloading cognitive processes, guided peer assessment, and formative feedback.
requirements: Approaches should be integrated with subject-specific instruction rather than taught as a separate entity
constraints: Themes were adapted from recommendations developed for secondary-level education and reviewed for university applicability
target_learning_goals: metacognitive strategy use
independent management of learning
examples: Modelling via think-aloud, gradual build in task complexity, guided/example questions for purposeful dialogue, checklists and quizzes
key_sources: O'Neill, E. J., Fulton, C., Matthews, J., & Hensey, C. (2026). Metacognition design framework to aid metacognitive skill development in university students supported by the virtual learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10574-y

article_title: The effects and interactions of rate of development, repetition, participation and room illumination on learning from a rear-projected film
citation: Research Abstracts. (1954). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=instructional+film+research+program
title: Fifteen produced film examples varying script, sound recording, lighting, camera speed, and photographer experience
description: As part of the billet analysis feasibility research, fifteen film examples were planned and produced to test recording approaches. They included "products of no-script and minimum script procedures", magnetic and single-system sound recording, lighting from simple to complex, five camera speeds, and pictures shot by individuals with differing photographic experience; film analysts reviewed the films to indicate their usefulness.
requirements: Film analysts reviewed the films to indicate their usefulness
target_learners: billet analysts and billet incumbents in naval training
target_learning_goals: recording and communicating job and equipment-use information visually
examples: Fifteen film examples were planned and produced, spanning script procedures, sound recording systems, lighting levels, five camera speeds, and photographers of differing experience.

article_title: ICT integration in the classroom: Challenging the potential of a school policy
citation: Tondeur, J., van Keer, H., van Braak, J., & Valcke, M. (2008). ICT integration in the classroom: Challenging the potential of a school policy. Computers & Education, 51, 212-223. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2007.05.003
title: Five areas of local ICT policy from a school improvement approach
description: The article organises local ICT school policy around five areas derived from the school improvement movement: an ICT policy plan with clear goals and strategies, leadership directing ICT integration, support and training for implementation, evaluation to monitor ICT use and guide planning, and between-school cooperation for disseminating ICT knowledge. The article states that "Table 1 distinguishes ﬁve key factors from the school improvement approach and links these concretely to school policies fostering ICT integration in the classroom." It uses this framework to structure both the principal interviews and the multilevel analysis of classroom ICT use.
requirements: Development of a local school policy guaranteeing conditions supporting continuous change processes, with clear goals and systematic strategies
constraints: The article notes this list of school factors cannot depict the complexity of school improvement
target_learning_goals: integration of ICT into teaching and learning practices
examples: Principals were interviewed about each of the five areas; 75% of schools developed partnerships with other schools to share an ICT coordinator

article_title: Factors influencing students’ perceived impact of learning and satisfaction in Computer Supported Collaborative Learning
citation: Pablo-César Muñoz-Carril, Nuria Hernández-Sellés, Eduardo-José Fuentes-Abeledo, Mercedes González-Sanmamed. (2021). Factors influencing students' perceived impact of learning and satisfaction in Computer Supported Collaborative Learning. Computers & Education, 174. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104310
title: Five-phase online collaborative learning experience with projects and case studies
description: The studied courses embedded "online collaborative working processes using project and case-study based methodologies" across five phases: pre-group identification of classmates, self-formed groups of 4 or 5 members via forums and Google Sheets, intra-group agreements on roles and communication tools, development of collaborative learning activities, and online self-assessment and peer-assessment of process and results. Teachers created virtual spaces, facilitated debates, gave feedback, and assessed group processes and products.
requirements: Virtual campus spaces, forums, and Google Sheets for group formation and communication
target_learners: master's students in four-month, 6-ECTS online courses
target_learning_goals: collaborative project and case-study learning
self- and co-evaluation of collaborative processes
examples: Phase 5 included online self-assessment and peer-assessment of process and results, plus a self-reflection of the learning process

article_title: Teacher agency and learner agency in teaching and learning a new school subject, Leaving Certificate Computer Science, in Ireland: Considerations for teacher education
citation: Scanlon, D & Connolly, C. (2021). Teacher agency and learner agency in teaching and learning a new school subject, Leaving Certificate Computer Science, in Ireland: Considerations for teacher education. Computers and Education, 174, 104291. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104291
title: Figurational sociology lens on teacher and learner agency as interdependent, fluctuating processes
description: The article uses figurational sociology to frame teacher agency and learner agency not as individual possessions but as processes emerging within figurations of interdependent relationships. It argues that achieving agency is 'a combination of the teacher and the students and the other interdependent relationships within their figurations, alongside contextual factors, and educational social processes'. This framework explains why agency fluctuates rather than being a stable product.
requirements: Analysis of agency must attend to interdependent relationships within figurations, not only individual teachers or students
constraints: Developed and illustrated in the context of a newly introduced Irish school subject, Leaving Certificate Computer Science
target_learners: Post-primary students studying Leaving Certificate Computer Science in Ireland
target_learning_goals: Understanding how teacher and learner agency develop in classroom figurations
key_sources: Scanlon, D & Connolly, C. (2021). Teacher agency and learner agency in teaching and learning a new school subject, Leaving Certificate Computer Science, in Ireland: Considerations for teacher education. Computers and Education, 174, 104291. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104291
