article_title: A Meta-Analysis of Instructional Management Model for Students' Creative Thinking Development: An Application of Propensity Score Matching
citation: Itsarangkul Na Ayutthaya, T., & Damrongpanit, S. (2022). A Meta-Analysis of Instructional Management Model for Students’ Creative Thinking Development: An Application of Propensity Score Matching. European Journal of Educational Research, 11(4), 2429-2444. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.11.4.2429
title: Taxonomy of five instructional management models for developing students' creative thinking
description: The article organizes 400 Thai studies on creative thinking development into five instructional management model groups: all-round creative thinking development (n=80), creative thinking skills stimulation (n=25), knowledge integration based on creative environment through technology media usage (n=68), self-knowledge construction with technology media (n=124), and creative learning activities and situations management (n=103). Each group bundles named instructional methods, e.g. the knowledge integration group includes "Science Technology Engineering and Math ematics Education (STEM Education)" and blended learning. The taxonomy structures the meta-analysis and the propensity score comparison of model effectiveness.
requirements: Studies must be experimental research with instructional management style as the primary variable and creative thinking as the dependent variable, reporting statistics sufficient for effect size calculation
constraints: Derived from graduate theses and research articles conducted in Thailand between 1971 and 2020, searched via ThaiLIS Digital Collection and university e-libraries
target_learners: primary and secondary school students in Thailand
target_learning_goals: creative thinking development
examples: Table 1 lists each model's instructional methods and frequencies, e.g. 45 art activities studies in the creative learning activities group and 42 programmed/online learning studies in the self-knowledge construction group
key_sources: Itsarangkul Na Ayutthaya, T., & Damrongpanit, S. (2022). A Meta-Analysis of Instructional Management Model for Students’ Creative Thinking Development: An Application of Propensity Score Matching. European Journal of Educational Research, 11(4), 2429-2444. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.11.4.2429

article_title: The Effects of Cooperative Learning on Mathematics Achievement in Turkey: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Turgut, S., & Gülşen Turgut, İ. (2018). The Effects of Cooperative Learning on Mathematics Achievement in Turkey: A Meta-Analysis Study. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 663-680. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11345a
title: Five essential elements define whether a group activity is cooperative learning
description: The article presents cooperative learning as small-group work in which students help each other's learning, and states that not every group activity qualifies: "An activity should include five main elements as positive interdependence, individual responsibility, supportive face-to-face communication, social skills and evaluation of group process in order to be cooperative." It then describes each element — positive interdependence created through task design, personal responsibility for one's own work, mutual support and encouragement, taught social skills such as leadership and communication, and evaluation of how well the group met its objectives and maintained relationships. The meta-analysis operationalizes cooperative learning through named techniques implementing this model.
requirements: Group members need to have acquired certain social skills to study together efficiently; the article says skills like leadership, communication, decision making and trust building should be taught to group members.
constraints: The meta-analysis covers studies done in Turkey between 2000 and 2017 comparing cooperative learning techniques with traditional teaching in mathematics; the article notes only Turkish studies were examined and more extended results could come from international studies.
target_learners: Elementary, middle school, high school and undergraduate mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement (mathematics and geometry domains)
examples: The synthesized studies implemented named techniques such as learning together, teams-games-tournaments, jigsaw, student teams achievement divisions and team-assisted individualization in experimental groups.
key_sources: Turgut, S., & Gülşen Turgut, İ. (2018). The Effects of Cooperative Learning on Mathematics Achievement in Turkey: A Meta-Analysis Study. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 663-680. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11345a

article_title: Evaluating the impact of simulation on patient outcomes in pediatric and neonatal critical care: a systematic review and critical appraisal of the evidence.
citation: Zanin A, Poletto E, Mencia S, Gawronski O, Jourdain G. (2026). Evaluating the impact of simulation on patient outcomes in pediatric and neonatal critical care: a systematic review and critical appraisal of the evidence. European Journal of Pediatrics 185(5):302. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00431-026-06925-3
title: Five-element model of influences determining simulation's clinical impact (SBR model)
description: To explain why simulation outcomes diverge across contexts, the review introduces a model asserting that success depends on "the alignment of five interconnected elements": (1) individual competence (technical/nontechnical skills); (2) team dynamics (communication and leadership); (3) institutional culture (psychological safety and administrative support); (4) physical resources (equipment and staffing availability); and (5) system-level integration (adherence to national or local protocols). The model explains why single-center studies, which can more easily align the five layers, often show more significant results than multicenter trials.
requirements: Future simulation-based research designs must account for the synergy between these five elements to bridge the gap between training and patient-level results
constraints: The model is introduced by the authors to illustrate contextual divergence; it is an interpretive framework, not a tested result
target_learners: healthcare providers and trainees in pediatric and neonatal intensive care
target_learning_goals: translating simulation-acquired competence into real-world clinical practice
examples: The review maps the model onto its research recommendations, arguing future studies should move beyond Level 1 and 2 outcomes
key_sources: Zanin A, Poletto E, Mencia S, Gawronski O, Jourdain G. (2026). Evaluating the impact of simulation on patient outcomes in pediatric and neonatal critical care: a systematic review and critical appraisal of the evidence. European Journal of Pediatrics 185(5):302. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00431-026-06925-3

article_title: Characterization of the learning environment for teaching pharmaceutical care: a scoping review.
citation: Ribeiro MAL, Hohenfeld DWA, Tavares TMA, Araújo-Neto FC, Mesquita AR, Brito GC, Lyra Jr DP. (2026). Characterization of the learning environment for teaching pharmaceutical care: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08876-7
title: Five-component conceptualization of learning environments (personal, social, organizational, physical, virtual)
description: The review adopts a concept of learning environment, following Gruppen et al. (2018), that "Refers to experiences and personal perceptions, social interactions, culture, and organizational practice, and the physical and virtual settings in which learning occurs". It decomposes environments into five components: personal (student perceptions, growth, professional identity), social (relationships with faculty, administration and patients), organizational (policies, accreditation rules, curriculum resources, workload), physical (campuses, hospitals, clinics, community settings), and virtual (curriculum management tools, digital assistants, learning forums). The review uses this framework to classify the components identified in each included study (Table 4).
requirements: Studies must describe the environment in terms of the five components for classification under this framework
constraints: The review notes the absence of consensus on the definition of learning environment in the healthcare field limits multicenter research
target_learners: Pharmacy students in undergraduate and professional programs
target_learning_goals: Patient-centered pharmaceutical care competencies
examples: Table 4 classifies each included study's components; for example, Brown & Vosper (2013) was classified as spanning Personal, Social, Organizational, Physical, and Virtual components
key_sources: Ribeiro MAL, Hohenfeld DWA, Tavares TMA, Araújo-Neto FC, Mesquita AR, Brito GC, Lyra Jr DP. (2026). Characterization of the learning environment for teaching pharmaceutical care: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08876-7

article_title: Exploring the Concept of Nurses' Healthcare Policy Competence: A Systematic Review and Qualitative Meta-Synthesis.
citation: Han, Nam Kyung, Kim, Jong Gun. (2026). Exploring the Concept of Nurses' Healthcare Policy Competence: A Systematic Review and Qualitative Meta‐Synthesis. Journal of Nursing Management. https://doi.org/10.1155/jonm/9182331
title: Five-factor conceptual framework of nurses' healthcare policy competence
description: The article synthesizes nurses' healthcare policy competence into an organizing framework of five factors: "intrinsic motivation, healthcare expertise, policy development, political skills, and policy intervention." Each factor is elaborated into themes and subthemes derived by meta-ethnographic synthesis of qualitative studies, and the authors state the framework "provides a conceptual framework for nurses' competence in healthcare policy and for developing political or policy education or programs to strengthen this competence."
requirements: Derived through meta-ethnographic synthesis of qualitative studies of nurses with healthcare policy intervention or political activism experience
constraints: Concept synthesized from 27 qualitative studies published in English up to December 31, 2023
target_learning_goals: healthcare policy competence
political competence for policy intervention
key_sources: Han, Nam Kyung, Kim, Jong Gun. (2026). Exploring the Concept of Nurses' Healthcare Policy Competence: A Systematic Review and Qualitative Meta‐Synthesis. Journal of Nursing Management. https://doi.org/10.1155/jonm/9182331

article_title: Validation status of definitive airway management simulators: a systematic review.
citation: McCarthy Roisin, Maher Liam, O'Dea Angela. (2026). Validation status of definitive airway management simulators: a systematic review. BJA: British Journal of Anaesthesia. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bja.2026.01.027
title: Five-domain validity framework for simulator evaluation (face, content, construct, concurrent, predictive)
description: The review organises simulator validation evidence using five validity domains defined from Van Nortwick and McDougall: face validity (realism to non-experts), content validity (expert-rated teaching effectiveness), construct validity (differentiating expertise levels), concurrent validity (correlation with a gold standard such as human anatomy), and predictive validity ("the extent to which performance on the simulator predicts future performance in real clinical settings"). Each domain carries specified assessment methods, e.g. I-CVI ≥0.80 for content and task time, errors, or OSATS scores for construct validity. The review uses this framework to categorise and rate all 29 simulators.
requirements: Studies must report empirical data on at least one validity domain to be included under this framework
constraints: Predictive validity for front-of-neck access procedures cannot be ethically or practically evaluated in real clinical settings, per the review
target_learning_goals: tracheal intubation
fibreoptic intubation
front-of-neck access procedures
examples: The review assigned each simulator a Level of Evidence (OCEBM-adapted, 1–4) and a Level of Recommendation (1 strongest to 4 weakest) based on validity evidence across these domains
key_sources: McCarthy Roisin, Maher Liam, O'Dea Angela. (2026). Validation status of definitive airway management simulators: a systematic review. BJA: British Journal of Anaesthesia. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bja.2026.01.027

article_title: Use of simulation for teaching biomedical sciences to undergraduate medical students- a scoping review.
citation: Owolabi Joshua O., Gardner Katresa, Agboola Rasheed, Yesudas Rekha R., Shaw Jennifer H. (2025). Use of simulation for teaching biomedical sciences to undergraduate medical students- a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07819-y
title: Five thematic areas of simulation use in biomedical science medical education
description: The review organizes its findings into five key thematic areas: "(1) simulation's role in skill acquisition, (2) simulation and technology-enhanced anatomy and physiology education, (3) virtual and augmented reality in medical training, (4) problem-based learning (PBL) and competency development, and (5) the integration of simulation into medical curricula". This taxonomy maps how simulation modalities (standardized patients, virtual labs, VR/AR, high-fidelity manikins) serve different educational purposes across biomedical disciplines.
requirements: Simulation methodologies categorized by fidelity, technology level, and purpose
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in accredited medical schools globally
target_learning_goals: biomedical sciences knowledge
clinical skills
professional attitudes
key_sources: Owolabi Joshua O., Gardner Katresa, Agboola Rasheed, Yesudas Rekha R., Shaw Jennifer H. (2025). Use of simulation for teaching biomedical sciences to undergraduate medical students- a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07819-y

article_title: AI in the Health Sector: Systematic Review of Key Skills for Future Health Professionals.
citation: Gazquez-Garcia J, Sánchez-Bocanegra CL, Sevillano JL. (2025). AI in the Health Sector: Systematic Review of Key Skills for Future Health Professionals. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/58161
title: Five-domain competency framework for AI use by health professionals
description: The review proposes a framework of five key competency areas deemed essential for integrating AI into clinical practice: "AI fundamentals, ethical and legal considerations, data analysis and management, communication and teamwork, and the evaluation of AI tools". Domains were derived by qualitative synthesis, with categories developed iteratively by grouping competencies that were conceptually aligned and ranked by frequency of appearance across the 7 included studies. Table S3 outlines competencies for each skill to guide educational programs and ongoing training.
requirements: Competencies should be considered only a first proposal, modifiable depending on the training program profile, technological developments, and evaluation of academic results
constraints: Derived from only 7 included studies with heterogeneous designs; no meta-analysis was performed due to heterogeneity
target_learning_goals: effective and safe use of AI technologies in clinical practice
key_sources: Gazquez-Garcia J, Sánchez-Bocanegra CL, Sevillano JL. (2025). AI in the Health Sector: Systematic Review of Key Skills for Future Health Professionals. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/58161

article_title: Online-Based and Technology-Assisted Psychiatric Education for Trainees: Scoping Review.
citation: Mohd Amiruddin Mohd Kassim, Sidi Muhammad Yusoff Azli Shah, Jane Tze Yn Lim, Tuti Iryani Mohd Daud. (2025). Online-Based and Technology-Assisted Psychiatric Education for Trainees: Scoping Review. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/64773
title: Five-method taxonomy of online-based and technology-assisted psychiatric education for trainees
description: The review organizes the literature on online-based and technology-assisted psychiatric education into five methods: videoconference, online modules/e-learning, virtual patients, software/applications, and social media. These methods were applied to objectives including "teaching theory knowledge, skills training, psychotherapy supervision, and information retrieval." The taxonomy is supported by a three-phase trend analysis (prior to 2015, 2015-2019, and 2020 onward) of 82 included articles.
requirements: Studies must include psychiatric trainees or residents and evaluate outcomes related to knowledge, skills, confidence, preference, or participant feedback
constraints: Based on English-language studies or those with English translations; review articles and purely descriptive accounts were excluded
target_learning_goals: psychiatric theory knowledge
clinical skills training
psychotherapy supervision
information retrieval
key_sources: Mohd Amiruddin Mohd Kassim, Sidi Muhammad Yusoff Azli Shah, Jane Tze Yn Lim, Tuti Iryani Mohd Daud. (2025). Online-Based and Technology-Assisted Psychiatric Education for Trainees: Scoping Review. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/64773

article_title: Self-directed learning and the student learning experience in undergraduate clinical science programs: a scoping review.
citation: Ashleigh Finn, Caitlin Fitzgibbon, Natalie Fonda, Cameron M Gosling. (2025). Self-directed learning and the student learning experience in undergraduate clinical science programs: a scoping review. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-024-10383-7
title: Five-factor framework for improving the student learning experience in self-directed learning
description: The review identifies five key factors that improve the student learning experience in undergraduate clinical science programs that utilise self-directed learning: "curricular elements; educator influence; impact of peers, environment; and clinical placement experiences". This framework organises the findings of 19 included studies and provides a structure for educators to consider when designing curricula that incorporate self-directed learning.
requirements: The review focuses on undergraduate clinical science programs that utilise self-directed learning
constraints: The majority of included literature sampled undergraduate medical students, which may affect generalisability to other clinical science disciplines
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning
lifelong learning
key_sources: Ashleigh Finn, Caitlin Fitzgibbon, Natalie Fonda, Cameron M Gosling. (2025). Self-directed learning and the student learning experience in undergraduate clinical science programs: a scoping review. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-024-10383-7

article_title: A systematic review identifying effective teaching methods and their combinations for increasing empathy in physicians: pairwise and network meta-analysis.
citation: Ngo Hazel, Sokolovic Nina, Hu Julia, Jenkins Jennifer. (2025). A systematic review identifying effective teaching methods and their combinations for increasing empathy in physicians: pairwise and network meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07917-x
title: Five teaching methods for empathy interventions: didactic, rehearsal, reflection, observation, and feedback
description: The article organizes behavioural empathy interventions around five teaching methods used singly or in combination: "didactic (lecture and reading and/or written information), rehearsal (practicing the empathy skill and/or role-playing as the patient), reflection (reflecting by oneself or in discussion with others), observation (watching enactments pertaining to the skill and/or exposure to a patient's perspective), and feedback (individualized from peer or facilitator)". Each method is mapped to a type of learning (surface, deep, or both) and a theoretical basis, such as cognitive, experiential, transformative, and social learning theories. The network meta-analysis uses combinations of these five methods as its treatment nodes.
requirements: Interventions must be classifiable into combinations of the five teaching methods for the network meta-analysis treatment nodes
constraints: Combinations represented by a single study were dropped from the network analysis to reduce heterogeneity
target_learning_goals: empathy skills
patient-centered communication
examples: Table 1 maps each method to its theoretical basis, e.g. rehearsal to experiential learning theories and observation to social learning theory
key_sources: Ngo Hazel, Sokolovic Nina, Hu Julia, Jenkins Jennifer. (2025). A systematic review identifying effective teaching methods and their combinations for increasing empathy in physicians: pairwise and network meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07917-x

article_title: Structured viva validity, reliability, and acceptability as an assessment tool in health professions education: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Abuzied Abdelhamid Ibrahim Hassan, Nabag Wisal Omer Mohamed. (2023). Structured viva validity, reliability, and acceptability as an assessment tool in health professions education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04524-6
title: Five criteria of a good assessment tool in medical education: validity, reliability, acceptability, feasibility, and educational impact
description: The review adopts a framework in which the usefulness of an assessment method in medical education is judged against five elements. As the article states, "validity, reliability and acceptability are considered parts of the criteria used for determining the usefulness of a particular method of assessment, together with the feasibility and educational impact those five elements are the criteria of good assessment tool." The review applies this framework by evaluating structured viva on the first three criteria against agreed medical education standards.
requirements: Assessment tools should be evaluated against all five criteria to determine their usefulness in medical education
constraints: This review evaluates only validity, reliability, and acceptability; feasibility and educational impact are named but not systematically reviewed
target_learners: Health professions education learners and faculty
target_learning_goals: Judging the quality and usefulness of assessment methods
examples: The review structures its Results and Discussion sections around the validity, reliability, and acceptability of structured viva
key_sources: Abuzied Abdelhamid Ibrahim Hassan, Nabag Wisal Omer Mohamed. (2023). Structured viva validity, reliability, and acceptability as an assessment tool in health professions education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04524-6

article_title: Validity Evidence for Procedure-specific Competence Assessment Tools in Orthopaedic Surgery: A Scoping Review.
citation: Li Yibo, Chan Robert, Menon Matthew R.G., Ryan Joanna F., Mador Brett, Campbell Sandra M., Turner Simon R. (2024). Validity Evidence for Procedure-specific Competence Assessment Tools in Orthopaedic Surgery: A Scoping Review. JAAOS Global Research & Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5435/JAAOSGlobal-D-23-00065
title: Five-domain validity evidence framework for appraising surgical assessment tools
description: The review applies a five-domain validity framework, based on Messick's unitary view of validity and operationalized by Ghaderi et al, in which each assessment tool is scored on content, response process, internal structure, relation to other variables, and consequences, with a maximum score of 15. Two independent reviewers scored each of the 24 tools on these domains, with disagreements resolved by consensus. The framework is presented as having "good interrater reliability" when used in prior surgical specialties' reviews.
requirements: Two independent reviewers scoring each tool, with disagreements resolved by consensus decision
constraints: Scores are appraisals of published validity evidence, capped by the quality of the underlying studies
target_learning_goals: assessment of procedural technical competence in surgery
examples: Each of the 24 tools received domain scores in Table 2, e.g., the Shoulder Objective Practical Assessment Tool scored 3,1,2,2,1 for a total of 9 of 15
key_sources: Li Yibo, Chan Robert, Menon Matthew R.G., Ryan Joanna F., Mador Brett, Campbell Sandra M., Turner Simon R. (2024). Validity Evidence for Procedure-specific Competence Assessment Tools in Orthopaedic Surgery: A Scoping Review. JAAOS Global Research & Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5435/JAAOSGlobal-D-23-00065

article_title: Simulation-Based Education in Trauma Management: A Scoping Review.
citation: Larraga-García, B., Quintana-Díaz, M., & Gutiérrez, Á. (2022). Simulation-Based Education in Trauma Management: A Scoping Review. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 19(20). https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph192013546
title: Fidelity-based classification of clinical simulators (low, medium, high)
description: The review organizes clinical simulators by fidelity, defined as "the simulated model's relation to its closeness to reality being the main classification". Low-fidelity simulators are anatomical representations for simple tasks and basic motor skills; medium-fidelity simulators integrate low-complexity software to manipulate physiological variables for decision-making assessment; high-fidelity simulators are life-size mannequins with mechanical devices and computer technology for advanced techniques and critical situations. The review uses this taxonomy to characterize the simulation methods of the included trauma training studies.
requirements: Simulation methods should be matched to the skills to be trained, as the review states one method can be better than another depending on the skills targeted
constraints: The review reports that, per cited systematic reviews and a randomized trial, high-fidelity simulators show no important long-term advantage over low-fidelity ones for knowledge and skill improvement
target_learning_goals: trauma management technical skills
non-technical skills such as communication, leadership and decision making
examples: The review classified the 35 included studies' simulation methods using this fidelity framework, finding high-fidelity mannequins in 51.4% of courses
key_sources: Larraga-García, B., Quintana-Díaz, M., & Gutiérrez, Á. (2022). Simulation-Based Education in Trauma Management: A Scoping Review. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 19(20). https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph192013546

article_title: Physical examination in undergraduate medical education in the field of general practice - a scoping review.
citation: Moßhammer D, Graf J, Joos S, Hertkorn R. (2017). Physical examination in undergraduate medical education in the field of general practice – a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1074-1
title: Five-category taxonomy of physical examination teaching and research in undergraduate medical education
description: The scoping review developed a content categorization of 117 articles using qualitative content analysis following Mayring. Articles were matched into five categories: "teaching methods" (CAT I), "teaching quality" (CAT II), "performance evaluation and assessment formats" (CAT III), "student views" (CAT IV) and "patient/ standardized patient perspective" (CAT V). Categories were derived inductively from the text material through an iterative six-step process, with inter-rater reliability of 0.88 (n = 103). The taxonomy represents the possible dimensions of assessment for physical examination education research.
requirements: Articles must concern undergraduate medical education with focus on general practice physical examination
constraints: Every article was assigned to only one category by main focus, though many articles could have been allocated to more than one category
target_learning_goals: physical examination skills
key_sources: Moßhammer D, Graf J, Joos S, Hertkorn R. (2017). Physical examination in undergraduate medical education in the field of general practice – a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1074-1

article_title: Blended learning models for introductory programming courses: A systematic review.
citation: Ali Alammary. (2019). Blended learning models for introductory programming courses: A systematic review. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0221765
title: Five blended learning components classified by interaction type
description: The review draws on a prior classification of blended learning building blocks: "Alammary, Carbone [28] identified five different blended learning components. Two of them are face-to-face, while the other three are online components." The components are face-to-face instructor-led, face-to-face collaboration, online instructor-led, online collaboration, and online self-paced, each classified by the type of interaction it supports and each described with its pedagogical advantages.
requirements: Instructors mix components thoughtfully, using each method for what it does best
constraints: Component classification is grounded in constructivist learning theory as described in the review
target_learning_goals: flexible and interactive learning across delivery modes
key_sources: Ali Alammary. (2019). Blended learning models for introductory programming courses: A systematic review. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0221765

article_title: Animation Model to Conceptualize ATP Generation: A Mitochondrial Oxidative Phosphorylation
citation: Jena, A. K. (2015). Animation model to conceptualize ATP generation: A study of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. European Journal of Science and Mathematics Education, 3(1), 61-76. https://scholar.google.com
title: Five-type taxonomy of misconceptions in the chemiosmotic hypothesis for ATP synthesis
description: The article organizes students' wrong responses on the OPCT into five types: "1) preconceptual notion 2) nonscientific beliefs 3) conceptual misunderstandings; 4) vernacular misconceptions; and 5) factual misconceptions". Preconceived notions (items 1, 5, 8, 10, 14) were acquired during everyday experience and memorized without confirming their reality, while conceptual misunderstandings (items 3, 6, 7, 9, 12, 13, 15) arose from lack of understanding during previous learning. The article reports conceptual misunderstanding was higher than the other types on the test.
requirements: A misconception test with items classified by type, evaluated to identify the levels and types of misconceptions of students
constraints: Taxonomy was derived from responses of sixty undergraduate students on one fifteen-item test in one topic area
target_learning_goals: diagnosing and classifying misconceptions about ATP generation and oxidative phosphorylation
examples: Item 1's solute misconception was described as the bigger one, negatively influencing understanding of other chemiosmosis concepts
key_sources: Jena, A. K. (2015). Animation model to conceptualize ATP generation: A study of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. European Journal of Science and Mathematics Education, 3(1), 61-76. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1107841

article_title: Exploration of the Factors That Support Learning: Web-Based Activity and Testing Systems in Community College Algebra [Contributed Report]
citation: Shandy Hauk, Bryan Matlen, Larry Thomas. (2017). Exploration of the Factors that Support Learning: Web-based Activity and Testing Systems in Community College Algebra. 20th Annual Conference on Research in Undergraduate Mathematics Education. https://sigmaa.maa.org/rume
title: Five-component framework for fidelity of implementation: Diagnostic, Procedural, Educative, Pedagogical, and Student Engagement
description: Drawing on Century and Cassata's summary of research, the article presents "five components to consider in fidelity of implementation: Diagnostic, Procedural, Educative, Pedagogical, and Student Engagement". Diagnostic components say what the "it" being implemented is; structural-procedural components tell the instructor what to do; structural-educative components state what users need to know; interaction-pedagogical components capture expected instructor actions and interactions; interaction-engagement components delineate expected student actions. The framework is operationalized through a rubric used as the guide for collecting and reporting implementation data.
requirements: A rubric articulating criteria and quality levels from low to high for each component, with measurable attributes per component
constraints: As Munter and colleagues point out, there is no agreement on how to assess fidelity of implementation; the component-based approach reflects a growing consensus rather than a settled standard
target_learners: community college instructors implementing a digital learning platform
target_learning_goals: faithful and productive implementation of a web-based learning intervention
examples: Table 6 gives rubric descriptors for the structural-educative component, rating instructors' math content proficiency, TPCK integration, and knowledge of the intervention's requirements at high, moderate, and low fidelity levels.
key_sources: Shandy Hauk, Bryan Matlen, Larry Thomas. (2017). Exploration of the Factors that Support Learning: Web-based Activity and Testing Systems in Community College Algebra. 20th Annual Conference on Research in Undergraduate Mathematics Education. https://sigmaa.maa.org/rume

article_title: Exploration of the Factors That Support Learning: Web-Based Activity and Testing Systems in Community College Algebra [Contributed Report]
citation: Shandy Hauk, Bryan Matlen, Larry Thomas. (2017). Exploration of the Factors that Support Learning: Web-based Activity and Testing Systems in Community College Algebra. 20th Annual Conference on Research in Undergraduate Mathematics Education. https://sigmaa.maa.org/rume
title: Fidelity-of-implementation rubric scoring system yielding a specific fidelity index for statistical modeling
description: The research team developed a rubric assigning numbers to fidelity levels (e.g., 3 for high, 2 for moderate, 1 for low, or weighted items). "The general score for the intervention will be the total number of points assigned in completing the rubric as a ratio of the total possible, across all instructors." Per-row scores for each instructor feed a "specific fidelity index" (Hulleman & Cordray, 2009), totaled by item, then component, then all components, for use in modeling the intervention's impact.
requirements: Rubric levels must be assigned numeric values, and component scores totaled from item scores to form an overall implementation index
target_learners: community college instructors implementing a WATS
target_learning_goals: measuring alignment between developer expectations and classroom enactment
examples: The rubric also aims to discover where productive adaptations by instructors may boost student achievement beyond implementations faithful to the developers' view.
key_sources: Shandy Hauk, Bryan Matlen, Larry Thomas. (2017). Exploration of the Factors that Support Learning: Web-based Activity and Testing Systems in Community College Algebra. 20th Annual Conference on Research in Undergraduate Mathematics Education. https://sigmaa.maa.org/rume

article_title: Effect of Field Trip on Students' Academic Performance in Basic Technology in Ilorin Metropolis, Nigeria
citation: Amosa, A. G. A., Ogunlade, O. O., & Atobatele, A. S. (2013). Effect of Field Trip on Students' Academic Performance in Basic Technology in Ilorin Metropolis, Nigeria. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Technology, 3(2). https://www.mojet.net
title: Field trip as an instructional strategy for Basic Technology practical skills
description: A field trip is defined in the article as "a group excursion away from the normal education environment for firsthand experience of an historic site or place of special interest". It is a planned study trip outside the classroom to obtain direct experience from a natural setting, letting learners experience theory in practice. In this study it was the treatment for the experimental group learning practical skills in Basic Technology, contrasted with expository teaching.
requirements: Planned by the teacher to benefit the student learning process
Used where schools lack basic equipment, via industrial visitations through community resources
target_learners: upper basic school students in Ilorin, Kwara State, Nigeria
target_learning_goals: practical skills in Basic Technology
examples: The experimental group received instruction via field trip while the control group was taught using the expository method, over weeks three to five with pre-test in week one and post-test in week six.

article_title: Teaching Vocabulary with Graphic Novels
citation: Ahmet Başal, Talat Aytan & İbrahim Demir. (2016). Teaching Vocabulary with Graphic Novels. English Language Teaching, 9(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n9p95
title: Figurative-idioms-embedded graphic novel teaching material
description: A teaching artifact built for the experimental group: forty figurative idioms listed by Grant (2007) from MICASE were used in a script that "was converted to a graphic novel with the use of computer software (www.storyboardthat.com)". Each week a required part of the novel including ten idioms was read in class, students guessed meanings, and the teacher checked meanings and gave extra example sentences.
requirements: A script embedding the target idioms and conversion software to produce the graphic novel
Weekly in-class reading with teacher-checked meanings and extra example sentences
constraints: The scenario was written by the lead researcher and converted by software, so the quality of the scenario and graphics may have affected results
target_learners: first-year English Language Teaching department students
target_learning_goals: figurative idiom knowledge
vocabulary learning
examples: Sample scenario pages and graphic-novel sections are reproduced in Appendices B and C

article_title: Teaching Problem-Solving Competency in Business Studies at Secondary School Level
citation: Meintjes A, Henrico A & Kroon J. (2015). Teaching problem-solving competency in Business Studies at secondary school level. South African Journal of Education, 35(3), Art. #1102. https://doi.org/10.15700/saje.v35n3a1102
title: Five-step problem-solving process conceptualisation (recognise, define/analyse, generate, choose, implement)
description: The article conceptualises problem-solving as a five-step process learners execute: "Step 1: Recognise the problem", Step 2 define and analyse the problem, Step 3 generate possible solutions without initially evaluating feasibility, Step 4 choose the best possible solution, and Step 5 implement the chosen solution. The study divided this into problem recognition (step 1) and problem-solving (steps 2-5), treating both as higher order cognitive abilities, and structured its test questions and assessment rubric around these steps.
requirements: Teaching should focus on the steps being executed by learners, with a focused problem statement needed for proper research of the problem
constraints: The article treats problem recognition and problem-solving as higher order cognitive abilities expecting higher levels of thinking than mere understanding or application of knowledge
target_learners: Grade 11 secondary school Business Studies learners
target_learning_goals: problem recognition
problem-solving as an entrepreneurial competency
examples: Test questions Q1-Q5 asked learners to recognise and identify the problem, define it, generate solutions, choose the best option, and describe implementation

article_title: Findings from a Multi-Year Scale-up Effectiveness Trial of Everyday Mathematics
citation: Vaden-Kiernan, M., Borman, G., Caverly, S., Bell, N., Ruiz de Castilla, V., Sullivan, K., & Rodriguez, D. (2015). Findings from a Multi-Year Scale-Up Effectiveness Trial of Everyday Mathematics. SREE Spring 2015 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: Fidelity of implementation as a latent construct with four components
description: The study conceptualizes implementation fidelity as a latent construct underlying four separate components: "dosage, adherence, quality of delivery, and student responsiveness." Fidelity was measured through classroom observations, interviews, and surveys with teachers and other key staff such as curriculum trainers. The framework structures the study's implementation analysis and its moderator analyses, in which class-level fidelity of implementation was examined as a potential moderator of EM's effects on math achievement.
requirements: Multiple data sources (classroom observations, interviews, and surveys with teachers and key staff) to capture the four components
constraints: In this trial, fidelity was low: only 55% of treatment teachers in year one and 44% in year two implemented the unique and essential components
target_learners: elementary school students in treatment and control classrooms
target_learning_goals: faithful delivery of curriculum-unique and essential instructional components in mathematics
examples: The implementation study classified teachers into a Unique Class when they showed evidence of implementing both the unique and essential components of EM.

title: FILA table (Facts, Ideas, Learning Issues, Action) used to scaffold PBL problem work
description: The FILA table is a four-column scaffold introduced to PBL-group students to structure their work on problems. The article describes preparing "the \"FILA\" table–a four-column table (Facts, Ideas, Learning Issues, Action)" as part of exposing participants to the PBL approach, alongside guidance on how to deal with problems and organize information for solving them. It functioned as one component of the 14-week experimental treatment in an undergraduate communication course.
requirements: Students work on given problems and organize information using the four columns: Facts, Ideas, Learning Issues, Action
constraints: Used here with first-year undergraduate management students in an Effective Communication subject over one semester

examples: PBL-group participants were trained in preparing the FILA table and organizing information before the post-test picture task

article_title: Music Activities as a Meaningful Context for Teaching Elementary Students Mathematics: A Quasi-Experiment Time Series Design with Random Assigned Control Group
citation: Song A. An, and Daniel A. Tillman. (2015). Music activities as a meaningful context for teaching elementary students mathematics: a quasi-experiment time series design with random assigned control group. European Journal of Science and Mathematics Education, 3(1), 45-60. https://ejsme.com
title: Five-phase lesson structure shifting instructional focus from music to mathematics
description: Each integrated lesson followed a five-phase model in which the instructional focus gradually shifted from music to mathematics. In phase one music was the focus; phases two through four progressively balanced and then privileged mathematics, and in phase five "music was not included and teachers focused only on mathematics topics". The article uses this structure to scaffold transfer from musical experiences to abstract mathematical content across the 14 intervention lessons.
requirements: Teachers need preparation in music-mathematics integrated instruction; the music group teacher received 10 hours of professional development seminars before the intervention
constraints: The model was implemented by one trained teacher with prior experience of 15 pilot integrated lessons, which the authors note may not be accessible to other teachers
target_learning_goals: mathematics content achievement
mathematics process ability (model, strategy, application)
examples: Lessons paired math content areas (number operation, data analysis, probability, algebra, measurement, geometry) with music foci such as melody, rhythm, chords, intervals, and instrument design (Table 2)

article_title: Examining the Effect of Teacher Guidance on Collaborative Argumentation in Middle Level Classrooms
citation: Hsu, P.-S., Van Dyke, M., & Chen, Y. (2015). Examining the effect of teacher guidance on collaborative argumentation in middle level classrooms. RMLE Online, 38(9). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Examining+the+Effect+of+Teacher+Guidance+on+Collaborative+Argumentation+in+Middle+Level+Classrooms
title: Five-feature framework for assessing the quality of verbal collaborative argumentation
description: Drawing on Chinn and Anderson's (1998) argumentation framework, the researchers assessed quality via argumentation diagrams whose core units are claim, datum, and warrant. They "identified the quality of the collaborative argumentation based on a number of features: size, breadth, depth, types of rhetorical moves, and co-construction of argumentation." Each feature has quantitative measures: size as node count, breadth as positions and lines of argumentation, depth as argumentations with five or fewer nodes, rhetorical moves as reasons, evidence, counterarguments, and rebuttals, and co-construction as argumentations built by two or more students.
requirements: Recording and transcription of verbal argumentation
Construction of argumentation diagrams with interrater consensus between two researchers
constraints: In this study only the depth feature was analyzed between groups; the other features were measured but not compared
target_learning_goals: collaborative argumentation quality assessment
examples: Class 1 (intervention) diagrams showed 42 nodes and nine lines of argumentation for four positions, with eight lines constructed collaboratively

article_title: The Effect of Simulation-Based Learning on Prospective Teachers' Inference Skills in Teaching Probability
citation: Timur Koparan, Gül Kaleli Yılmaz. (2015). The Effect of Simulation-based Learning on Prospective Teachers’ Inference Skills in Teaching Probability. Universal Journal of Educational Research 3(11). https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2015.031101
title: Five-step simulation-based learning model for teaching probability (problem, prediction, model, test, evaluation)
description: The article builds its learning environment on Cobb's 3R logic (randomize-repeat-reject), extended by combining it with a simulation-based learning approach into "a 5 -step simulation -based learning model was created". The stages are: Problem (introducing real-life problems), Prediction (taking estimations for the solution), Model (creating a simulation consisting of reasonable random processes), Test (producing data from the created model), and Evaluation (querying the distribution of the data and reaching a conclusion to generalization). The model structured the four-week TinkerPlots activities in the experimental group.
requirements: Activities require dynamic statistical software such as TinkerPlots so learners can build simulation models and change the number of trials
constraints: Activities in the paper are about a finite sample space and discrete probability calculations; the study does not include all activities relating to probability theory
target_learners: prospective mathematics teachers in statistics/probability courses
target_learning_goals: inference and prediction skills in experimental probability
understanding of randomness and variability
examples: The experimental group created coin-flipping simulation models in TinkerPlots, produced data for 20, 50 and 100 trials, and evaluated tables and graphics against their predictions
key_sources: Timur Koparan, Gül Kaleli Yılmaz. (2015). The Effect of Simulation-based Learning on Prospective Teachers’ Inference Skills in Teaching Probability. Universal Journal of Educational Research 3(11). https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2015.031101

article_title: Developing a Fidelity Measure of Early Intervention Programs for Children with Neuromotor Disorders
citation: Mihee An, Jayden Nord, Natalie A Koziol, Stacey C Dusing, Audrey E Kane, Michele A Lobo, Sarah W McCoy, Regina T Harbourne. (2020). Developing a fidelity measure of early intervention programs for children with neuromotor disorders. Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology. https://doi.org/10.1111/dmcn.14702
title: Five-dimensional construct of intervention fidelity
description: The article frames intervention fidelity as "a multidimensional construct with five dimensions: adherence, dosage, quality of intervention delivery, participant responsiveness, and program differentiation". Adherence is accurate delivery of key components; dosage is the amount delivered in time, frequency, or rate; quality concerns the manner of implementation; responsiveness is participant engagement; and program differentiation indicates whether the target intervention can be distinguished from others. The START-Play measure operationalizes all five dimensions, which the authors say improves accurate presentation, implementation, examination, and replicability of interventions.
requirements: Adequate measurement and reporting across all five dimensions to ensure accurate presentation, implementation, and examination of the target intervention
constraints: Studies using fidelity measurement in rehabilitation generally focus on only adherence and not the other dimensions
target_learners: infants with neuromotor disorders in early intervention
target_learning_goals: faithful and accurate implementation of a designed intervention
identifying active ingredients of an intervention
examples: The START-Play trial coded 103 videos on all five dimensions, comparing the START-Play and uEI groups
key_sources: Mihee An, Jayden Nord, Natalie A Koziol, Stacey C Dusing, Audrey E Kane, Michele A Lobo, Sarah W McCoy, Regina T Harbourne. (2020). article_title: On the Effectiveness of Team Teaching in Promoting Learners' Grammatical Proficiency
citation: Mohammad Aliakbari and Ali Mansouri Nejad. (2013). On the Effectiveness of Team Teaching in Promoting Learners' Grammatical Proficiency. Canadian Journal of Education / Revue canadienne de l'éducation 36:3. https://www.cje-rce.ca
title: Five models for implementing co-teaching, varying in how students and content are divided
description: Citing Friend, Reising, and Cook (1993), the article presents five co-teaching models that all use two teachers but differ in arrangement: "One teaches, one observes", parallel teaching (students divided into two groups taught simultaneously and separately), station teaching (content and students divided, each teacher taking a small part), alternative teaching (one instructor with the larger group, the other with a smaller group needing specialized attention), and team teaching, described as "one brain in two bodies", in which both teachers give instruction mutually and simultaneously. The taxonomy frames the study's model choice.
requirements: Successful execution rests on exploiting a suitable model; selection depends on factors such as district, classroom situation, and amount of cooperation
constraints: The article notes team teaching "to some extent depends on teachers' styles"
target_learning_goals: grammar instruction
classroom instruction across content areas
examples: The study adopted team teaching because, unlike other models, it does not necessitate dividing students and shares autonomy between both teachers
key_sources: Mohammad Aliakbari and Ali Mansouri Nejad. (2013). On the Effectiveness of Team Teaching in Promoting Learners' Grammatical Proficiency. Canadian Journal of Education / Revue canadienne de l'éducation 36:3. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1057969

article_title: The Adoption of Tablet and E-Textbooks: First Grade Core Curriculum and School Administration Attitude
citation: Ibtesam Al-Mashaqbeh and Muneera Al Shurman. (2015). The Adoption of Tablet and e-Textbooks: first grade core curriculum and school administration attitude. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.21. http://www.iiste.org
title: E-textbook with interactive components loaded on first-grade students' tablets
description: A curriculum package designed by a software company in communication with teachers, downloaded onto each student's tablet, covering science, math, English and Arabic. It included e-textbooks, activities, games, and worksheets, with a table of content, worksheets, table of figures, storage area, search engine, games, and group project area. The article also describes e-textbook components such as "Interactive galleries: students can see collection of interactive photos, use highlighting with different colors, and write notes", study cards, sharing, and interactive textbooks.
requirements: Teachers were trained by the software company to use the items in a suitable way, and students used the tablets under teacher supervision
constraints: The article states tablets cannot be considered a replacement of the traditional teaching method
target_learners: first grade students in a private elementary school
target_learning_goals: achievement in core curriculum subjects (science, math, English, Arabic)
examples: Students followed teachers' lesson plans, sometimes engaged in self-learning using tablet activities and practice sheets, and sometimes worked in groups to solve problems, games, or activities

article_title: The Effectiveness of Educational Games on Scientific Concepts Acquisition in First Grade Students in Science
citation: Mohammad Hasan Al-Tarawneh. (2016). The Effectiveness of Educational Games on Scientific Concepts Acquisition in the First Grade Students in Science. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.3. https://www.iiste.org
title: Teaching guide of eight educational games for the five-senses unit
description: The researcher developed a teaching guide for the first-grade five-senses unit, containing study plans for educational games across eight lessons. The games — "surprise box, close your eyes, identify sounds and fragrances, say then taste, what’s in the bag, cold and hot, I’m the doctor" — are purposeful activities practiced individually or in groups under pre-set rules to acquire scientific concepts. The guide was reviewed by a jury of six reviewers and revised per their recommendations.
requirements: Study plans allocating a specific number of classes to each of the eight lessons
Teacher briefing: the researcher met the science teacher and intensively discussed the guide and how to apply the games
constraints: Validated for first graders and the five-senses unit only
target_learning_goals: acquisition of scientific concepts about the five senses
examples: Appendix (1) gives a lesson plan for the game Close your eyes, teaching shapes, colors, near/far and big/small through objects presented while eyes are closed

article_title: Efficacy, Intent to Teach, and Implementation of Nutrition Education Increases after Training for Health Educators
citation: Fahlman M, McCaughtry N, Martin J, Shen B. (2011). School health educators' self-efficacy, intentions to teach, and implementation of nutrition education increases after in-service training. Am J Health Educ. 2011;42(3):181-190. https://doi.org/10.1080/19325037.2011.10599191
title: Five research-based best-practice components of teacher in-service professional development
description: The professional development was engineered around five recommendations the authors identify as research-based: (1) workshops "should use active learning methods and avoid didactic lectures"; (2) workshops should be conducted by expert educators with knowledge of school contexts who do not work for the participating schools; (3) teachers should be compensated for their time; (4) programs should be supported by school administrators; and (5) teachers should be given all curriculum materials and instructional/supplementary resources needed to teach the full curriculum in their home classrooms. The workshop used non-lecture, skill-based, active learning techniques where teachers first learned and then practiced with their peers.
requirements: Expert workshop leader unaffiliated with teachers' home districts
Administrator support for implementation
Compensation for teachers' time
Complete curriculum and supplementary materials provided
constraints: The training took place outside contractual hours, requiring a stipend and continuing education credits
target_learning_goals: Improving teacher capability and willingness to implement a nutrition curriculum
examples: Eight hours of Saturday in-service training on the Michigan Model nutrition module, with all materials provided, weekly researcher support visits, and a six-week classroom implementation window

article_title: Revisiting an Old Methodology for Teaching Counting, Computation, and Place Value: The Effectiveness of the Finger Calculation Method for At-Risk Children
citation: Stegemann, K. C., & Grünke, M. (2014). Revisiting an Old Methodology for Teaching Counting, Computation, and Place Value: The Effectiveness of the Finger Calculation Method for At-Risk Children. Learning Disabilities: A Contemporary Journal, 12(2), 191-213.
title: Finger representation as embodied cognition supporting numerical cognition
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that fingers furnish a natural, permanently available representation of numerical information that reflects the one-to-one principle and, because hands encode numbers as sums or multiples of ten, can support understanding of the base-10 system. Finger representation is described as a type of "embodied cognition" that supports the internalization of numerical information, and the permanency of finger depictions helps reduce working memory load during calculation, which the authors argue buffers performance against math anxiety. The study applies this framework by testing Chisanbop, a systematic finger calculation method, as a remedial approach for counting, computation, and place value.
requirements: Instruction must be matched to the child's developmental phase; the article warns it is not productive to teach a skill that antecedes a competence level the child has not yet mastered.
constraints: The Chisanbop system as described represents only values between zero and ninety-nine; numbers beyond 99 require paper and pencil and a variation of the standard algorithm.
The framework is presented as relevant during a certain phase in the development of arithmetic abilities, and older students may view finger use as embarrassing.
target_learners: Elementary school children, particularly grade 2 students and children at-risk for math failure or with dyscalculia
target_learning_goals: Number sense, counting, computation, place value, and positive attitudes toward mathematics
examples: The experimental teachers delivered about 20 minutes of daily Chisanbop instruction within math lessons, using direct instruction or review followed by a cooperative game and/or worksheets.
key_sources: Stegemann, K. C., & Grünke, M. (2014). Revisiting an Old Methodology for Teaching Counting, Computation, and Place Value: The Effectiveness of the Finger Calculation Method for At-Risk Children. Learning Disabilities: A Contemporary Journal, 12(2), 191-213. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1047461

article_title: The Effects of Cooperative Learning on the Academic Achievement and Knowledge Retention
citation: Van Dat Tran. (2014). The Effects of Cooperative Learning on the Academic Achievement and Knowledge Retention. International Journal of Higher Education, 3(2). https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v3n2p131
title: Five basic elements of cooperative learning
description: The article defines cooperative learning as instructional methods in which teachers organize students into small groups that work together to learn academic content, and states that "Cooperative learning consists of five basic elements: positive inte rdependence, promotive interaction, individual accountability, teaching of interpersonal and social skills, and quality of group processing." Each element is described as necessary: without positive interdependence a situation is not cooperative, and without individual accountability some members may do all the work while others do nothing.
requirements: Positive interdependence must be constructed in the groups; learning situations are not cooperative if students are arranged into groups without it.
Social and interpersonal skills such as listening attentively, questioning cooperatively and negotiating respectfully need to be taught.
Group processing requires reflecting on a group session to describe helpful and unhelpful member actions and decide what to continue or change.
target_learners: tertiary students in small cooperative groups
target_learning_goals: academic content learning
interpersonal and social skills
examples: The experimental treatment applied the Learning Together technique with group formation, mutual help, and student presentations of their understanding of each unit.
key_sources: Van Dat Tran. (2014). The Effects of Cooperative Learning on the Academic Achievement and Knowledge Retention. International Journal of Higher Education, 3(2). https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v3n2p131

article_title: Teaching Arithmetic Combinations of Multiplication and Division to Students with Learning Disabilities or Mild Intellectual Disability: The Impact of Alternative Fact Grouping and the Role of Cognitive and Learning Factors
citation: Ioannis Agaliotis & Afroditi Teli. (2016). Teaching Arithmetic Combinations of Multiplication and Division to Students with Learning Disabilities or Mild Intellectual Disability: The Impact of Alternative Fact Grouping and the Role of Cognitive and Learning Factors. Journal of Education and Learning, 5(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v5n4p90
title: Five-step effective-instruction intervention for teaching arithmetic combinations of multiplication and division
description: The control intervention was a 12-lesson (6 multiplication, 6 division) program built on "principles of effective instruction", delivered by 18 trained Resource Room teachers to groups of 2-3 students. It comprised five structural components: review of prerequisite ACs, direct teaching through the three modes of knowledge representation, guided practice with reinforcement, independent practice with a success criterion of at least 16 correct oral answers to 20 written ACs in one minute, and final assessment with a progress table. Implementation fidelity was rated on a 4-point scale and showed high quality of application in all cases.
requirements: Teachers received 8 hours of training by the researchers plus weekly feedback on quality of program application
constraints: The success criterion of at least 16 correct oral answers to 20 ACs in one minute applied to the independent-practice step
target_learners: primary students with LD or MID, aged 9-12
target_learning_goals: fluent and accurate recall of multiplication and division arithmetic combinations
examples: The control group of 30 students (LD = 20, MID = 10) received this intervention, and its content covered 120 randomly selected ACs out of the 190 existing for both operations

article_title: Efficacy Validation of the Revised First Step Program: A Randomized Controlled Trial
citation: Feil, E. G., Walker, H. M., Frey, A. J., Seeley, J. R., Small, J. W., Golly, A., Lee, J., & Forness, S. R. (2020). Efficacy Validation of the Revised First Step Program: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Exceptional Children. https://journals.sagepub.com/home/ecx
title: First Step Next (FSN) Tier 2 early intervention program
description: First Step Next is a Tier 2 early intervention for pre-K through grade 2 children targeting social skills and academic enablers central to school success. "The program includes three major tasks: social skills instruction, the green-card game, and home-school connections." A trained coach delivers the first 5-7 days (coach phase), then transitions control to the teacher from day 11 onward. The program was evaluated in the reported RCT with 160 at-risk preschoolers.
requirements: A trained behavioral coach delivers initial implementation and provides one-on-one teacher consultation
Parent participation in the home-school connection component, including a parent workbook and daily feedback via note or phone call
constraints: The home component focus shifted from parent engagement and support to only parent engagement, reducing intervention dosage with parents
target_learners: at-risk preschool children (pre-K through grade 2) with elevated externalizing behavior
target_learning_goals: social-emotional skills such as following directions, anger management, and asking for help appropriately
academic enabling skills supporting school success
examples: In the RCT, 21 coaches across three cohorts delivered the program after a two-day training with role-played lessons, and students received 78% of requisite program days on average

article_title: An Empirical Study on the Application of Cooperative Learning to English Listening Classes
citation: Min Han. (2015). An Empirical Study on the Application of Cooperative Learning to English Listening Classes. English Language Teaching, 8(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n3p177
title: Sharan's five basic elements of cooperative learning
description: The article presents, citing Sharan (1999), five elements it calls "essential for CL": "positive interdependence, individual accountability, interpersonal and small group skills, promotive interaction and group processing". Positive interdependence is described as the core, existing when members know one cannot succeed unless everyone succeeds; group processing is regular reflection on how well the group cooperated. The article treats these as both characteristics of good CL groups and disciplines for effective learning.
requirements: Group members must realize the importance of common goals and be accountable for their own work and for helping others
Students must acquire interpersonal and small-group skills, since they are not born knowing how to interact
target_learners: college non-English majors in English listening classes
target_learning_goals: listening comprehension
communicative competence
cooperative skills
examples: The author taught students basic CL knowledge and required end-of-class reflection reports on what the group accomplished and what needed improvement

article_title: Innovation in Early Math Education: The Whole Teacher Approach to Professional Development
citation: McCray, J. & Chen, J.-Q. (2013). Innovation in Early Math Education: The Whole Teacher Approach to Professional Development. The EMC program embodies all five.
requirements: Sustained engagement over time rather than single workshops
Follow-up mechanisms such as coaching that link learning to classroom practice
target_learners: In-service teachers, especially early childhood generalists
target_learning_goals: Improved teaching quality and student learning through teacher PD
examples: The EMC program pairs yearlong learning labs with between-session on-site coaching and guided classroom implementation
