article_title: The Use of Animation Film in Forming Representations about the Planet Earth and the Solar System
citation: Vereș, S. & Magdaș, I. (2020). The Use of Animation Film in Forming Representations about the Planet Earth and the Solar System. Romanian Review of Geographical Education, 9(1), 38-59. https://doi.org/10.23741/RRGE120183
title: Film-plus-mediation lesson pattern: view, discuss with teacher, then consolidate with 2D/3D models, colouring tokens, and a mnemonic
description: A lesson-level instructional pattern in which an animated film is first viewed, then reviewed and discussed with the teacher, and finally consolidated with complementary materials. The article describes using a geographical globe and 3D model to explain Earth's rotation, schematic drawings of the planets, colouring tokens for each planet, and a mnemonic phrase. The authors state the second activity used "the animation film, 2D and 3D representati on of the Solar System" addressed to several analysers (auditory, visual, tactile, kinaesthetic), which helped capture and maintain attention.
requirements: A teacher mediates the discussion and explanations after viewing
Complementary visual and tactile materials (globe, 3D model, drawings, tokens) are available
constraints: Stated for Science learning in primary education with the Solar System topic in the Romanian Mathematics and Environmental Exploration subject
target_learning_goals: forming representations of the Solar System's structure and functioning
knowing planet names, order, and characteristics
understanding how days and nights form
examples: Students reviewed the film, answered teacher questions about its plot, observed a globe and 3D Solar System model, coloured planet tokens, ordered them from the Sun, and learned the mnemonic "MÂINE VOI PRIMI MULTE JUCĂRII SAU UNA NEMAIPOMENITĂ"
key_sources: Vereș, S. & Magdaș, I. (2020). The Use of Animation Film in Forming Representations about the Planet Earth and the Solar System. Romanian Review of Geographical Education, 9(1), 38-59. https://doi.org/10.23741/RRGE120183

article_title: Predictors and Moderators of Teacher Learning and Changes in Practice: Evidence from a Randomized Trial of a Teacher-Adapted Literacy Program
citation: Quinn, D. M., & Kim, J. S. (2016). Predictors and Moderators of Teacher Learning and Changes in Practice: Evidence from a Randomized Trial of a Teacher-Adapted Literacy Program. SREE Spring 2016 Conference abstract.
title: Fidelity versus adaptive implementation approaches to scaling up educational programs
description: The article contrasts two program-management frameworks for scale-up. Under the fidelity approach, "the teacher's job is to achieve the program ideal envisioned by the program developers," supported by top-down management. Under the adaptive approach, teachers diagnose problems, devise and test solutions, and adapt programs to context, which the authors link to a "context-focused approach to scale-up" requiring teacher control and collaborative work structures. The study tests these approaches empirically as Traditional versus Adaptive READS.
requirements: Under the adaptive approach, teachers must be able to recognize what is working and what is not, and collaborate in work structures; the fidelity approach requires adherence to researcher-designed procedures
constraints: The authors note that program effects often vary by context, so approaches showing promise in efficacy trials may fail to replicate elsewhere
target_learners: elementary school teachers implementing a literacy intervention
target_learning_goals: teacher learning about literacy instruction
incorporation of intervention practices into regular classroom teaching
examples: Twenty-seven schools were randomly assigned within matched pairs to Traditional READS (scripted lessons, two-hour training) or Adaptive READS (orientation on program principles, data examination in grade-level teams, and formal meetings to finalize adaptation plans)
key_sources: Quinn, D. M., & Kim, J. S. (2016). Predictors and Moderators of Teacher Learning and Changes in Practice: Evidence from a Randomized Trial of a Teacher-Adapted Literacy Program. SREE Spring 2016 Conference abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567622

article_title: The Effect of Two Types of Feedback on Iranian EFL Learners' Tense-Marker Production
citation: Somayeh Kazemi Tari. (2008). The Effect of Two Types of Feedback on Iranian EFL Learners' Tense-marker Production. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.2n.1p.108
title: 20-item fill-in-the-blank tense-marker test used as both pretest and posttest
description: A written 20-item fill-in-the-blank test, completed in 25 minutes, assessed learners' accurate use of the three target tense markers (simple present, simple past, present continuous). The same test served as pretest and posttest, and t-tests on its scores measured each feedback type's effectiveness and compared the two groups. In a pilot with 15 students at the same level, Kuder-Richardson reliability was "about 0.70", which the author judged "within an acceptable range".
requirements: Administered identically as pretest and posttest so pre-post and between-group t-tests can be computed
constraints: Teacher-made test piloted on 15 students at the same level; reliability about 0.70
target_learning_goals: Accurate production of English simple present, simple past, and present continuous tense markers
examples: Appendix A prints the test: completing conversations with correct verb forms, e.g. 'She ______ (work) in a restaurant now'
key_sources: Somayeh Kazemi Tari. (2008). The Effect of Two Types of Feedback on Iranian EFL Learners' Tense-marker Production. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.2n.1p.108

article_title: Applying Computer-Assisted Musical Instruction to Music Appreciation Course: An Example with Chinese Musical Instruments
citation: Lou, S.-J., Guo, Y.-C., Zhu, Y.-Z., Shih, R.-C., & Dzan, W.-Y. (2011). Applying computer-assisted musical instruction to music appreciation course: An example with Chinese musical instruments. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(1). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Five-stage CAMI software production flow
description: The article describes a five-stage development process for the CAMI software: "preparation stage, software design and development stage, materials integration stage, software test stage, and modification stage." Preparation includes understanding teachers' teaching demands and students' learning situations; design includes choosing teaching materials, determining teaching design and completing script design; the final stages combine components with the script, test the software and modify it into complete teaching software.
requirements: Understanding teachers' teaching demand and students' learning situation in the preparation stage
Regular team discussion with the computer engineer during production
target_learners: vocational senior high school students in music appreciation courses
target_learning_goals: understanding and appreciating Chinese musical instruments
examples: The team spent six months collecting and editing characters, pictures and audio/video materials, then commissioned a computer company for follow-up production
key_sources: Lou, S.-J., Guo, Y.-C., Zhu, Y.-Z., Shih, R.-C., & Dzan, W.-Y. (2011). Applying computer-assisted musical instruction to music appreciation course: An example with Chinese musical instruments. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ926553

article_title: CALL, Prewriting Strategies, and EFL Writing Quantity
citation: Sajad Shafiee, Mansour Koosha & Akbar Afghari. (2015). CALL, Prewriting Strategies, and EFL Writing Quantity. English Language Teaching, 8(2). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n2p170
title: Instructional package of five prewriting strategies for EFL writing
description: A compiled instructional package drawn from three writing textbooks (Zemach and Islam 2011; White 2006; Smally, Ruetten, and Kozyrev 2011) covering "freewriting, brainstorming, listing, clustering, and asking wh-questions during the planning stage of writing". The same materials were used for the conventional, web-based, and hybrid groups, with only the mode of input delivery differing. The package was reviewed by the researchers and two colleagues before use.
requirements: Review and revision of the materials by the researchers and two colleagues, with feedback from academic writing instructors
constraints: The control group's textbook (Paragraph Development) deliberately contained no prewriting strategies, so the package applies only to the experimental conditions
target_learning_goals: Idea generation and planning before writing
Increased writing quantity (idea units)
examples: Chapter and page selections from the three textbooks specified which lessons taught listing, clustering, freewriting, wh-questions, brainstorming, and outlining
key_sources: Sajad Shafiee, Mansour Koosha & Akbar Afghari. (2015). CALL, Prewriting Strategies, and EFL Writing Quantity. English Language Teaching, 8(2). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n2p170

article_title: Automatic Speech Recognition Technology as an Effective Means for Teaching Pronunciation
citation: Amal Khalil Elimat & Ali Farhan AbuSeileek. (2014). Automatic speech recognition technology as an effective means for teaching pronunciation. The JALT Call Journal, 10(1), 21-47. https://jaltcall.org
title: Five-phase model of ideal ASR-based computer-assisted pronunciation training
description: The article describes, citing Neri, Cucchiarini, and Strik (2003), the ideal ASR-based CAPT program as "a sequence of five phases": speech recognition, scoring, error detection, error diagnosis, and feedback presentation. The engine translates incoming speech into words using internal phonetic and syntactic models; scoring compares the student's utterance with a native utterance to give a global quality score; error detection locates problematic sounds to raise learner awareness; error diagnosis identifies the error type and suggests improvement; and feedback presentation shows the overall score as a graded bar or number on a scale, which the authors call fundamental because learners benefit only if information is presented meaningfully.
requirements: Feedback must be presented in a meaningful way for learners to benefit from the information ASR obtains
constraints: The model is presented as a description of ideal CAPT programs, attributed to Neri, Cucchiarini, and Strik (2003), not tested in this study
target_learning_goals: Improved pronunciation quality through awareness of specific errors
examples: The Tell Me More program used in the study instantiates this cycle: students listen to a model, record, and receive automatic feedback comparing their attempts to a native speaker's
key_sources: Amal Khalil Elimat & Ali Farhan AbuSeileek. (2014). Automatic speech recognition technology as an effective means for teaching pronunciation. The JALT Call Journal, 10(1), 21-47. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1107929

article_title: First Step Next: A Best-Evidence Synthesis of Replication Randomized Controlled Trials from 2009 to 2021
citation: Andy J. Frey, Jason W. Small, Hill M. Walker, Brandon Mitchell, John R. Seeley, Edward G. Feil, Jon Lee, and Steven R. Forness. (2023). First Step Next: A Best-Evidence Synthesis of Replication Randomized Controlled Trials From 2009 to 2021. Remedial and Special Education, 44(1), 60-72. https://doi.org/10.1177/07419325211068145
title: First Step Next early intervention program
description: First Step Next is a targeted early intervention for pre-K through Grade 2 students with moderately severe, primarily externalizing behavioral challenges, implemented by general education teachers in collaboration with a coach. "FSN contains the following elements: social skills (SS) instruction, green card game, and home-school connections; it is implemented across four implementation phases (i.e., preparation, coach, teacher, and maintenance phase)." The coach teaches seven super student skills one-to-one, the class-wide green card game provides non-verbal feedback and points on a fixed interval schedule, and parents sign daily notes and run reinforcement activities at home.
requirements: Implementation requires a trained coach (often a provider of special education services) working with the general education teacher, with training via a 1- or 2-day workshop and weekly supervision of 1 hr during implementation.
constraints: Cost analyses have estimated the FSN coach invests approximately 45 hr of time per additional student, with coordination and collaboration activities taking 2 to 3 months depending on case difficulty.
target_learners: pre-K through Grade 2 students with moderately severe, primarily externalizing behavioral challenges
target_learning_goals: improve social functioning and prosocial behavior
decrease problem behaviors that disrupt the teaching-learning process
examples: In the five replication RCTs, the coach ran the green card game for approximately 10 days before turning responsibility over to the teacher for a 10-day teacher phase and a 10-day maintenance phase.
key_sources: Andy J. Frey, Jason W. Small, Hill M. Walker, Brandon Mitchell, John R. Seeley, Edward G. Feil, Jon Lee, and Steven R. Forness. (2023). First Step Next: A Best-Evidence Synthesis of Replication Randomized Controlled Trials From 2009 to 2021. Remedial and Special Education, 44(1), 60-72. https://doi.org/10.1177/07419325211068145

article_title: The Effect of TMPT Program on Pre-School Children's Social Problem Solving Skills
citation: Gur, C. & Kocak, N. (2018). The Effect of TMPT Program on Pre-school Children's Social Problem Solving Skills. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 73, 77-94. https://doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2018.73.5
title: Five-dimension perspective-taking progression from self to universal perspectives
description: The TMPT Program organizes Thinking Training as a progression through five perspectives: the self ('I' point of view), the other (empathic perspective), a third person or object, the group (pluralist perspective), and finally universal perspectives evaluating conditions from five or more viewpoints. Each dimension is discussed for one month with 20 classroom activities built on ordinary materials such as stories, films, paintings, and discussion questions. The design assumes perspective-taking supports social problem-solving; the article states the aim is for children "to learn how to think, not what to think."
requirements: One dimension per month across the school year, with teachers trained monthly and given materials
Discussion rather than judgment: the adult should not judge the child's ideas
constraints: Developed and tested for preschool children aged 5-6
target_learning_goals: perspective-taking
multidimensional thinking
social problem-solving
examples: Dimension activities include comparing horses and zebras for the 'you' step, discussing a van Gogh painting for the third-person step, and discussing sea pollution for the group perspective.
key_sources: Gur, C. & Kocak, N. (2018). The Effect of TMPT Program on Pre-school Children's Social Problem Solving Skills. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 73, 77-94. https://doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2018.73.5

article_title: Interactive Methods of Teaching Physics at Technical Universities
citation: Krišťák, Ľ., Němec, M., Danihelová, Z. (2014). Interactive Methods of Teaching Physics at Technical Universities. Informatics in Education, 13(1), 51–71. https://doi.org/10.15388/infedu.2014.03
title: Five ways of assigning problem tasks within interactive lessons
description: Within the P&E method each problem task can be assigned in five ways, summarised in Table 1: text solved theoretically; text solved via a real or computer-aided experiment; an unfinished experiment/video-experiment/simulation where students predict the result and the experiment is then carried out to verify the theory; a finished experiment whose physical course or result must be reasoned theoretically; and a finished experiment solved via video-analysis. The authors report that "various variations of problem task solving influence students very positively", teaching them that a problem can be assigned and solved in different ways and that a procedure effective in one case need not be effective in another.
requirements: Students' worksheets and teachers' guidelines created for each way of problem task assignment
constraints: Assignment formats rely on available experiments, video-experiments, simulations and applets
target_learning_goals: physical reasoning and analysis of phenomena
flexibility in problem-solving procedures
connecting formalism to everyday life
examples: Example text task: how a ship's draught changes after shipping out from a river into the sea
key_sources: Krišťák, Ľ., Němec, M., Danihelová, Z. (2014). Interactive Methods of Teaching Physics at Technical Universities. Informatics in Education, 13(1), 51–71. https://doi.org/10.15388/infedu.2014.03

article_title: Modifying a Research-Based Problem-Solving Intervention to Improve the Problem-Solving Performance of Fifth and Sixth Graders with and without Learning Disabilities
citation: Krawec, J., & Huang, J. (2017). Modifying a Research-Based Problem-Solving Intervention to Improve the Problem-Solving Performance of Fifth and Sixth Graders With and Without Learning Disabilities. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 50(4), 468–480. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219416645565
title: Five modifications adapting a grades 7–12 strategy intervention for fifth and sixth graders
description: The article enumerates five targeted modifications: increased explicitness of instruction (expanding one routine lesson into three lessons on modeling, paraphrasing, and visualizing), expanded emphasis on metacognition with additional sequenced prompts, a new prerequisite lesson on concepts of the four operations, extension of initial instructional sessions from 3 to 6 days, and added visual supports (operations decision tree, paraphrasing and visualizing frameworks). The authors state: "we extended the initial instructional sessions from 3 to 6 days, expanded the focus on paraphrasing and visualizing strategies, increased the explicitness of the meta-cognitive components, taught and then reinforced concepts of the four arithmetic operations, and added visual supports."
requirements: Modifications were based on previous research, developmental characteristics of fifth and sixth graders, and a pilot study identifying deficits in concepts of operations
constraints: The weekly practice session script was not altered from the original intervention
target_learners: Fifth and sixth grade students, including those with LD
target_learning_goals: Math problem solving, including paraphrasing, visualizing, and solution planning
examples: Instead of the self-instructive prompt to make a drawing, students first asked themselves "What am I looking for? Am I looking for the total?" before continuing with drawing prompts
key_sources: Krawec, J., & Huang, J. (2017). Modifying a Research-Based Problem-Solving Intervention to Improve the Problem-Solving Performance of Fifth and Sixth Graders With and Without Learning Disabilities. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 50(4), 468–480. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219416645565

article_title: Modifying a Research-Based Problem-Solving Intervention to Improve the Problem-Solving Performance of Fifth and Sixth Graders with and without Learning Disabilities
citation: Krawec, J., & Huang, J. (2017). Modifying a Research-Based Problem-Solving Intervention to Improve the Problem-Solving Performance of Fifth and Sixth Graders With and Without Learning Disabilities. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 50(4), 468–480. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219416645565
title: Five IRT-calibrated curriculum-based measures of math problem solving
description: The research team developed five CBMs of math problem solving, "calibrated using Item Response Theory methods to achieve equivalent difficulty level." Each measure combined two 5-item blocks from a pool of nine blocks of 45 discrete word problems, with each block containing approximately one 1-step, three 2-step, and one 3-step problem. Each of the five measures consisted of 10 textbook-type problems using all four operations with whole numbers and decimals. Internal consistency ranged from .82 to .84, and equated scores were used in analysis.
requirements: Equated CBM scores (Montague et al., 2010) were used in the study
constraints: Administered five times: prior to intervention, 1 month following, then every other month; the fifth administration in the final week of the year showed a noticeable performance fall-off the authors attribute to end-of-year disengagement
target_learners: Fifth and sixth grade students of varying ability
target_learning_goals: Measuring growth in math word problem solving performance
examples: CBMs were administered to each participating math class period prior to intervention, 1 month after, and every other month for the remainder of the school year
key_sources: Krawec, J., & Huang, J. (2017). Modifying a Research-Based Problem-Solving Intervention to Improve the Problem-Solving Performance of Fifth and Sixth Graders With and Without Learning Disabilities. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 50(4), 468–480. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219416645565

article_title: Development of Junior Pupils Research Skills in Interrelation with Universal Learning Activities
citation: Sabirova, E. G., Zakirova, V. G. & Masalimova, A. R. (2016). Development of Junior Pupils Research Skills in Interrelation with Universal Learning Activities. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(4), 505-514.
title: Organize pupils' research process according to five principles: naturalness, awareness, independent activity, obviousness, and cultural conformity
description: The article states that a scientific approach to the research process in pedagogical practice demands using a number of principles. Under the "principle of naturalness", the problem has to be not fictional but existing and the interest real; under the "principle of independent activity", the pupil masters the research process only through living it, through one's own experience; and the "principle of cultural conformity" requires taking into account traditions of sensing the world in the chosen culture and of interrelation in the observed social community. The remaining two principles require awareness of the problem, purpose, task, process and results, and obviousness, whereby the pupil learns the world not only by books but as it is.
requirements: Problems posed to pupils must be real rather than fictional, and the interest genuine rather than false
constraints: The principles are stated for organizing the research process in elementary-school pedagogical practice, not tested as a manipulated variable in the experiment
target_learning_goals: development of research skills and research approach to practical work
examples: The article applies the principles when listing subject-embedded tasks, e.g. environment tasks built on observation of natural phenomena and conversations with relatives about real holidays and family genealogy.
key_sources: Sabirova, E. G., Zakirova, V. G. & Masalimova, A. R. (2016). Development of Junior Pupils Research Skills in Interrelation with Universal Learning Activities. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(4), 505-514. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1094583

article_title: The Effects of Professional Development Initiatives on EFL Teachers' Degree of Self Efficacy
citation: Mohammad Nabi Karimi. (2011). The Effects of Professional Development Initiatives on EFL Teachers' Degree of Self Efficacy. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, Vol 36, 6, May 2011.
title: Five-model professional development package (In-service Training, Fellow Observation/Assessment, Development/Improvement Process, Mentoring, Study Groups)
description: The treatment combined five of the seven PD models identified in prior reviews: in-service training, observation/assessment, development/improvement process, mentoring, and study groups. The article states that "in the present study attempts have been made to provide various experiences for the participant teachers through the employment of five different PD models", contrasting this with prior studies that targeted only one source of efficacy. Activities included group-based work, critiqued teaching demonstrations, review of organizational programs, observation of successful teachers, and four-to-six-member study groups, delivered across three 16-session courses of 90-minute sessions.
requirements: Delivered through courses whose content aligns with the models' characteristics; attendance records were used to ensure participation
constraints: Evaluated only with Iranian junior high school EFL teachers in a convenience-sample treatment group
target_learning_goals: teachers' sense of efficacy for engagement, instructional strategies, and classroom management
examples: Treatment teachers taught a critiqued lesson, investigated curricular issues in study groups of four to six, and observed classes of successful Ilam teachers, submitting observation reports
key_sources: Mohammad Nabi Karimi. (2011). The Effects of Professional Development Initiatives on EFL Teachers' Degree of Self Efficacy. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, Vol 36, 6, May 2011. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ936991

article_title: The Effect of Cooperative Learning Method and Systematic Teaching on Students' Achievement and Retention of Knowledge in Social Studies Lesson
citation: Korkmaz Toklucu, S., & Tay, B. (2016). The effect of cooperative learning method and systematic teaching on students' achievement and retention of knowledge in social studies lesson. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 66, 315-334. http://dx.doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2016.66.18
title: Five basic principles of cooperative learning (Johnson, Johnson & Holubec)
description: The article presents cooperative learning as students working together to achieve shared learning goals, and identifies the conditions needed for such activities to succeed: "These five basic principles include: positive interdependence, face-to-face interaction, individual accountability, social skills, and group process (Johnson, Johnson & Holubec, 1992)." These principles frame the cooperative learning lesson plans used in experiment group 1.
requirements: Group tasks must be structured so that all five principles are taken into consideration for cooperative activities to succeed
constraints: As cited in the article from Johnson, Johnson & Holubec (1992); the article does not elaborate each principle in detail
target_learners: Elementary students working in cooperative groups
target_learning_goals: Achievement of shared learning goals through structured group work
examples: Experiment group 1 used techniques including combining, ask together learn together, student team achievement parts, learning together, and group inquiry
key_sources: Korkmaz Toklucu, S., & Tay, B. (2016). The effect of cooperative learning method and systematic teaching on students' achievement and retention of knowledge in social studies lesson. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 66, 315-334. http://dx.doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2016.66.18

article_title: The Use of Music as a Way of Formation of Communicative Skills of Students in Teaching English Language
citation: R. M. Akhmadullina, A. R. Abdrafikova & N. V. Vanyukhina. (2016). The Use of Music as a Way of Formation of Communicative Skills of Students in Teaching English language. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(6), 1295-1302.
title: Five types of music and musical information used in English language teaching
description: The study operationalises "music" in English language teaching as five types: "1. Instrumental performance of various musical works; 2. Song (acapella, solo and choral); 3. Video clips from recordings of songs; 4. Verbal information from the world of the music industry" (articles, interviews, advertising, programmes), and "5. Non-verbal information" (photographs of musicians, instruments, studio and concert-hall interiors). Each type received its own set of classroom techniques in the formation stage.
requirements: Techniques must be selected for each type of musical information separately, as the abstract states the best techniques are analysed "for each type of information separately"
target_learning_goals: communicative skills in English
examples: Classical instrumental works by Mozart, Beethoven, Rachmaninoff, Strauss, Bach and programme music by Mussorgsky, Shostakovich, Prokofiev and Tchaikovsky were selected
key_sources: R. M. Akhmadullina, A. R. Abdrafikova & N. V. Vanyukhina. (2016). The Use of Music as a Way of Formation of Communicative Skills of Students in Teaching English language. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(6), 1295-1302. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1114401

article_title: Towards a Practical Framework of the Remediation of Cognitive Skills at Primary Level
citation: Outi Kyrö-Ämmälä & Kaarina Määttä. (2011). Towards a Practical Framework of the Remediation of Cognitive Skills at Primary Level. World Journal of Education. https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v1n1p28
title: Five core functions of the guiding teaching style for cognitive remediation
description: The article names "five essential pedagogical actions to improve a child's cognitive development", which "form the core functions of the cognitive remediation": process questions that make pupils discuss their thinking; bridging, where "the cognitive functions as the teaching subjects are connected to surroundings that are familiar to a learner"; demanding arguments for both right and wrong answers; teaching rule formation and the generalisation of rules; and a teacher attitude emphasising predictability, consecution and strategies. The pattern operates at lesson level within a guiding teaching style.
requirements: A teacher must pay attention to pupils' feedback and develop teaching style and strategies based on it
Bridging examples should be simple and logically straightforward so learners realise the connection themselves
constraints: The functions are the core of remediation but insufficient alone; the pedagogical general prerequisites of Section 5.1 are also needed
target_learners: primary-level pupils with weak cognitive skills
target_learning_goals: thinking processes
generalisation of cognitive strategies
precise reasoning and language
examples: Process questions printed in the article include 'How do you know this?' and 'What do you have to do first?'
key_sources: Outi Kyrö-Ämmälä & Kaarina Määttä. (2011). Towards a Practical Framework of the Remediation of Cognitive Skills at Primary Level. World Journal of Education. https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v1n1p28

article_title: Elementary Teachers Integrate Music Activities into Regular Mathematics Lessons: Effects on Students' Mathematical Abilities
citation: Song An, Mary Margaret Capraro, Daniel A. Tillman. (2013). Elementary Teachers Integrate Music Activities into Regular Mathematics Lessons: Effects on Students' Mathematical Abilities. Journal for Learning through the Arts, 9(1). http://escholarship.org/uc/item/0js732gf
title: Five-phase instructional model for music-mathematics integrated lessons
description: An (2012) proposed an instructional model in which "The model has five phases, with each phase containing varying levels of focus on music and mathematics." Phase one focuses solely on music; phase two shifts focus toward mathematics while music retains more focus; phase three gives music and mathematics equivalent focus during student activity; phase four uses students' music products to design mathematics tasks with greater emphasis on mathematics; phase five focuses on pure mathematics with no music. The model underpinned the study's intervention design.
requirements: Teachers need professional development and familiarity with music-math integration; participant teachers received 10 hours of PD seminars and pilot-lesson feedback before implementing the model.
constraints: The article presents the model as a hypothesis-generating framework tested in one exploratory quasi-experiment; the authors do not suggest their activities are a prototype for all mathematics classroom activities.
target_learning_goals: mathematical modeling, strategy, and application abilities
examples: Teachers designed weekly lessons following the model, e.g., introducing music knowledge first, then engaging students in composition or instrument activities, then assigning mathematics word problems based on students' own musical works.
key_sources: Song An, Mary Margaret Capraro, Daniel A. Tillman. (2013). Elementary Teachers Integrate Music Activities into Regular Mathematics Lessons: Effects on Students' Mathematical Abilities. Journal for Learning through the Arts, 9(1). http://escholarship.org/uc/item/0js732gf

article_title: The Role of Cognitive Style in the Collocational Knowledge Development of Iranian EFL Learners through Input Flood Treatment
citation: Elaheh Hamed Mahvelati & Jayakaran Mukundan. (2012). The Role of Cognitive Style in the Collocational Knowledge Development of Iranian EFL Learners through Input Flood Treatment. English Language Teaching, 5(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n10p105
title: Cognitive style of field dependence-independence as a moderator of implicit instruction effectiveness
description: Field dependence-independence is a cognitive-style dimension describing how globally or analytically a learner approaches a task or processes information. The article adopts Witkin and Goodenough's definitions: a field-dependent individual "can insufficiently separate an item from its context and who readily accepts the dominating field or context", whereas a field-independent individual "can easily ‘break up’ an organised perceptual field and separate readily an item from its context". The study uses this dimension to explain which learners benefit from implicit, exposure-based collocation instruction.
requirements: Learners' cognitive style must be measured (here via the GEFT) before instruction can be matched to style
constraints: The article states field-dependent learners need directive, supportive teaching and external support to focus attention, while field-independent learners prefer discovery methods and minimum direction
target_learning_goals: collocational knowledge (receptive and productive)
examples: The study classified learners as field-dependent, field-independent, or field-intermediate using GEFT scores relative to the sample mean ± ¼ SD, excluding field-intermediates.
key_sources: Elaheh Hamed Mahvelati & Jayakaran Mukundan. (2012). The Role of Cognitive Style in the Collocational Knowledge Development of Iranian EFL Learners through Input Flood Treatment. English Language Teaching, 5(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n10p105

article_title: Adolescents' Self-Regulation Development via the Sensory Room System
citation: Aydar M. Kalimullin, Elena A. Kuvaldina & Julia Koinova-Zoellner. (2016). Adolescents' Self-Regulation Development Via the Sensory Room System. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(5), 663-671.
title: The "Find yourself" program: an 8-lesson sensory-room intervention for adolescent self-regulation
description: The program "Find yourself" was developed and implemented as the formative stage of the experiment, aimed at developing adolescents' self-regulation through the system of sensory room. It comprised 8 lessons using sensory-room facilities such as transforming armchairs, musical beanbag chairs, bubble columns and an audio system with relaxation records. The article states "The program included 8 lessons" and lists four purposes: teaching behavior self-regulation skills, teaching relaxation, developing cooperation and communication skills, and creating an emotionally comfortable environment.
requirements: A sensory room equipped with facilities such as transforming armchairs, musical beanbag chairs, bubble columns and an audio system with relaxation records
Group work with classmates, since peers create a reference environment for adolescents
constraints: Tested only with 50 pupils from the 7th grades of one gymnasium in Kirov during the 2014-2015 academic years
target_learning_goals: behavior self-regulation skills
relaxation
cooperation and communication skills
emotional comfort
examples: Lesson 1 "Stars" used visualization of a starry sky; Lesson 7 "The Sea" used the game "Siamese twins" for interaction; the final lesson "Clouds" used exercises such as "My portrait in sunrays"

article_title: The Effect of the Process Writing Approach on Writing Success and Anxiety
citation: Nihat BAYAT. (2014). The Effect of the Process Writing Approach on Writing Success and Anxiety. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 14(3). https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2014.3.1720
title: Five-stage process writing cycle with peer and self evaluation in small groups
description: The article describes classroom application of process writing through five stages: "prewriting, drafting, editing, revising, and publishing". In the study, students worked in groups of four who "decided on the topics of essays, plans, and conclusions to be drawn by discussing them with each other, and then proceeded to write". Members used a stage checklist with interrogative questions rated 1 to 5 to evaluate their own and friends' essays, while the professor guided students where needed. Texts were produced over two weeks per essay.
requirements: A checklist of writing stages reminding participants what to do at each stage and how to evaluate essays
Small groups in which members discuss topics, plans, and conclusions before writing
Extended time for essay completion rather than a limited period
constraints: The article notes some participants could not use the allotted time efficiently, and individual differences led some to finish earlier than others
target_learners: first-year university students in teacher education
target_learning_goals: academic essay writing
self- and peer-assessment of writing
organization, content, word choice, and language use
examples: Experimental-group students devised their own topics through brainstorming while control-group students received professor-provided topics and weekly essay feedback only after completion

article_title: Development of Learning Management Model Based on Constructivist Theory and Reasoning Strategies for Enhancing the Critical Thinking of Secondary Students
citation: Dudduan Chaipichit, Nirat Jantharajit and Sumalee Chookhampaeng. (2015). Development of learning management model based on constructivist theory and reasoning strategies for enhancing the critical thinking of secondary students. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2015.2193
title: Five-step instructional sequence: motivation, comprehension, hypothesis, pondering, evaluation
description: The developed model's implementation component has five aspects: "motivation, creation of understanding in various incidents or situations, associating the basic experience with previous understanding, considering and accepting the consensus through reference and negotiation, and the evaluation and assessment of performance practice". In Phase 2 the researcher elaborated these as five learning-management steps: motivation, comprehension, hypothesis, pondering, and evaluation, each with described activities such as stimulating curiosity through problem situations and making decisions to accept or reject a hypothesis.
requirements: Steps are synthesized from Constructivist Theory and the reasoning strategies model of Joyce, Weil and Calhoun (2004)
constraints: Applied within science curriculum instruction for secondary students in this study
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
reasoning from evidence
decision making
examples: Instruction focused on five steps including interpreting a situation, explanation and reference, considering and pondering the reliability of information, conjecture and analysis of negotiation, and evaluating alternatives of decision making and opinion

article_title: The Web Quest: Its Impact on Developing Teaching Skills of Physical Education Student Teachers
citation: Haythem Abdel Mageed Mohamed & Rasha Nageh Ali Abd El Rheem. (2008). The Web Quest: Its Impact on Developing Teaching Skills of Physical Education Student Teachers. Journal of Research, volume 5, issue 1. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=The+Web+Quest+Its+Impact+on+Developing+Teaching+Skills+of+Physical+Education+Student+Teachers
title: Five-cycle WebQuest intervention pattern: surf, teamwork, information exchange, teaching and feedback
description: The intervention pattern organized instruction into five cycles of four 120-minute sessions each, preceded by an orientation session on the WebQuest. In each cycle "participants were required to choose one lesson from the WebQuest and prepare a lesson plan to peer-teach at the end of the cycle." Session 1 was surfing the WebQuest in the university lab, Session 2 teamwork within sub-groups, Session 3 exchanging of information in one big circle, and Session 4 teaching and feedback with a post conference assessing performance against the WebQuest's evaluation rubric. Target teaching skills were rotated among sub-groups across cycles.
requirements: A university Internet lab, a designed WebQuest with lessons and an evaluation rubric, sub-groups of candidates, and an instructor monitoring and offering help when needed
constraints: The pattern was studied only with third-year male PE teacher candidates aged 19 to 20 at one university over three months
target_learning_goals: planning, implementation and evaluation of PE lessons; information gathering and synthesis from Internet resources
examples: In Session 4 three chosen candidates presented their planned lessons in 90 minutes, one each for equipment arrangement, teaching, and the evaluation stage, followed by a 30-minute post conference

article_title: The Impact of Task Type and Cognitive Style on Vocabulary Learning
citation: Gholam Reza Haji Pour Nezhad & Nasrin Shokrpour. (2012). The Impact of Task Type and Cognitive Style on Vocabulary Learning. English Language Teaching, 5(9). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n9p17
title: Field dependence/independence as a cognitive style affecting language learning
description: The article describes field in/dependence, introduced by Witkin et al. (1977), as the degree to which one perceives analytically or globally. Field independence is "the ability to perceive a particular relevant item or factor in a field of distracting items", involving cognitive restructuring ability; field dependency is "the tendency to depend on the field so that the parts embedded within the field are not easily perceived". Field-independent learners are analytic, independent, and socially insensitive, while field-dependent ones tend to be holistic, dependent, and socially aware. The study uses the Group Embedded Figures Test to assign learners to these styles.
requirements: Assessment of cognitive style via an instrument such as the standard Group Embedded Figures Test before assigning learners to conditions
constraints: Research cited in the article suggests field in/dependency is under the influence of factors such as age, sex, hemisphere lateralization, child rearing, and socioeconomic status
target_learning_goals: vocabulary learning
second language learning
examples: 84 participants were given a Cognitive Style Test and matched into homogeneous groups based on cognitive style type and vocabulary performance
key_sources: Gholam Reza Haji Pour Nezhad & Nasrin Shokrpour. (2012). The Impact of Task Type and Cognitive Style on Vocabulary Learning. English Language Teaching, 5(9). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n9p17

article_title: Developing the Mathematics Learning Management Model for Improving Creative Thinking in Thailand
citation: Sriwongchai, A., Jantharajit, N., & Chookhampaeng, S. (2015). Developing the Mathematics Learning Management Model for Improving Creative Thinking in Thailand. International Education Studies, 8(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v8n11p77
title: Five-step learning process sequence for creative thinking in mathematics lessons
description: The model's learning process is a five-step activity sequence: "1) engagement and connection to prior knowledge, 2) encounter of problem and thoughtful incubation, 3) analyzing alternative an d investigating solutions, 4) applying and modifying thinking pattern, and 5) concluding and evaluating creative thinking." It structures each lesson or unit so students connect prior knowledge, confront open-ended problems with incubation time, investigate alternative solutions, modify their thinking patterns, and conclude and evaluate their creative thinking. The sequence was implemented across 30 hours of 9th-grade mathematics instruction.
requirements: Open-ended problems that support divergent thinking, which the article says most teachers previously lacked
constraints: Applied to 9th-grade Probability and Statistics content in Thai secondary schools
target_learning_goals: Creative thinking through divergent thinking on open-ended problems
examples: Lesson plans for improving creative thinking in mathematics learning were written for the overall 30 hours of instruction following this sequence.
key_sources: Sriwongchai, A., Jantharajit, N., & Chookhampaeng, S. (2015). Developing the Mathematics Learning Management Model for Improving Creative Thinking in Thailand. International Education Studies, 8(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v8n11p77

article_title: Valuing a More Rigorous Review of Formative Assessment's Effectiveness
citation: Apthorp, H., Klute, M., Petrites, T., Harlacher, J., & Reale, M. (2016). Valuing a more rigorous review of formative assessment's effectiveness. SREE Spring 2016 Conference Proposal. https://www.relcentral.org/news-and-events/the-essence-of-formative-assessment-creating-a-common-understanding-of-the-formative-assessment-process/
title: Five-category characterization of formative assessment effects using benchmark effect size and statistical significance
description: For studies meeting WWC standards, the review characterized findings "according to a benchmark effect size, statistical significance, and the direction of effect into one of five mutually exclusive categories": statistically significant positive, substantively important positive, indeterminate, statistically significant negative, and substantively important negative. Figure B.3 sets criteria, e.g., a substantively important positive effect requires an estimated effect greater than .25 but not statistically significant, and an indeterminate effect falls between .25 and -.25 and is not statistically significant.
requirements: Effect sizes and significance information must be available or derivable for outcomes in each study after applying any needed corrections
constraints: When effect size information is not available for multiple outcomes in the same domain, the criteria fall back on the proportion of statistically significant positive or negative effects
target_learning_goals: characterizing the direction and practical importance of formative assessment effects
examples: Figure B.3 criteria: substantively important positive effect if one outcome's estimated effect is greater than .25 but not statistically significant
key_sources: Apthorp, H., Klute, M., Petrites, T., Harlacher, J., & Reale, M. (2016). Valuing a more rigorous review of formative assessment's effectiveness. article_title: Studying the Effectiveness of Physical Education in the Secondary School (by the Example of Kazakhstan)
citation: Тulegen A. Botagariyeva, Svetlana S. Kubiyeva, Venera E. Baizakova, Nurolla Mambetov, Yerkin K. Tulegenov, Alpysbay S. Aralbayev and Dulat U. Kairgozhin. (2016). International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(10), 3575-3594. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
title: Computer program for processing physical fitness test results
description: The authors developed software (Frolov, 2009) to process results of reaching school qualifying standards on "Physical Training" and the Presidential physical fitness tests. The program "provides tools to determine the individual and group characteristics of schoolchildren as well as to draw methodical conclusions related to the correction of physical qualities of schoolchildren." Each school receives a database with standards values, statistical parameters, and an individual card of each student, plus graphic distribution of results in intervals showing frequency of occurrence. Analysis showed the highest frequency of results fell within the range of improper national preparedness for the Presidential level.
requirements: The data to be processed is interrelated with the processing tasks
Technical skills are required to interpret the results in accordance with the tasks
target_learners: ninth-grade secondary school students in Aktobe, Kazakhstan
target_learning_goals: physical fitness assessment and correction of physical qualities
examples: The program provided a graphic distribution of results in intervals to determine frequency of occurrence, revealing that most results were below the national preparedness level for the Presidential tests.

article_title: Direct versus Indirect Explicit Methods of Enhancing EFL Students' English Grammatical Competence: A Concept Checking-Based Consciousness-Raising Tasks Model
citation: Đặng, T. T. Đ., & Nguyễn, H. T. (2012). Direct versus Indirect Explicit Methods of Enhancing EFL Students' English Grammatical Competence: A Concept Checking-based Consciousness-raising Tasks Model. English Language Teaching, 6(1), 112. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n1p112
title: Five-stage concept checking-based consciousness-raising task sequence for grammar lessons
description: The article's instructional model divides each grammar lesson into five stages adapted from Harding and Taylor (2005) and Cunningham and Moor (2005): "(1) lead-in, (2) providing input, (3) consciousness-raising tasks, (4) checking and summarizing, and (5) practice." Learners first encounter the target form in contextualized input, then discover rules through pair and group tasks, receive teacher checking and feedback, and finally practice independently without teacher interference. The direct explicit group followed the same sequence except that step 3 replaced tasks with teacher presentation and explanation of the rules.
requirements: Contextualized input (reading or listening) containing examples of the target structure
Pair and group work on rule-searched tasks
Teacher checking, feedback, and rule summary after the task stage
constraints: The treatment phase lasted eight weeks with 90-minute sessions in this study; both groups received the same amount of time, contextualized input, and practice
target_learners: EFL high school students at pre-intermediate level
target_learning_goals: Discovery of the form and meaning of target grammatical structures
Retention and productive use of English tenses
examples: In the implementation stage, inductive students were engaged in rule-searched condition tasks in pairs and groups, then given feedback and confirmation of what they had searched before

citation: Seifoori, Z. (2016). Metacognitive awareness and the fluency of task-based oral output across planning conditions: The case of Iranian TEFL students. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research, 4(1), 11-26. https://www.urmia.ac.ir/ijltr
title: Fifteen-session topic-based metacognitive awareness listening and speaking course
description: The treatment was a fifteen-week topic-based listening and speaking course "based on Cotterall's (2000) principles of autonomous learning". Six metacognitive strategies drawn from Oxford (1990) were taught at three levels: centering learning (overviewing, focusing attention), arranging and planning learning (identifying task purpose and planning), and evaluating learning (self-editing, self-evaluation). Tasks were linked to the recognition-to-production (PPP) model from Communicative Language Teaching and practiced under the study's three planning conditions.

Opportunities to discuss and practice strategies known to facilitate task performance
constraints: The tasks were not authentic and focused on a limited set of grammatical structures (simple past and past continuous)

oral fluency
strategic self-planning of speech
examples: Experimental classes completed the course alongside narrative picture-strip tasks performed under PTP, OLP, or POLP planning conditions

article_title: The Effect of Talking Story Books on Saudi Young EFL Learners' Reading Comprehension
citation: Hashem Ahmed Alsamadani. (2017). The Effect of Talking Story Books on Saudi Young EFL Learners’ Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 10(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n5p204
title: Weekly five-task talking-story-book cycle integrating listening, retelling, comprehension checking, phonics and story completion
description: The article describes a weekly instructional cycle built around one talking story book, in which learners listen once or twice, then complete sequenced tasks across the week: "Task One Memory-Based Understanding", narrative retelling, true-false questions, phonics word completion, and a written conclusion or completion of 3-5 lines. Each task was assigned to a specific day and was designed to assess a component of reading comprehension such as auditory memory, sequencing and phonics discrimination.
requirements: Each participant needs a well-illustrated talking story book with audio played at a child-like pace and tone
Tasks are spread across the week, one talking story book per week
constraints: Evaluated only with Saudi sixth-grade EFL learners over four weeks using Lady Bird Level 3 stories of 1300 to 1600 words

retelling
spelling
phonics
auditory memory
examples: Over four weeks the experimental group heard Rapunzel, Jack and the Beanstalk, Little Red Riding Hood and the Wolf and the Seven Little Kids, completing five tasks per book, with a written 3-5 line completion on day 5

article_title: The Enhancement of Mathematical Critical Thinking Ability of Aliyah Madrasas Student Model Using Gorontalo by Interactive Learning Setting Cooperative Model
citation: Husnaeni. (2016). The Enhancement of Mathematical Critical Thinking Ability of Aliyah Madrasas Student Model Using Gorontalo by Interactive Learning Setting Cooperative Model. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(8). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1099553
title: Five-aspect framework for measuring mathematical critical thinking ability (MCTA)
description: The study operationalizes mathematical critical thinking ability through five aspects: (1) trigger event — identifying completeness of the premise of a statement and concepts needed to prove it; (2) exploration — constructing meaning and investigating mathematical ideas; (3) drawing conclusions — making and deciding mathematical ideas inductively or deductively; (4) clarification — evaluating and explaining, defining context of mathematical ideas; and (5) resolution — proposing or repairing measures of mathematical proof of a statement. Five description test items, one per aspect, are used for measurement.
requirements: A set of five description-form test items, each targeting one aspect
constraints: The maximum ideal MCTA score is 50
target_learning_goals: Mathematical critical thinking ability
examples: Question 1 targets the trigger event aspect, Question 2 targets exploration, Question 3 targets drawing conclusions, Question 4 targets clarification, and Question 5 targets resolution

engaged learning
collaboration

article_title: The Effects of Vocabulary Instructions on Students' Reading Comprehension across Cognitive Styles in ESP
citation: Kusumawati, E., & Widiati, U. (2017). The Effects of Vocabulary Instructions on Students’ Reading Comprehension across Cognitive Styles in ESP. Journal of Education and Practice, 8(2). https://journals.iiste.org/index.php/JEP/article/view/2894
title: Field dependence–independence cognitive style framework applied to ESP reading instruction
description: The article applies the field dependence/field independence cognitive style framework (Witkin et al., 1971) to ESP reading instruction. FI learners “perceive things as distinct from their background field” and tend toward analytic, abstract interests, while FD learners tend to see things more holistically and are more attentive to social context. The article stresses that FI and FD are tendencies rather than discrete categories, and uses the Group Embedded Figures Test (GEFT) to classify students. It treats cognitive style as an attribute variable that may interact with instructional treatment in determining reading comprehension outcomes.
requirements: A classification instrument such as the Group Embedded Figures Test (GEFT) to identify students’ cognitive style
constraints: The framework describes tendencies, not fixed categories: “the term of FI and FD do not divide people into two distinct groups: there is simply a tendency in any person toward one mode or the other”
target_learning_goals: Matching vocabulary instruction to learners’ cognitive styles
ESP reading comprehension
examples: The study classified 54 Mechatronics students into FI and FD groups using the GEFT before assigning them to explicit or implicit vocabulary instruction conditions
key_sources: Kusumawati, E., & Widiati, U. (2017). The Effects of Vocabulary Instructions on Students’ Reading Comprehension across Cognitive Styles in ESP. Journal of Education and Practice, 8(2). https://journals.iiste.org/index.php/JEP/article/view/2894

Modeling by the instructor

Stakeholder involvement and community participation

Scaffolded acquisition of English as an additional language

Lesson planning templates and lesson plans for training purposes

citation: Al Ansari Ahmed Mohamed. (2026). Managerial perceptions of core competencies for healthcare middle managers in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia: a qualitative study. International Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5116/ijme.6957.fb46
title: Five-domain competency framework for healthcare middle managers
description: The article proposes that successful healthcare middle managers require competencies organized into five overarching domains: "personality, managerial skills, work ethics, mental ability and interaction". The framework emerged from inductive thematic analysis of 27 semi-structured interviews using Braun and Clarke's six-step framework, with selective coding consolidating eight initial themes into the five domains. The authors state these domains "collectively define the core attributes of successful healthcare middle managers in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia" and recommend embedding them into competency-based leadership training.
requirements: Requires input from managers across hierarchical levels (senior, middle, frontline) to capture the full competency picture
constraints: Derived from managers in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia; the authors state this limits generalizability of findings to other regions
target_learning_goals: leadership and management competency development for middle managers
examples: Thematic analysis of 27 interviews in KSA and Bahrain produced the five domains, with subthemes such as integrity, time management, teamwork, communication, and decision-making

title: The final retraining program comprises 11 learning modules and 38 learning directories with 28 theoretical courses and 10 practical components, delivered through online and offline methods.
description: The final retraining program included 11 learning modules covering ideological and political courses and practices, knowledge areas (including professional practice, teaching, research, and management), and skills in the same domains. Training materials included PowerPoint presentations, instructional videos, and a case library. Online learning activities, assessments, and evaluations were conducted through an online platform, while offline components were delivered through continuing education courses organized by the Peritoneal Dialysis Nursing Group of the Zhejiang Nursing Association, as well as grassroots training programs or nursing salons.
requirements: A three-tier responsibility system was established for the development of teaching materials, with a three-level review process involving course experts, peer experts, and the project leader.
constraints: The usage standards: at least half of the nurses' working hours are dedicated to specialized nursing, teaching, research, and management related to peritoneal dialysis, and they have been doing so for at least 3 years.

title: Fixed disease-module curriculum architecture combining contouring, structured plan review, MDT debriefing and narrative feedback
description: The curriculum was designed backward from core clinical tasks rather than lecture topics, organized into three fixed disease modules (locally advanced NPC without induction chemotherapy, middle/lower thoracic esophageal cancer, FIGO 2018 IB3–IIIC1 cervical cancer). Each module combined "one contouring task, one structured plan-review task, one multidisciplinary team (MDT)-style case presentation, and one narrative-feedback encounter", delivered over about 2 weeks with 6–8 hours of supervised faculty contact. The authors regard this architecture as making contouring and plan review explicit and assessable within routine training.

Preparatory packages (contouring atlas, planning note, pitfalls summary) before each module

Structured treatment-plan review
Multidisciplinary clinical reasoning
examples: Each module was delivered over approximately 2 weeks with 2–3 h of supervised contouring review, 2 h of structured plan-review discussion, one MDT-style case session and one narrative-feedback session

title: Five-category modular teaching resource repository for Endodontics education
description: The repository comprises five categories: a Multi-level Video Repository (standardized procedures, micro-lectures, virtual simulation demonstrations), an Exemplary Teaching Resource Bank (lesson plans, mind maps, 3D anatomical diagrams, assessment questions), a Hotspot and Frontier Knowledge Link Library, a Stomatology-Specific Ideological and Political Case Database, and a Student Advanced Work Exhibition Repository. article_title: The Impact of Scaffolding on Academic Achievement in Undergraduate Emergency Language Courses.
citation: Zhu An, Ye Jian-Hong. (2026). The Impact of Scaffolding on Academic Achievement in Undergraduate Emergency Language Courses. Journal of Psycholinguistic Research. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10936-026-10254-9
title: Five-phase scaffolding instructional design for language courses
description: The article applies He's (1997) five-component scaffolding model to an emergency language course: building the scaffold (pre-testing to determine learning situation), entering the context (using movies or pictures to create emergency situations), independent exploration (teacher guidance gradually decreasing as student ability increases), collaborative learning (group work and discussion), and evaluation (student presentations with timely teacher feedback). This sequence structures an 8-week course across four emergency-event teaching units. The article describes it as a design in which "the teacher's guidance gradually decreases as the students' problem-solving ability increases until the students are able to complete the tasks independently."
requirements: Teacher capacity to design graduated learning units and provide timely feedback
Pre-testing to determine students' starting point
constraints: Validated only for a foreign-language (English) emergency language course with Chinese undergraduates; the article notes other language types (Mandarin, dialects, sign languages) were not studied
target_learners: Undergraduate students of teaching Chinese to speakers of other languages
target_learning_goals: Emergency language proficiency in English
Professionalism as emergency personnel
examples: The 8-week course covered four units: public health events, natural disasters, social security emergencies, and sudden accidents and disasters, culminating in student presentations and teacher assessment.
key_sources: Zhu An, Ye Jian-Hong. (2026). The Impact of Scaffolding on Academic Achievement in Undergraduate Emergency Language Courses. Journal of Psycholinguistic Research. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10936-026-10254-9

citation: Cummins MR, Perri Moore Seneca S, Sward KA. (2026). Inflection Point: Artificial Intelligence, Digital Health, and the Evolution of Pre-Licensure Nursing Informatics Competencies. Computers, Informatics, Nursing. https://doi.org/10.1097/CIN.0000000000001506
title: Fifth wave of nursing informatics competencies: digital health practice as user, contributor, evaluator, and steward
description: The review proposes a logical fifth wave in the evolution of pre-licensure nursing informatics competencies, characterized by digital health and building on the prior four waves. It argues "This phase requires nurses to function not only as users of technology, but also as informed contributors, evaluators, and ethical stewards of digital health systems that increasingly shape care delivery." The wave builds on, rather than replaces, established foundations such as clinical decision support, workflow integration, and ethical deployment of health IT.
requirements: Consensus-driven competency development building on existing frameworks while incorporating AI and digital health demands
Intentional and practical faculty development strategies
constraints: The review frames this as a proposed direction requiring research: "research to guide this evolution is urgently needed"
target_learning_goals: critical evaluation of digital health applications
ethical stewardship of digital health systems
use of emerging digital health technologies
examples: The review presents the fifth wave as a shift toward advanced digital health practice responding to telehealth, AI, and sensor-based monitoring integration into care

citation: Rahimi A. Masie, van Emden Michael, Hardon Sem F., Simons Maarten, Bonjer H. Jaap, Horeman Tim, Daams Freek. (2026). title: Fix4Life embalmed cadaver model for high-fidelity laparoscopic training
description: Fix4Life (F4L) is a novel embalming technique for human cadavers used as a training modality for laparoscopic surgery. The article describes it as "a novel embalming technique without phenol and with low formaldehyde concentration, resulting in flexible and pliable tissue without discoloration". Unlike fresh frozen cadavers, F4L specimens allow long-term preservation and repeated use across courses, which the authors note is relevant ethically and financially, with preparation costs comparable to traditional embalming.

constraints: Traditional embalmed cadavers cause discoloration and stiffening, which F4L was designed to avoid
target_learning_goals: laparoscopic procedural skills
anatomical knowledge
tissue manipulation

description: The article structures its blended sim-lab module into five sequential parts: pre-class preparation and quiz, theoretical lecture, teacher's demonstration, guided students' operation, and post-class support. Demonstrations use dual-view filming (long-range and close-range), and an endoscopic demonstration shows "the placement of the fulcrum during operation, the way the instrument entered, and the movement form of the instrument under the gingiva." Guided practice occurs on standardized typodonts with instructor supervision, followed by post-class on-site preceptorship and synchronous tele-mentoring.

Instructors with pedagogical training, collaborative lesson planning and procedural calibration
An instructor-to-student ratio of 1:7.5 (2:15 per group) during practical instruction

Access to Complete Anatomy and QuPath during sessions

citation: Stochlinski Caroline, Maleczek Mathias, Korn Lukas, Gleiss Andreas, Breckwoldt Jan, Roessler Bernhard. (2026). Skill retention of advanced airway techniques after simulation training – a randomized prospective study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08646-5
title: Fiction contract in simulation pre-briefing
description: The fiction contract is a psychological agreement used during the theoretical input and pre-briefing of simulation-based education. "It describes an explicit agreement between facilitators and learners who share the common goal of experiencing the simulation as realistically as possible": teachers design an authentic scenario while learners actively engage and treat the simulated situation as a real clinical encounter. The article states the literature emphasises this contract, particularly in pre-briefing, as contributing to psychological immersion, active participation and learning success, and recommends it as an integral part of planning simulation formats.
requirements: Facilitators design an authentic scenario; learners actively engage and treat the simulated situation as a real clinical encounter
constraints: The article attributes its importance to the simulation literature rather than testing it in this trial

examples: In this study the fictional contract was a central element during the theoretical input led by the same instructor for all participants

article_title: Artificial Intelligence in Couple and Family Therapy: Introduction of the AI Competencies.
citation: Hertlein Katherine M. and Springer Paul. (2026). Artificial Intelligence in Couple and Family Therapy: Introduction of the AI Competencies. Journal of Marital and Family Therapy. https://doi.org/10.1111/jmft.70121
title: First-order versus second-order conceptualizations of AI use in CMFT
description: The article proposes an organizing axis for AI in CMFT: first-order use treats AI as a tool, but "viewing AI as only a tool is a limited view" that "discounts how AI alters the process of therapy in a second‐order way." Second-order use treats AI as a "third actor/third entity" whose rules must be negotiated, changing the roles of therapist, client, and AI in treatment.
requirements: Second-order use requires the therapist to acknowledge their own role in the system, negotiate and govern new rules with AI as a third entity, and shift from human-to-human dyads to human–human–technology triads.
constraints: The article states that AI's focus on dynamics and reflection affects the rules of therapy and may maintain the problem, and that first-order tool use alone discounts AI's second-order impact.
target_learning_goals: understand AI's systemic, second-order impact on therapeutic practice
key_sources: Hertlein Katherine M. and Springer Paul. (2026). Artificial Intelligence in Couple and Family Therapy: Introduction of the AI Competencies. Journal of Marital and Family Therapy. https://doi.org/10.1111/jmft.70121

title: 5-AI-role model decomposing AI functions across the OSCE life cycle
description: The article proposes a 5-AI-role model—learning assistant, AI-augmented standardized patient, assessment assistant, case generator, and learning analyst—mapped to pre-OSCE, peri-OSCE, and post-OSCE workflows. Its stated intention is to "augment, not replace, human expertise and make the assessment enterprise more transparent and improvable." Each role carries specified inputs, outputs, governance artifacts, human control points, and key risks (Table 1), e.g., the assessment assistant produces "time-stamped evidence links and suggested checklist marks" that raters verify, edit, or reject.

constraints: The model is conceptual; the article states it does not provide prospective evidence that AI-augmented OSCEs improve reliability, validity, equity, or learning outcomes
target_learning_goals: clinical communication, reasoning, and procedural skills assessed in OSCEs
examples: Table 1 assigns each role a primary function, governance artifacts, human control points, and risks to monitor, such as overscaffolding for the learning assistant and construct underrepresentation for the assessment assistant

description: The article proposes that a common competency core underpins safe redistribution of tasks, organized into five domains. As printed, "Five domains are central: task‐level clinical decision‐making, technical safety management, interprofessional communication, equipment operation, and troubleshooting." Each domain is specified behaviorally: decision-making means recognizing salient cues, applying protocols, and escalating; safety management covers sterile technique, device and medication checks, fallbacks and stop rules; communication uses shared frameworks such as SBAR and closed-loop confirmation; equipment operation covers setup, parameter verification, and maintenance; troubleshooting combines systematic fault finding with judgment to pause and request assistance at thresholds.
requirements: Assessment scenarios must map simulation features to the five domains to offer "practical routes to measurable proficiency"
constraints: The domains are proposed for well-defined clinical activities moved under protocols and supervision, not unrestricted task transfer
target_learning_goals: task-level clinical decision-making
technical safety management
interprofessional communication
equipment operation
troubleshooting
examples: The article maps simulation features, debriefing approaches, and psychological safety closely to the five competency domains as routes to measurable proficiency.

article_title: Effect of simulator fidelity on skill acquisition and trainee satisfaction in arthroscopic surgery training for novices: a prospective randomized comparative study.
citation: Kutsuna Tatsuhiko, Kinoshita Tomofumi, Hino Kazunori, Watamori Kunihiko, Tsuda Takashi, Yamaoka Shintaro, Takao Masaki. (2025). Effect of simulator fidelity on skill acquisition and trainee satisfaction in arthroscopic surgery training for novices: a prospective randomized comparative study. International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11548-025-03528-5
title: Use high-fidelity simulation to enhance novice trainee satisfaction and motivation even when it does not outperform low-fidelity simulation for short-term skill acquisition
description: The article concludes that simulator fidelity influences not only technical skill development but also learner satisfaction: "high-fidelity simulators significantly improve training satisfaction compared to low-fidelity simulators", evident after a single session. Because training satisfaction is described as a determinant of learning motivation and engagement, the authors suggest fidelity's value for novices lies in the immersive, engaging experience it provides, and call for more cost-effective high-fidelity simulators to expand access to high-quality surgical training.
requirements: A well-designed high-fidelity simulator with realistic graphics and haptic feedback to create an immersive surgical environment
constraints: The skill-acquisition advantage was not demonstrated: no significant skill differences were observed after a single session, and long-term effects of repeated training remain unclear per the authors

examples: In the study, ArthroSim trainees reported significantly higher satisfaction with instrument handling (p = 0.024) and overall knee arthroscopy training (p = 0.033) despite equivalent ASSET scores and completion times

citation: Zhao Juan, Hu Zhongjun. (2025). Big data analytics platform enhances teaching abilities in normal university students through triple helix collaboration. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-27799-9
title: Five-dimension teaching ability development framework spanning cognitive, procedural, social, reflective, and technological competencies
description: The article proposes a multidimensional construct of teaching ability for normal university students, tracked along five dimensions: cognitive (subject knowledge and pedagogical content knowledge), procedural (instructional planning and implementation), social (classroom management and student relationships), reflective (self-assessment and adaptation), and technological (educational technology integration). Each dimension encompasses "hierarchical competency levels from foundational to transformative, with specific observable indicators that can be automatically extracted and analyzed from digital teaching artifacts". Development is modeled as a non-linear growth trajectory from novice to expert.
requirements: Observable indicators extractable from digital teaching artifacts (videos, lesson plans, journals)
constraints: The growth-function and reliability formulas are presented as conceptual/theoretical frameworks rather than operational calculation tools
target_learning_goals: Progressive development of teaching ability from novice toward expert integration of theory and practice
examples: The framework enables continuous formative assessment, personalized development pathways, and evidence-based interventions throughout professional preparation programs

citation: Güdük Ömer Faruk, Berberoğlu İpek Nur, Akturan Selçuk. (2025). A single-group pre–post OSCE evaluation of a simulation-based clinical readiness module in pediatric dentistry. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08215-2
title: Five-station pediatric dentistry OSCE with weighted checklists and standardized patients
description: An objective structured clinical examination with five stations (one comprising two scored procedures) covering Medical History Taking, Child–Parent Communication, Team Dynamics, Oral Hygiene Instruction, and Topical Fluoride and Fissure Sealant Application. Checklists were adapted from DEPAD-accredited open-access resources, aligned with the DUÇEP-2024 national core curriculum, and scored on a 3-point scale with weighted items: "Certain critical steps were designated as gold standard behaviours and weighted more heavily in the scoring". Scores ranged 0–100 per outcome.
requirements: Content validity established through review by three subject-matter experts and one medical educator with consensus finalization
Evaluator training in OSCE methodology before implementation
Scripted scenarios and rehearsal sessions for standardized patients
constraints: No additional validity or reliability testing was conducted beyond the expert review; evaluators were not blinded to pre/post status and no formal calibration session was conducted
target_learning_goals: assessment of technical skills, communication, and professional behaviors in pediatric dentistry
examples: Trained standardized patients were used in three stations, including a live child's voice behind a glass panel and a simulated distressed-parent syncope scenario (observed but not scored)
