description: A novel scoring system developed by the authors to assess the quality of ChatGPT-4 responses to clinical cases. It comprises five items: "Diagnostic ranking (DR) (0–10 points)", diagnostic strategy and investigation proposal accuracy (0–5), completeness (0–5), clarity and understandability (0–5), and appropriate use of medical terminology (0–5), for a maximum of 30 points. Three independent expert internal medicine physicians scored each response with it, and detailed criteria were provided in Appendix S1.
requirements: Three independent expert IM physicians, not involved in case selection or participation, to score each response
constraints: Only the diagnostic ranking item demonstrated excellent inter-rater reliability (ICC = .98); clarity and terminology showed poor reliability
target_learning_goals: evaluating AI-generated diagnostic responses in clinical reasoning
examples: Used to score ChatGPT-4 responses to five NEJM Case Challenge cases presented by 15 participants of varying medical expertise

title: Five-part LLM prompt template for AI-assisted grading of short-answer questions
description: The approach gives large-language models instructor-guided few-shot prompt templates for grading: "The prompt includes the text of the SAQ, the instructor’s criteria for a good answer, multiple examples of student responses paired with the instructor’s grades and personalized feedback, and a new, ungraded student answer." In all classes instructors implemented the approach with OpenAI's GPT-4, and generated grades and feedback were entered into the course's learning platform.

constraints: GPT-4 was chosen over an open-source model, prioritizing ease of use and stronger performance over replicability and transparency, since model parameters are not public

target_learning_goals: critical thinking through short-answer questions with personalized instructor feedback
examples: Across four undergraduate classes in 2023/2024, 88% of 3,080 SAQ answers from 271 students were graded with AI assistance

citation: Anyinkeng A, Mesfin GS, Taryim M, Efuetlateh J, Tsion H, Ahmed AK. (2025). The role of remote and virtual surgical training in expanding cardiothoracic surgical capacity in low-resource regions. BMC Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12893-025-03142-x
title: Five-phase implementation framework for virtual surgical training in low-resource settings
description: The review proposes a structured five-phase implementation framework (Fig. 2) to translate policy into action for institutions adopting virtual surgical training. It begins with a readiness and needs assessment, followed by resource and technology planning, design and integration aligning virtual training with existing curricula and validated assessments such as OSATS and the Global Rating Scale, implementation through pilot programs with routine monitoring and iterative feedback, and finally credentialing and scale-up aligned with national certification bodies. The authors state it offers "step-by-step, practical guidance that practicing surgeons and institutional leaders can use to translate policy into action".
requirements: Readiness and needs assessment identifying local training gaps, infrastructure capacity, and faculty engagement
Cost-effective, context-appropriate tools and platforms
Validated assessment methods such as OSATS and the Global Rating Scale
constraints: Aimed at low-resource settings; the review notes implementation is difficult without reliable electricity, stable internet, and suitable physical spaces for simulation labs
target_learners: Practicing surgeons, institutional leaders, and surgical trainees in low- and middle-income countries
target_learning_goals: Safe transition from simulation-based training to patient care and sustainable surgical workforce development
examples: The framework's design and integration phase incorporates validated assessment methods and continuous assessment with supervised practice to ensure a smooth transition to patient care

article_title: Training the trainees in robotic surgery - a pilot scheme in the United Kingdom.
citation: Al-Ani Mohammed, Massias Samuel, Jayawardena Panduka, Khanderia Esha, Franklyn Joshua, Hashmi Khawar, Patel Vanash. (2025). Training the trainees in robotic surgery – a pilot scheme in the United Kingdom. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07749-9
title: Five-step sequential robotic training pathway with benchmark-gated progression
description: The article describes a structured, sequential training pathway for surgical trainees new to robotic console surgery. It "included sequential steps: online didactic modules, a first-assist course, performance-tracked virtual simulation exercises using the Versius Trainer, basic surgical skills assessment, and supervised training in live operating lists". Progression was contingent on meeting defined objective benchmarks at each stage, and live operating used a modular, step-by-step deconstruction of procedures adapted from laparoscopic training paradigms, with case segmentation based on trainee competence to protect patient safety.
requirements: Consultant trainers who have completed their own robotic learning curve and been approved to train trainees
Access to the robotic platform's e-learning, first assist course and Versius Trainer simulation resources
constraints: Rolled out at a single centre using a single robotic platform, which the authors state could limit generalisability
Trainees received no dedicated time off from service; training was embedded in clinical schedules
target_learners: General surgical specialist trainees (ST4–ST8) with no prior robotic console experience
target_learning_goals: Robotic console surgical competence, including system set-up, instrument and endoscope use, suturing, knot-tying and live procedural skills
examples: Anterior resections were taught via a modular approach: medial-to-lateral dissection, vascular control, lateral mobilisation of the sigmoid colon, and total mesorectal excision
The Versius Trainer component comprised 16 proficiency-based tasks, some requiring two consecutive and three total passes

article_title: Proposing core competencies for physicians in using artificial intelligence tools in clinical practice.
citation: Scott IA, Shaw T, Slade C, Wan TT, Barmanray R, Coorey C, Johnson SLJ, Bell L, Herd M, Sullivan CM. (2025). Proposing core competencies for physicians in using artificial intelligence tools in clinical practice. Internal Medicine Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/imj.70112
title: Five-domain core competency framework for physicians using AI tools in clinical practice
description: The article proposes a framework of core competencies for practising physicians using AI tools, organised into five domains: foundational knowledge of AI tools, critical appraisal of AI tools, use of AI tools, patient interaction with AI tools, and professionalism and AI tools. Each domain is framed by a guiding question (e.g. 'Should this AI tool be used?') and enumerated subcompetencies. The authors define competencies as 'the demonstrable knowledge, skills, abilities and behaviours that contribute to individual and organisational performance'. The framework targets practising physicians, a group the authors say prior competency proposals did not target.
requirements: Physicians are not expected to become AI experts; competencies are scoped to proper use of AI tools within their areas of practice
constraints: The list is explicitly non-exhaustive and proposed as a starting point for further discussion
Additional competency domains and subcompetencies may be required for different specialties and as AI tools evolve
target_learning_goals: understand AI tool types and limitations
appraise AI tools critically
use AI tools effectively and ethically
involve patients when using AI tools
fulfil professional responsibilities in AI adoption
examples: Table 1 enumerates the five domains and their subcompetencies, from differentiating machine learning, deep learning and generative AI to assuming responsibility for patient care decisions involving AI support

citation: Tam, C. Y. W., Dizon, J. I. W. T., Sin, S. W. C., Tang, G. K. Y., Lai, V. Y. W., Wong, Y. Y., Ganotice, F. A., & Yeung, N. P. (2025). Implementation of hybrid simulation training to promote collective and self-efficacy in medical students: a two-pronged approach. Annals of Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2025.2527362
title: Two-dimensional fidelity framework: physical resemblance versus functional task alignment
description: The article adopts Hamstra et al.'s stratification of simulation fidelity into two dimensions: "physical resemblance – characterized by the tactile, visual, auditory and olfactory appearance of the simulator relative to the simulation concept in mind" and "functional task alignment – the simulator's functional property in alignment with the learning objectives at hand". This distinction underpins the study's argument that low-fidelity basic manikins can achieve functional alignment (e.g. compression rhythm mastery in CPR) at low cost, while VPS supplies clinical information and haemodynamics that a high-fidelity manikin would otherwise relay.
requirements: Simulator selection must be judged against the learning objectives at hand via functional task alignment, not overall fidelity labels
constraints: The article notes that unequivocal interpretations of 'high-fidelity' in wider literature complicate model selection, particularly in resource-limited settings
target_learners: medical and healthcare students in simulation-based training
target_learning_goals: aligning simulator modality choice with acute-care learning objectives
examples: The study paired a basic CPR manikin with BodyInteract VPS so the manikin handled functional task alignment while the VPS relayed physical exam findings and emulated haemodynamics.

title: Five-factor model of e-learning utilization among health professions students
description: The article proposes and validates a model in which e-learning utilization among undergraduate health professions students is explained by five latent constructs: purpose of using the internet (PUR), confidence/perceived ease of using technology (CON), perceived advantages of e-learning (PAE), perceived limitations of e-learning (PLE), and perceived educational impact (PEI). constraints: Developed and tested in a single South Indian institution with first-year medical and dental students; incremental fit indices fell below recommended thresholds, and three hypothesized factors (AVL, PRE, LXE) did not hold in this setting

examples: The hypothesized eight-factor model (Fig. 1) was reduced to the validated five-factor CFA/SEM model (Fig. 2) using split-sample EFA and CFA

article_title: Enhancing clinical reasoning skills in medical students through team-based learning: a mixed-methods study.
citation: Ishizuka K, Shikino K, Takada N, et al. (2025). Enhancing clinical reasoning skills in medical students through team-based learning: a mixed-methods study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06784-w
title: Fink's taxonomy of significant learning as an organizing framework for TBL's advantages in clinical reasoning education
description: Fink's taxonomy of significant learning is a six-level framework the article used to set the analytic categories of its qualitative content analysis: "learning how to learn, caring, human dimension, integration, application, and foundational knowledge." Each level was given a specific meaning in the study: "Learning how to learn" included self-regulated learning strategies, "caring" included emotional engagement and motivation, "human dimension" included teamwork and peer interactions, "integration" captured connecting ideas across clinical contexts, "application" included practical use of clinical reasoning skills, and "foundational knowledge" focused on core medical concepts. The framework organized 233 codes of students' perceived advantages of TBL.
requirements: Open-ended questionnaire data coded inductively, with subcategories examined for alignment with one of the six levels
constraints: Applied here to fourth-year medical students' self-perceptions in a single TBL course at one Japanese institution
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning skills
significant learning across knowledge, application, integration, human dimension, caring, and learning how to learn
examples: Content analysis mapped 89 codes to the human dimension, 69 to integration, 40 to application, 20 to learning how to learn, 8 to caring, and 7 to foundational knowledge
key_sources: Ishizuka K, Shikino K, Takada N, et al. (2025). Enhancing clinical reasoning skills in medical students through team-based learning: a mixed-methods study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06784-w

article_title: Assessment of first-year medical student perceptions in the development of self-directed learning skills in a single medical school course.
citation: Beck Amanda P. (2025). Assessment of first-year medical student perceptions in the development of self-directed learning skills in a single medical school course. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06890-9
title: Five-item Student Self-Assessment of Acquisition of Skills for Self-Directed Learning rubric
description: A five-item self-report rubric developed in-house to aid students' self-assessment of SDL competency during the CRE course. Items cover independently identifying/analyzing/synthesizing information, assessing source credibility, teamwork and communication, critical thinking, and using facilitator and peer feedback, each rated on a four-level proficiency scale (1 = Initial to 4 = Proficient) loosely based on the NIH Proficiency Scale, with behavioral anchors. Exploratory factor analysis yielded one factor ("SDL Competency") accounting for 76.05% of variance, with Cronbach's alpha of 0.92.
requirements: Voluntary student completion via Qualtrics at defined time points; total score ranges from 5 to 20
constraints: The article states a major limitation is that it is based on voluntary self-assessment and "is not a direct measure of their SDL abilities"; the very short length and lack of detailed psychometric analysis of items are also stated limitations
target_learning_goals: self-assessment of SDL competency
formative self-evaluation of skill development
examples: Items were selected from a larger pool written by the NYMC SDL Subcommittee, refined to five statements, and validated with principal components extraction and varimax rotation
key_sources: Beck Amanda P. (2025). Assessment of first-year medical student perceptions in the development of self-directed learning skills in a single medical school course. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06890-9

article_title: Perceived mental health skills and competence among occupational health physicians.
citation: Majuri M, Malin M, Antila A, Luukkonen R, Palosaari M, Reijula K. (2024). Perceived mental health skills and competence among occupational health physicians. Occupational Medicine (Oxford, England). https://doi.org/10.1093/occmed/kqae080
title: Five-factor taxonomy of mental health competences for OH specialist physician training
description: The article derives, by exploratory factor analysis of its 23-item questionnaire, a five-factor structure of OH mental health competence: "general mental health, workplace risks and resources, rehabilitation, promotion and prevention, and special skills". General mental health skills are achieved in medical school; workplace risks and resources correspond to core EPAs done at workplace level; rehabilitation covers individual employee-level medical and vocational rehabilitation; promotion and prevention target sickness-absence prevention. All factors showed internal consistency with Cronbach's alpha over 0.83.
requirements: The questionnaire was built on the current Finnish curriculum and legislation and validated with university personnel, clinical lecturers and pedagogies before data collection
constraints: The factor structure was derived from a 9%-response survey sample dominated by the University of Helsinki area, and the authors state results must be interpreted with caution in the international context because the OH physician role varies among countries
target_learners: trainee physicians in OH specialist training
target_learning_goals: mental health competence in occupational health practice, spanning diagnosis, work ability assessment, rehabilitation, and workplace-level promotion and prevention
examples: Factor loadings were assigned with a 0.40 threshold and communality over 0.30, with a panel of experienced OH specialists resolving items loading on two factors
key_sources: Majuri M, Malin M, Antila A, Luukkonen R, Palosaari M, Reijula K. (2024). Perceived mental health skills and competence among occupational health physicians. Occupational Medicine (Oxford, England). https://doi.org/10.1093/occmed/kqae080

article_title: Small programs, big challenges: Reimagining the evaluation of clinical teaching in genetic counseling.
citation: Randall Armel, S. (2025). Small programs, big challenges: Reimagining the evaluation of clinical teaching in genetic counseling. Journal of Genetic Counseling, 34, e1924. https://doi.org/10.1002/jgc4.1924
title: Five-dimension framework of effective clinical teaching-learning
description: A framework for conceptualizing effective "clinical teaching‐learning" that the review reports from Ahmady & Khani (2022), organizing quality clinical teaching into "five dimensions including behavioral (learner, teacher, and patient factors), social (interactions between the learner, patient, and healthcare workers), pedagogical (instructional design and teaching‐learning opportunities), contextual (positive learning environment), and educational leadership". The review uses it to show that quality teaching is multidimensional and that no single student perspective can capture it. It also notes a medicine review identified 49 themes of good clinical teaching categorized as physician, teacher, or humanistic traits.
requirements: Requires defining effective teaching before measuring it, since the review states measuring effective teaching first requires defining it
constraints: The review notes whether these characterizations apply across all health professions remains largely unanswered, with some studies suggesting the definition is context-specific
target_learners: health professions students in clinical placements
target_learning_goals: effective clinical teaching and supervision
quality of the clinical learning environment
examples: The review contrasts this framework with a genetic counseling Delphi study that ranked 142 of 158 proposed supervisor competencies as highly important, grouped into six domains including student evaluation and student-centered supervision
key_sources: Randall Armel, S. (2025). Small programs, big challenges: Reimagining the evaluation of clinical teaching in genetic counseling. Journal of Genetic Counseling, 34, e1924. https://doi.org/10.1002/jgc4.1924

article_title: Automated performance metrics and surgical gestures: two methods for assessment of technical skills in robotic surgery.
citation: Olsen RG, Svendsen MBS, Tolsgaard MG, Konge L, Røder A, Bjerrum F. (2024). Automated performance metrics and surgical gestures: two methods for assessment of technical skills in robotic surgery. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-024-02051-0
title: Five-category surgical gesture taxonomy for annotating simulated robot-assisted radical prostatectomy videos
description: The gesture assessment method uses five manually annotated gesture types: "regular dissection, hemostatic control, application of clips, needle handling, and suturing". Gesture totals were transformed into idle time (time between phases with no annotations) and active time (total duration of gesture phases), then into z-scores and a composite score across three part-procedures and three repetitions. A pass/fail score of −0.4 standard deviations was set using the contrasting groups' method.
requirements: Videos need to be recorded, manually annotated, and analyzed before being presented
constraints: The method is still in the early stages of development as it requires manual interpretation and video annotation
target_learners: novice robotic surgeons in simulation-based training
target_learning_goals: technical skills assessment in robotic surgery
examples: 144 videos of bladder neck dissection, neurovascular-bundle dissection, and urethrovesical anastomosis were manually annotated with the five gestures.
key_sources: Olsen RG, Svendsen MBS, Tolsgaard MG, Konge L, Røder A, Bjerrum F. (2024). Automated performance metrics and surgical gestures: two methods for assessment of technical skills in robotic surgery. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-024-02051-0

article_title: Time for a simulation strategy?
citation: Shiner N. (2023). Time for a simulation strategy? Journal of Medical Radiation Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1002/jmrs.685
title: Five-stage scaffolded integration of simulation into healthcare curricula
description: Browne and Philips offer "a 5‐stage scaffolded approach to integrating simulation into healthcare curricula": (1) online learning; (2) facilitated practical (task training); (3) simulation consolidation (facilitated simulation); (4) simulation days (remote facilitation); (5) clinical practice. The editorial recommends integrating SBE early so students' confidence and competence build along with scenario complexity, consistent with cognitive load theory.
requirements: Educators should ensure a scaffolded approach to learning is used, offering a reduced-risk environment to build from prior to clinical practice
constraints: Mastery does not come with one-off simulations, so frequency of simulation in the curriculum must be planned
target_learning_goals: Building confidence and competence progressively before clinical practice
examples: The editorial presents the five stages as a sequence from online learning through facilitated practical and consolidation to clinical practice.
key_sources: Shiner N. (2023). Time for a simulation strategy? Journal of Medical Radiation Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1002/jmrs.685

article_title: The effect of e-learning on point-of-care ultrasound education in novices.
citation: Lien Wan-Ching, Lin Phone, Chang Chih-Heng, Wu Meng-Che, Wu Cheng-Yi. (2022). The effect of e-learning on point-of-care ultrasound education in novices. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2022.2152522
title: Five-stage interactive e-learning platform for point-of-care ultrasound (FAST) training
description: An interactive e-learning platform for PGY-1 PoCUS training structured in five irreversible stages: "Stage 1 was Pretest Stage with multiple-choice questions", a Teaching Stage for core knowledge, a Self-Learning Stage recognizing at least 20 US images with interactive interpretation, a Self-Testing Stage, and a Case-Simulation Stage for clinical judgments. User activity and time per stage were automatically recorded, and a satisfaction survey preceded logout. Most users finished Stages 1–3 at first access and accessed the platform via desktops or laptops (95% of accesses).
requirements: Internet access and unique user authorization to access the platform
US machines and a hands-on FAST curriculum (30-min didactics and 2-hour hands-on training) alongside the platform
constraints: The learning process was irreversible among stages and steps within a stage
In this study only FAST performance was evaluated, at a single academic hospital
target_learners: first postgraduate year (PGY-1) residents, novice sonographers
target_learning_goals: FAST image acquisition and interpretation
clinical judgment in point-of-care ultrasound
examples: 70 PGY-1 users made 324 accesses (median 3, IQR 1–6) and reported high satisfaction with platform design (median 4.5), content (5), image quality (5), and the training course (5)
key_sources: Lien Wan-Ching, Lin Phone, Chang Chih-Heng, Wu Meng-Che, Wu Cheng-Yi. (2022). The effect of e-learning on point-of-care ultrasound education in novices. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2022.2152522

article_title: Can virtual-reality simulation ensure transthoracic echocardiography skills before trainees examine patients?
citation: Nielsen Martine S., Clausen Jesper H., Hoffmann-Petersen Joachim, Konge Lars, Nielsen Anders B. (2022). Can virtual-reality simulation ensure transthoracic echocardiography skills before trainees examine patients? International Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5116/ijme.6321.8e5d
title: Fitts and Posner three-stage model of motor skill acquisition
description: The article uses the Fitts and Posner model to interpret its observed score patterns: "Fitts and Posner presented three sequential stages of learning, where movement eventually becomes automatic as competency is gathered." In the cognitive stage individuals rely on working memory and declarative knowledge; the associative stage decreases dependence on working memory and yields more fluent movement; the autonomous stage requires minimal cognitive effort, creating better error detection, decision-making and anticipation with minimal variation. The authors map novices to the first stage and experienced physicians to the last.
requirements: Time in each stage depends on the trainee's level of skills, knowledge and behaviours; supporting each learning pace with no time restraint is essential in the educational setup
target_learners: medical trainees acquiring procedural skills such as TTE
target_learning_goals: automatisation of scanning and projection-finding skills
examples: Novices used more time and often struggled to find correct projections, while experienced physicians' scores and test times indicated they had reached the autonomous stage
key_sources: Nielsen Martine S., Clausen Jesper H., Hoffmann-Petersen Joachim, Konge Lars, Nielsen Anders B. (2022). Can virtual-reality simulation ensure transthoracic echocardiography skills before trainees examine patients? International Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5116/ijme.6321.8e5d

article_title: Developing a best practice framework for clinical competency education in the traditional East-Asian medicine curriculum.
citation: Han Sang Yun, Lee Seung-Hee, Chae Han. (2022). Developing a best practice framework for clinical competency education in the traditional East-Asian medicine curriculum. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03398-4
title: Five core clinical competencies designated for traditional Korean medicine graduates
description: The program defines "five core competencies designated for the clinical education of traditional Korean medicine": maintaining a clean and sterile clinical setting, accurate physical examination, correct traditional diagnosis with patient explanation, safe performance of acupuncture, moxibustion, cupping and pharmacopuncture, and "Proficient preparation, processing, and prescription of medical herbs". These competencies organize the curriculum, facilities, and assessment design described in the framework.
requirements: Curriculum modules, practice facilities and test stations aligned so each competency is taught and assessed
target_learners: students training as primary care traditional Korean medicine practitioners
target_learning_goals: safe and effective clinical procedures, diagnosis, and herbal preparation
examples: Each competency maps to specific test items, e.g. medical herbs are assessed in the Practice Lab for Medical Herb
key_sources: Han Sang Yun, Lee Seung-Hee, Chae Han. (2022). Developing a best practice framework for clinical competency education in the traditional East-Asian medicine curriculum. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03398-4

article_title: Effective principal leadership behaviors to improve the teacher performance and the student achievement.
citation: Pardosi J and Utari TI. (2021). Effective principal leadership behaviors to improve the teacher performance and the student achievement. F1000Research, Volume 10, 465. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.51549.1
title: Fiedler's Leadership Contingency Model as the framework for effective principal leadership behaviors
description: The article adopts Fiedler's Leadership Contingency Model to operationalize effective principal leadership behaviors. It states that "According to the Leadership Contingency Model developed by Fiedler (1967), there are three main situational variables to determine whether the situation is suitable or effective for the leadership": the leader-member relationship, the degree of task structure, and position power. The study's questionnaire and SEM measurement model build the leadership effectiveness latent variable from these three manifest variables, and the article concludes effective principal leadership behaviors were limited to these three factors.
requirements: Leadership effectiveness is assessed through the three situational variables: leader-follower relationship, task structure, and position power
constraints: The article concludes effective principal leadership behaviors were limited to the three factors (a) leader-follower relationship, (b) task structure, and (c) position power
target_learning_goals: improving teacher performance and student achievement through effective leadership behavior
examples: The study measured leadership behavior effectiveness through 30 questionnaire items covering followers' belief, respect, familiarity and affection for the leader; clarity of goals and tasks; and the leader's power to direct, evaluate, reward and punish
key_sources: Pardosi J and Utari TI. (2021). Effective principal leadership behaviors to improve the teacher performance and the student achievement. F1000Research, Volume 10, 465. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.51549.1

article_title: Scalable Science Education via Online Cooperative Questioning.
citation: Hilton, C. B., Goldwater, M. B., Hancock, D., Clemson, M., Huang, A., & Denyer, G. (2022). Scalable Science Education via Online Cooperative Questioning. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 21(1). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.19-11-0249
title: Five-step scaffolded sequence of question answering, evaluation, and solo-then-cooperative authoring
description: This pattern organizes a semester of PeerWise-supported activities so that answering and evaluating existing questions precedes solo authoring, which precedes cooperative authoring with peer feedback. The exercises "leverage analogical comparison, self-explanation, and confronting misconceptions," and generative prompts ask what would happen if a step were inhibited or activated and invite analogies. Each step was two weeks apart, with questions assigned to randomly distributed learning outcomes covering exam content.
requirements: An online question bank platform (PeerWise) with rating and comment functions
Instructor-led tutorial on Bloom's taxonomy and reflective questioning
Learning outcomes allocated across the cohort
constraints: Steps 3 (solo) and 4 (cooperative) targeted different content domains, confounding their comparison
target_learners: second-year undergraduate biochemistry students in large classes
target_learning_goals: deep conceptual understanding of molecular biology and metabolism beyond rote recall
examples: Students first wrote true-false statements, then found and critiqued web MCQs and answered at least 40 from the bank, then solo-authored one MCQ, then cooperatively authored and refined questions in groups over steps 4 and 5.
key_sources: Hilton, C. B., Goldwater, M. B., Hancock, D., Clemson, M., Huang, A., & Denyer, G. (2022). Scalable Science Education via Online Cooperative Questioning. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 21(1). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.19-11-0249

article_title: Is it valid to assess an individual's performance in team training simulation when the supporting team are confederates? A controlled and randomized clinical trial.
citation: Traoré Jérémie, Balen Frédéric, Geeraerts Thomas, Charpentier Sandrine, Dubucs Xavier, Houzé-Cerfon Charles-Henri. (2022). Is it valid to assess an individual's performance in team training simulation when the supporting team are confederates? A controlled and randomized clinical trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03747-3
title: Fiction contract and perceived realism as the assumed mechanism linking confederates to simulation performance
description: The article frames confederate use within an explanatory account of simulation realism: "A fundamental assumption of simulation is that learning is enhanced when the environment seems realistic." Full-scale simulation tries to recreate every element of a real situation to persuade participants to accept the "fiction contract" and engage fully; the confederate, a scripted member of the pedagogical team, is thought to increase realism and immersion by providing realism, challenges or information the simulator cannot transcribe. The trial tested, and did not confirm, a performance effect of this mechanism.
requirements: Perceived realism is assumed to depend on interactions between participant and environment, which the confederate is meant to facilitate
constraints: The study's results suggest confederates "do not seem to limit the biases related to the simulated environment that could influence the performance of the participants"
target_learners: Health professional learners in full-scale simulation
target_learning_goals: Engagement and immersion in simulated crisis scenarios
examples: Confederates in the study were trained across five days in active teaching techniques plus three days specifically in the confederate role, reflecting the standards-of-practice requirement for formally trained confederates
key_sources: Traoré Jérémie, Balen Frédéric, Geeraerts Thomas, Charpentier Sandrine, Dubucs Xavier, Houzé-Cerfon Charles-Henri. (2022). Is it valid to assess an individual's performance in team training simulation when the supporting team are confederates? A controlled and randomized clinical trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03747-3

article_title: The influence of personality traits on university performance: Evidence from Italian freshmen students.
citation: Corazzini Luca, D'Arrigo Silvia, Millemaci Emanuele, Navarra Pietro. (2021). The influence of personality traits on university performance: Evidence from Italian freshmen students. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0258586
title: Five-Factor Model of personality traits as measured by the Ten-Item Personality Inventory
description: The article adopts the Five-Factor Model, "an internationally well-established framework of personality traits," comprising extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, emotional stability and openness to experience. Traits are measured at matriculation with the Italian adaptation of the Ten-Item Personality Inventory, a short-form questionnaire whose paired items respondents rate on a seven-point Likert-type scale; reverse-scored items are recoded and item pairs averaged per scale. The framework serves as the set of explanatory regressors for first-year GPA.
requirements: Personality measurement must occur before students have information about course attendance and exam outcomes to avoid reverse causality
constraints: TIPI is a short-form instrument; the article notes a detailed discussion of its limitations and advantages in the S1 Appendix
target_learning_goals: academic achievement (first-year GPA)
key_sources: Corazzini Luca, D'Arrigo Silvia, Millemaci Emanuele, Navarra Pietro. (2021). The influence of personality traits on university performance: Evidence from Italian freshmen students. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0258586

article_title: Low-tech intraocular ophthalmic microsurgery simulation: A low-cost model for home use.
citation: Golash Vidushi, Kaur Simerdip, Naveed Hasan, Nanavaty Mayank A. (2021). Low-tech intraocular ophthalmic microsurgery simulation: A low-cost model for home use. Indian Journal of Ophthalmology. https://doi.org/10.4103/ijo.IJO_242_21
title: Five-exercise home simulation set covering incision, capsulorhexis, dexterity and suturing
description: The article defines a reusable set of five simulation exercises, each mapping a household material to an ophthalmic skill: corneal incisions on grape skin, capsulorhexis on boiled potato under a lozenge-packet 'anterior chamber', 'Loop the hoops' straw-threading, 'Dot the cross' poppy-seed placement with the non-dominant hand, and suturing an orange-peel graft disc. The authors state "Four important and basic skills of performing the corneal incisions, capsulorhexis, improving manual dexterity, and suturing were identified" and built one or more exercises per skill using validated techniques agreed among all authors.
requirements: Each exercise requires its listed low-cost equipment (e.g. keratome and 15-degree blade for incisions; cystotome and rhexis forceps for capsulorhexis) and a prepared lozenge-packet incision port setup
constraints: The dexterity exercises emulate manipulation in a confined space rather than replicating actual ophthalmic surgical steps
target_learning_goals: basic intraocular surgical skills
manual dexterity
suturing technique
examples: The capsulorhexis exercise marks a 7-10 mm diameter circle on a boiled potato slice, covers it with a lozenge packet with a 5 mm main port, and completes a simulated rhexis with cystotome and forceps
key_sources: Golash Vidushi, Kaur Simerdip, Naveed Hasan, Nanavaty Mayank A. (2021). Low-tech intraocular ophthalmic microsurgery simulation: A low-cost model for home use. Indian Journal of Ophthalmology. https://doi.org/10.4103/ijo.IJO_242_21

article_title: Experiences and Perceptions of Ophthalmic Simulation-Based Surgical Education in Sub-Saharan Africa.
citation: Annoh R, Banks LM, Gichuhi S, Buchan J, Makupa W, Otiti J, Mukome A, Arunga S, Burton MJ, Dean WH. (2021). Experiences and Perceptions of Ophthalmic Simulation-Based Surgical Education in Sub-Saharan Africa. Journal of Surgical Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsurg.2021.04.005
title: Five-theme framework of experiences and perceptions of ophthalmic surgical training in sub-Saharan Africa
description: The article organizes its qualitative findings into a thematic framework of "Five over-arching themes and sub-themes": benefits of conventional training, ethical challenges in conventional training, attributes of ophthalmic surgeons and surgeon educators, value of simulation in ophthalmic surgical education, and barriers to implementation of ophthalmic simulation-based surgical education. Each theme carries sub-themes such as stress reduction, technical skill development, confidence building, repetitive practice and reflective learning under the simulation theme. The framework was derived inductively using constant comparative thematic analysis of interviews with trainees and educators.
requirements: Semi-structured interview data from both trainee ophthalmologists and surgeon educators, coded inductively and reviewed by two researchers using the constant comparative method
constraints: The article states the views were largely from Eastern and Southern Africa and "cannot be generalized to other African regions"
target_learning_goals: intraocular surgical competence
safe surgical practice
examples: Table 3 lists the five main themes and their associated sub-themes as identified in the thematic analysis
key_sources: Annoh R, Banks LM, Gichuhi S, Buchan J, Makupa W, Otiti J, Mukome A, Arunga S, Burton MJ, Dean WH. (2021). Experiences and Perceptions of Ophthalmic Simulation-Based Surgical Education in Sub-Saharan Africa. Journal of Surgical Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsurg.2021.04.005

article_title: The effect of flipped classroom in multiple clinical skills training for clinical interns on Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCE).
citation: Zhang Weihao, Gu Jiaoyang, Li Fan, Feng Feifei, Chen Huiqiang, Xing Xiaowei, Liu Lan. (2021). The effect of flipped classroom in multiple clinical skills training for clinical interns on Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCE). Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2021.2013405
title: Five-station OSCE for assessing intern clinical skills
description: The study used an Objective Structured Clinical Examination with five stations to assess interns' clinical skills: "heart physical examination, lung physical examination, abdominal physical examination, neurological physical examination, and CPR". Each station had one professionally trained examiner and a standard simulator with physical examination equipment in an independent assessment space, following national standardized training skills examination references. Assessment took place on the third day after the end of all skills teaching.
requirements: Stations equipped with simulated persons and physical examination equipment
Examiners with professional OSCE training
Independent assessment space per station
target_learning_goals: clinical skills assessment
physical examination skills
CPR skills
examples: The hospital clinical skills examination center prepared the location and materials; station order was heart, lung, abdominal, neurological examination, then CPR.
key_sources: Zhang Weihao, Gu Jiaoyang, Li Fan, Feng Feifei, Chen Huiqiang, Xing Xiaowei, Liu Lan. (2021). The effect of flipped classroom in multiple clinical skills training for clinical interns on Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCE). Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2021.2013405

article_title: The Effect of a Paired Lab on Course Completion and Grades in Nonmajors Introductory Biology.
citation: DeFeo, D. J., Bibler, A., & Gerken, S. (2020). The Effect of a Paired Lab on Course Completion and Grades in Nonmajors Introductory Biology. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 19(3). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.20-03-0041
title: Five categories of learning objectives for science labs
description: From a review of literature published since the 1990s, the authors identify five categories of science-lab learning objectives "generally aligned with previous analyses that have considered these outcomes across science disciplines": 1) "promote deeper critical thinking or problem-solving skills"; 2) develop content knowledge; 3) apply scientific methods and understand the nature of science; 4) develop practical and technical skills; and 5) develop positive attitudes including confidence, interest, and engagement. This taxonomy frames the study, whose outcome measure (grades) covers only content knowledge.
requirements: Research about labs should be explicit in describing the lab experience, given extreme variability in how labs are administered
constraints: The study's own outcome measure (final grades) assessed only the content-knowledge objective, not the other four categories
target_learners: Undergraduate nonmajors in introductory science courses
target_learning_goals: Science-lab learning outcomes including critical thinking, content knowledge, nature of science, technical skills, and attitudes toward science
examples: The syllabus review of 291 BIOL 102 sections found grades composed primarily of three multiple-choice exams, online homework, and weekly quizzes, largely measuring discrete content knowledge
key_sources: DeFeo, D. J., Bibler, A., & Gerken, S. (2020). The Effect of a Paired Lab on Course Completion and Grades in Nonmajors Introductory Biology. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 19(3). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.20-03-0041

article_title: Implementation of a rapid response system at an isolated radiotherapy facility through simulation training.
citation: Kawamura Hidemasa, Komatsu Yasuhiro, Tanaka Kazumi, Kanamoto Masafumi, Tobe Masaru, Usami Chisato, Hinohara Hiroshi, Oshima Kiyohiro, Kitada Yoko, Tsuda Kazuhisa, Ogano Tomoaki, Shimada Hirofumi, Ohno Tatsuya. (2022). Implementation of a rapid response system at an isolated radiotherapy facility through simulation training. BMJ Open Quality. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjoq-2021-001578
title: Five-phase framework for analysing emergency response from detection to transport
description: The article organises emergency response analysis by dividing "the time course from detection of the emergency to transport to the hospital emergency department into five phases": detecting the emergency, calling the MET, transportation of the MET to the site, on-site response, and patient transportation to the emergency department. For each phase the core group identified what needed to be addressed and what action to take, and problems were summarised for each phase before improvement measures were discussed. The framework structured the protocol modification, equipment renovation and simulation design.
requirements: A multidisciplinary core group reviewing facility characteristics and previous efforts to identify problems in each phase
constraints: Developed for a radiotherapy facility with poor access to an emergency department and patients immobilised with fixation devices
target_learners: multidisciplinary radiotherapy facility staff including physicists, technicians, nurses and physicians
target_learning_goals: emergency detection and response
MET activation and communication
patient transport to emergency care
examples: The core group used the phases to identify problems such as limited voice reach, complex interior structure, and difficult patient monitoring
key_sources: Kawamura Hidemasa, Komatsu Yasuhiro, Tanaka Kazumi, Kanamoto Masafumi, Tobe Masaru, Usami Chisato, Hinohara Hiroshi, Oshima Kiyohiro, Kitada Yoko, Tsuda Kazuhisa, Ogano Tomoaki, Shimada Hirofumi, Ohno Tatsuya. (2022). Implementation of a rapid response system at an isolated radiotherapy facility through simulation training. BMJ Open Quality. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjoq-2021-001578

article_title: Measuring attitudes towards biology major and non-major: Effect of students' gender, group composition, and learning environment.
citation: Almasri Firas, Hewapathirana Gertrude I., Ghaddar Fatme, Lee Nick, Ibrahim Bashar. (2021). Measuring attitudes towards biology major and non-major: Effect of students’ gender, group composition, and learning environment. PLoS ONE 16(5): e0251453. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0251453
title: Semester-long fixed jigsaw-style collaborative groups of four with worksheet activities occupying most class time
description: The article’s CL implementation placed students in fixed groups of four for the entire semester, using a jigsaw method in which students divide lecture material beforehand, explain different parts to their group, then discuss instructor-provided worksheet activities. "these activities take up almost 70% of the class time for around 45 minutes for each class", with three activities per lecture and intensity increasing "every 2–3 sessions". Activities align partially with upcoming examinations, and the instructor uses remaining time to summarize.
requirements: Fixed group membership across the semester to build a motivated, friendly teamwork environment
Groups of four, which the article cites as more effective for the flow of ideas than bigger groups
Instructor guidance, feedback quality, and activity quality
Activities comprising real-life scenarios, fill-in-the-blanks, or true/false questions
constraints: Recommended when the subject consists of independent portions such as Biology
Activities are similar but not identical to examination questions
target_learners: Undergraduate introductory biology students in single-gender and mixed-gender classes
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of basic biology and applying understanding to solve biological questions
examples: Students prepared topics and divided lecture material between group members before class, then solved worksheets under instructor supervision

Measuring attitudes towards biology major and non-major: Effect of students’ gender, group composition, and learning environment. PLoS ONE 16(5): e0251453. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0251453

article_title: Undergraduate medical education amid COVID-19: a qualitative analysis of enablers and barriers to acquiring competencies in distant learning using focus groups.
citation: Reinhart A, Malzkorn B, Döing C, Beyer I, Jünger J, Bosse HM. (2021). Undergraduate medical education amid COVID-19: a qualitative analysis of enablers and barriers to acquiring competencies in distant learning using focus groups. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2021.1940765
title: Five-theme explanatory model of enablers and barriers to clinical competency-based e-learning under lockdown
description: The article develops an explanatory model arranged as a Venn diagram linking five major themes emerging from student and teacher focus groups: 'Mental wellbeing, Communication, Structure and self-organization, Technical issues, and Learning and commitment'. Learning and commitment sits at the centre of the model, with enablers and barriers of the other themes and their overlaps depicted around it. The authors position it as guidance for 'a thoughtful, necessary transition to future e-learning and hybrid programs for a competency-based medical education'.
requirements: Themes were derived from focus groups with prior participants of the online-only course, coded deductively against Regmi and Jones' framework plus inductive additions
constraints: Findings are described as 'not generalizable regarding e-learning as such' and tied to a setting of comprehensive social distancing in summer 2020
The study addresses views only, not measured effects on skills or patient outcomes
target_learning_goals: clinical competencies such as evidence-based case management, history taking, and communication under distant-learning conditions
examples: The authors aligned the five themes and their overlaps in a Venn diagram and mapped eight Regmi and Jones enablers/barriers onto three of the five themes in Table 2
key_sources: Reinhart A, Malzkorn B, Döing C, Beyer I, Jünger J, Bosse HM. (2021). Undergraduate medical education amid COVID-19: a qualitative analysis of enablers and barriers to acquiring competencies in distant learning using focus groups. article_title: Impact of guided self-study on learning success in undergraduate physiotherapy students in Switzerland - a feasibility study of a higher education intervention.
citation: Rogan Slavko, Taeymans Jan, Zuber Stefan, Zinzen Evert. (2021). Impact of guided self-study on learning success in undergraduate physiotherapy students in Switzerland – a feasibility study of a higher education intervention. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02794-6
title: Five-phase guided self-study procedure for higher education
description: The article operationalizes guided self-study (G-SS) as a structured procedure in which "students are supported by lecturers or tutors during G-SS", in contrast to free self-study where students are self-reliant. Drawing on Landwehr and Mueller, it defines five phases: a preparatory phase in which students receive a learning assignment with clear-cut learning objectives; realization stages of tutor coaching and checking; presentation of learning outcomes in a plenum session; reflection on the learning process by students and tutor; and peer feedback on presentations and learning processes. The study instantiated this as an eight-day cycle per clinical case, with six cases aligned to module contents.
requirements: A tutor or lecturer guides preparation, presentation, reflection and feedback phases
Clinical cases aligned with curriculum contents and clear-cut learning objectives
Scheduled sessions (90 min at day 8) for presentation, reflection and feedback
constraints: The article reports no standardized procedure for G-SS existed at BFH before this study, and empirical evidence for the underlying theoretical model was still lacking
target_learning_goals: practical physiotherapy skills such as examination protocols, massage techniques and gait analysis
independent acquisition of knowledge and skills
examples: Six clinical cases (e.g. thoracic massage after heart surgery, gait analysis, knee pain examination) were each processed in an eight-day cycle: case emailed on day 1, tutor-supported or independent preparation days 2–7, presentation, oral reflection and moderated plenary feedback on day 8
key_sources: Rogan Slavko, Taeymans Jan, Zuber Stefan, Zinzen Evert. (2021). Impact of guided self-study on learning success in undergraduate physiotherapy students in Switzerland – a feasibility study of a higher education intervention. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02794-6

article_title: Simulation-based education for selected communication skills: exploring the perception of post-graduate dental students.
citation: Mascarenhas Sharon, Al-Halabi Manal, Otaki Farah, Nasaif Mohamed, Davis Dave. (2021). Simulation-based education for selected communication skills: exploring the perception of post-graduate dental students. Korean J Med Educ 33(1):11-25. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2021.183
title: Five-phase system framework (input, process, output, outcome, impact) for structuring qualitative SBE research findings
description: The study's conceptual framework organizes 16 thematic categories into five sequential phases of a system: input (facilities, personnel, teaching materials), process (pre-brief, simulation, debrief), output (direct effects on knowledge, attitude, skills), outcome (effects on learning and teaching at the college), and impact (long-term effects on curriculum, quality of care, and the profession). The researchers fitted categories to the general system theory, stating it "can reveal the multidisciplinary nature of the phenomenon under investigation". They conclude that using it "proved to be useful for structuring and analyzing qualitative data in SBE research".
requirements: Categories generated through multi-staged participant-focused thematic analysis that can be related to differing phases of the SBE system
constraints: Participants without prior knowledge of systems theory found it challenging to understand the temporal differences between output, outcome, and impact themes during respondent validation
target_learning_goals: communication skills (consent, breaking bad news, unexpected outcome)
examples: The framework was presented to participants in a 2-hour respondent-validation discussion using three PowerPoint slides, after which students agreed with all identified codes
key_sources: Mascarenhas Sharon, Al-Halabi Manal, Otaki Farah, Nasaif Mohamed, Davis Dave. (2021). Simulation-based education for selected communication skills: exploring the perception of post-graduate dental students. Korean J Med Educ 33(1):11-25. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2021.183

article_title: Application of the educational method of realistic simulation in the treatment of pressure injuries.
citation: Baracho Valéria da Silva, Chaves Maria Emília de Abreu, Lucas Thabata Coaglio. (2020). Application of the educational method of realistic simulation in the treatment of pressure injuries. Revista Latino-Americana de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/1518-8345.3946.3357
title: Five-phase realistic simulation program for pressure injury education
description: The article describes a five-phase in-service education program: pre-test with an adapted 13-item true/false Pieper questionnaire, clinical case problematization in teams of five, realistic simulation with a mannequin, reusable artificial wounds and trained student actors, structured debriefing, and an identical post-test. The simulation scenario lasted 80 minutes with alternating 20-minute sessions and 7-minute interrogations. It was designed so professionals "move from being a listener to being a protagonist and autonomous of their own knowledge".
requirements: Teams of five professionals meeting across three discussion days; a private room; a mannequin with reusable artificial wounds; two student actors previously trained by the researchers; two registered nurses with more than 5 years of clinical experience to conduct interrogations
constraints: The post-test was applied immediately after the simulation, which the authors state may have influenced the knowledge improvement; the study covered only hospitalization clinics, excluding emergency, ICU and hemodialysis staff
target_learning_goals: pressure injury prevention, assessment, cleaning and dressing techniques
clinical reasoning for wound evaluation and topical therapy
examples: Phase III used kidney dishes, sterile dressing kit, gauze, gloves, 0.9% saline solution, bandage, adhesive tape, dressings, and artificial blood
key_sources: Baracho Valéria da Silva, Chaves Maria Emília de Abreu, Lucas Thabata Coaglio. (2020). Application of the educational method of realistic simulation in the treatment of pressure injuries. Revista Latino-Americana de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/1518-8345.3946.3357

article_title: Executive functions mediate the relationship between cardiorespiratory fitness and academic achievement in Spanish schoolchildren aged 8 to 11 years.
citation: Visier-Alfonso ME, Sánchez-López M, Martínez-Vizcaíno V, Jiménez-López E, Redondo-Tébar A, Nieto-López M. (2020). Executive functions mediate the relationship between cardiorespiratory fitness and academic achievement in Spanish schoolchildren aged 8 to 11 years. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0231246
title: Fitness-induced vascularization, neural growth and synaptic transmission in prefrontal regions underlying executive functions explain fitness effects on learning
description: The article advances a neurobiological mechanism account in which "physical fitness induces vascularization, neural growth and synaptic transmission in the regions of the brain underlying executive functions, especially the prefrontal cortex". Executive function in turn "provides neural substrates that underlie successful learning", so fitness effects on academic achievement may travel through improved inhibition and cognitive flexibility rather than only through a direct path.
constraints: The authors note their correlational design "leaves open the possibility that the observed behavioral and structural fitness-related differences between high and low-fit groups are caused by some unmeasured factor".
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement in language and mathematics
Executive functioning (inhibition, cognitive flexibility, working memory)
examples: The mediation findings that inhibition and cognitive flexibility carried part of the CRF–achievement effect, while working memory did not, are the article's own evidence for this mechanism account.
key_sources: Visier-Alfonso ME, Sánchez-López M, Martínez-Vizcaíno V, Jiménez-López E, Redondo-Tébar A, Nieto-López M. (2020). Executive functions mediate the relationship between cardiorespiratory fitness and academic achievement in Spanish schoolchildren aged 8 to 11 years. article_title: Inter-rater reliability in clinical assessments: do examiner pairings influence candidate ratings?
citation: Faherty Aileen, Counihan Tim, Kropmans Thomas, Finn Yvonne. (2020). Inter-rater reliability in clinical assessments: do examiner pairings influence candidate ratings? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02009-4
title: Five-Factor Model of Personality as a framework for studying examiner rating behaviour
description: The article adopts the Five-Factor Model of Personality (the 'Big Five') as the framework for measuring examiner individual differences, describing it as "an integrative framework for studying individual differences in personality" that is "among the most well accepted taxonomies of personality in the literature with wide application in different domains and across cultures due to its empirical validity". Scores represent degrees of neuroticism, extroversion, openness to experience, agreeableness and conscientiousness, expressed as T scores. The study used the 60-item NEO-FFI to measure these traits and relate them to examiner scoring behaviour.
requirements: A validated instrument such as the NEO Five Factor Index to measure the five trait domains
constraints: No single cut-off separates those who have a trait from those who do not; scores represent degrees of each trait
target_learning_goals: understanding and reducing examiner variability in clinical assessment
examples: Examiners completed the NEO-FFI after solo scoring; 75% scored below average for neuroticism and 75% high or very high for extroversion
key_sources: Faherty Aileen, Counihan Tim, Kropmans Thomas, Finn Yvonne. (2020). Inter-rater reliability in clinical assessments: do examiner pairings influence candidate ratings? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02009-4

article_title: Can e-learning improve the performance of undergraduate medical students in Clinical Microbiology examinations?
citation: Stevens Niall T., Holmes Killian, Grainger Rachel J., Connolly Roisín, Prior Anna-Rose, Fitzpatrick Fidelma, O'Neill Eoghan, Boland Fiona, Pawlikowska Teresa, Humphreys Hilary. (2019). Can e-learning improve the performance of undergraduate medical students in Clinical Microbiology examinations? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1843-0
title: Online Clinical Microbiology e-learning resource with glossary, question/answer activities, podcasts with MCQ quizzes, antibiotic content, pathogen index and clinical case scenarios
description: An online module hosted on Moodle designed to complement didactic teaching in the Foundations in Microbiology module. It contained "an alphabetical glossary of important terms in Clinical Microbiology and question/answer-type activities on core concepts", podcasts with MCQ-style quizzes, antibiotic activities, and clinical case scenarios for each important genus or family with feedback and unlimited attempts. Each pathogen name was hyper-linked to an alphabetical index summarising epidemiology, virulence, pathogenesis, laboratory diagnosis and antimicrobial management. Students could track their progress and compare it to the class.
requirements: Students were expected to complete all components of the online content, with expectations outlined in the Marks and Standards document and a face-to-face introductory session
constraints: There were no academic consequences for not engaging
target_learning_goals: characteristics of medically important bacteria, viruses and fungi
pathogenicity and spread of infection
antibiotic chemotherapy and stewardship
laboratory diagnosis
infection prevention
examples: The HCAI core-concepts activity was accessed 71,737 times and the pathogen index by 329/334 (98.5%) of registered students

article_title: Effects of native language on CPR skills and willingness to intervene in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest after film-based basic life support training: a subgroup analysis of a randomised trial.
citation: Hollenberg Jacob, Claesson Andreas, Ringh Mattias, Nordberg Per, Hasselqvist-Ax Ingela, Nord Anette. (2019). Effects of native language on CPR skills and willingness to intervene in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest after film-based basic life support training: a subgroup analysis of a randomised trial. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2018-025531
title: Film-based CPR training method with individual Mini Anne manikins and a 31-minute Swedish instruction film
description: A standardised whole-class CPR training method advocated by the Swedish Resuscitation Council, in which students each use an individual training manikin (Mini Anne) and follow "instructions in Swedish on a 31 min film" to practise identifying cardiac arrest, raising the alarm, compressions, ventilations and the recovery position, per ERC guidelines 2010. The teacher acts as a facilitator who introduces the lesson, starts and pauses the film, gives advice and answers questions. Skills were measured with the modified Cardiff test (12 items, total score 12–48 points) on a Resusci Anne manikin.
requirements: Requires individual training manikins for all students, the instruction film, and a teacher trained (here 5 hours) to act as facilitator
constraints: Training was delivered in Swedish only; the instructors acted only as facilitators, and the article notes an individual instructor's enthusiasm and/or characteristics may affect students' learning
target_learning_goals: Basic life support skills: identifying cardiac arrest, calling emergency services, chest compressions, ventilations, recovery position
examples: 68 school classes were cluster randomised; the prespecified film-based subgroup of 641 students was analysed with tests directly after training and at 6 months

article_title: Development of simulation education debriefing protocol with faculty guide for enhancement clinical reasoning.
citation: Bae Juyeon, Lee JuHee, Jang Yeonsoo, Lee Yoonju. (2019). Development of simulation education debriefing protocol with faculty guide for enhancement clinical reasoning. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1633-8
title: Five clinical reasoning attributes (perception, information processing, analysis, deliberation, metacognition) as the organizing framework for debriefing questions
description: The article organizes its debriefing protocol around clinical reasoning attributes extracted from the literature. More than half of reviewed studies emphasized seven attributes, but "The attributes of heuristics and intuition, however, were excluded in this protocol" because prior research indicates those are used by expert-level nurses. The remaining "5 clinical reasoning attributes, i.e. perception, information processing, analysis, deliberation, and metacognition were included", each matched to core questions at the corresponding debriefing stage.
requirements: Core questions must be matched to the learning outcome of each debriefing stage
constraints: Heuristics and intuition were excluded as attributes appropriate to expert-level nurses rather than undergraduates
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning: perceiving patient problems, processing information, analyzing, deliberating, and metacognitive reflection
examples: Perception core questions such as 'let's discuss what health issues this patient has now' were deduced from the literature
key_sources: Bae Juyeon, Lee JuHee, Jang Yeonsoo, Lee Yoonju. (2019). Development of simulation education debriefing protocol with faculty guide for enhancement clinical reasoning. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1633-8

article_title: Promoting innovation in the objective structured teaching examination and feedback: clustering teachers to aid teaching evaluation.
citation: Hsieh, M.-C. and Chen, T.-Y. (2019). Promoting innovation in the objective structured teaching examination and feedback: clustering teachers to aid teaching evaluation. Medical Education Online, 24(1). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6567259/
title: Flanders interaction analysis system (FIAS) as a 10-category observational tool for quantifying teacher–student verbal interaction
description: The FIAS is an observational coding system that classifies verbal behaviors of teachers and pupils during classroom interaction into 10 categories: seven teacher-talk categories (accepting feelings, praising, accepting/using ideas, asking questions, lecturing, giving direction, criticizing/justifying authority), two pupil-talk categories (response and initiation), and one silence/confusion category. The article states it is "an observational tool used to classify the verbal behaviors of teachers and pupils as they interact in the classroom". In this study, the FIAS was applied to videotaped OSTE feedback stations, with recordings made at 20–25 observations per minute over 15 minutes, and only 9 of the 10 categories (F0–F8) were analyzed after excluding standardized student responses.
requirements: Trained coders watching recorded teaching sessions to assign categories reliably (Kappa 0.73–0.90 in this study)
constraints: Only verbal communication is considered; nonverbal gestures are not taken into account
Some clinical interactive activities (e.g., content expertise, interpersonal attributes) cannot be perceived by FIAS
Extended dialogue between students and faculty cannot be analyzed at present
target_learners: Clinical teachers in faculty development programs
target_learning_goals: Teaching behavior self-awareness
Feedback-giving skills
Teaching reflection
examples: In this study, two coders rated 38 videotaped OSTE feedback stations using FIAS categories F0–F8, achieving Kappa values of 0.73 to 0.90
key_sources: Hsieh, M.-C. and Chen, T.-Y. (2019). Promoting innovation in the objective structured teaching examination and feedback: clustering teachers to aid teaching evaluation. Medical Education Online, 24(1). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6567259/

article_title: Competencies required for general practitioners/family physicians in urban areas versus non-urban areas: a preliminary study.
citation: Mitsuyama Toshichika, Son Daisuke, Eto Masato. (2018). Competencies required for general practitioners/family physicians in urban areas versus non-urban areas: a preliminary study. BMC Family Practice. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-018-0869-4
title: Five-group taxonomy of general practitioner competencies and contexts in urban and non-urban areas
description: The study organizes its qualitative findings into a five-group taxonomy: "competencies characteristic of general practitioners in urban areas; contexts characteristic of general practitioners in urban areas; competencies characteristic of general practitioners in non-urban areas; contexts characteristic of general practitioners in non-urban areas; and common competencies between both groups of general practitioners." Each group contains enumerated concepts, such as broad biomedical care scope and effective use of limited resources for non-urban areas, and integration of fragmented care for urban areas. The taxonomy can structure curriculum planning for regional primary care training.
requirements: Interview or experiential data from physicians with clinical experience in both urban and non-urban areas to ground the comparison
constraints: Theoretical sufficiency was not confirmed for competencies of general practitioners in non-urban (rural) areas, so that branch may be incomplete
target_learners: Medical educators designing primary care curricula
target_learning_goals: Distinguishing region-specific from common primary care competencies
Understanding practice contexts in urban versus non-urban settings
examples: Table 2 lists concepts per group, including 'Integration of fragmented care in urban areas' under urban competencies and 'Judgment to make effective use of limited medical resources' under non-urban competencies.

description: A tutor-completed evaluation form developed by the authors from literature review and their school's PBL objectives. Each of the five domains — "participation, preparation, communication skills, critical discussion, and teamwork" — is rated on five levels worth 20 scores, and students are evaluated by their tutors immediately after case learning. article_title: High-fidelity is not superior to low-fidelity simulation but leads to overconfidence in medical students.
citation: Massoth C, Röder H, Ohlenburg H, Hessler M, Zarbock A, Pöpping DM, Wenk M. (2019). High-fidelity is not superior to low-fidelity simulation but leads to overconfidence in medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1464-7
title: Realism-competence level account: higher simulator fidelity benefits higher-level competency acquisition only for more qualified trainees
description: The authors propose, using the Miller pyramid of clinical competence (knows, knows how, shows how, does), that a relationship exists between simulation fidelity and the competency level achievable. They argue that even if high realism favors acquiring the top "does"-action level, it "requires for the condition of more qualified trainees proportionally to the degree of realism, to surpass the level of 'shows how'", suggesting lower-level trainees such as medical students benefit more from lower-fidelity training. This account explains their finding that HF training conferred no advantage and induced overconfidence in novices.
requirements: Trainee educational level must be considered when selecting simulator fidelity
constraints: The authors state it remains unclear whether their results transfer to medical professionals, as findings may be tied to the specific educational level of their fourth-year student cohort
target_learning_goals: advanced life support procedural skills
resuscitation team performance
accurate self-assessment of clinical skills
examples: In this trial, fourth-year medical students trained on either a SimMan 3G high-fidelity simulator in a simulated ICU room or a Rescue Anne Simulator in a regular ward room, with identical teaching content
key_sources: Massoth C, Röder H, Ohlenburg H, Hessler M, Zarbock A, Pöpping DM, Wenk M. (2019). High-fidelity is not superior to low-fidelity simulation but leads to overconfidence in medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1464-7

article_title: A middle-range model for improving quality of nursing education in Malawi.
citation: Bvumbwe, T.M. & Mtshali, N.G., 2018, 'A middle-range model for improving quality of nursing education in Malawi', Curationis 41(1), a1766. https://doi.org/10.4102/curationis.v41i1.1766
title: Five-strategy configuration for transforming and scaling up nursing education
description: The model organises its intervention space into five sub-concepts serving as key strategies. As stated: "Key main strategies in the model included curriculum reforms, regulation, transformative learning, provision of infrastructure and resources and capacity building." Curriculum reform is described as central to transforming quality and relevance, regulation operates through accreditation and licensure, and capacity building spans institutional productive capacity and faculty development. The configuration is meant to prevent using one strategy to solve all problems.
requirements: Implementation through collaborative academic–practice partnership at national, institutional and programme levels
constraints: Developed for the Malawian context; the article states it can transfer to countries with similar nursing education contexts
target_learners: nursing education planners, regulators and faculty in Malawi and similar settings
target_learning_goals: improving quality, quantity and relevance of nursing education
examples: Table 3 lists the sub-concepts with supporting extracts from panel and focus group participants

article_title: A program to train medical physicists for direct patient care responsibilities.
citation: Brown DW, Atwood TF, Moore KL, MacAulay R, Murphy JD, Mundt AJ, Pawlicki T. (2018). A program to train medical physicists for direct patient care responsibilities. Journal of Applied Clinical Medical Physics. https://doi.org/10.1002/acm2.12472

description: The article presents a training program comprising five sequenced components: a 1-day Clinician-Patient Communication Workshop, two 2-hour Communication Strategies for Radiation Oncology sessions, Simulated Patient Interactions with trained patient actors, Faculty-Observed Patient Consults, and a Case-Based Treatment Toxicity Course. The program "emphasizes experiential, practice‐based learning over didactic presentations" and was designed with the UC San Diego School of Medicine for physicists moving into clinical roles with direct patient contact.
requirements: Trainees complete all five components, with competencies assessed during Simulated Patient interactions and Faculty-Observed Patient Consults
constraints: developed for medical physicists transitioning into a clinical role with direct patient care responsibilities in radiation oncology
target_learning_goals: patient communication skills
clinical communication competencies for physicist-patient consults
examples: Trainees perform mock physicist-patient consults with trained patient actors, each consult scheduled for 30 minutes

article_title: A patient safety education program in a medical physics residency.
citation: Ford Eric C., Nyflot Matthew, Spraker Matthew B., Kane Gabrielle, Hendrickson Kristi R. G. (2017). A patient safety education program in a medical physics residency. Journal of Applied Clinical Medical Physics. https://doi.org/10.1002/acm2.12166
title: Five topic focus areas structure a patient safety and quality curriculum for medical physics residents
description: The program organizes its content around five topic focus areas selected from published recommendations (AAPM Report No. 249, CAMPEP standards, TG-100, ASTRO's "Safety is No Accident"): accidents and outcomes, failure mode and effect analysis, incident learning and safety culture, principles in error proofing and quality improvement, and quality audits. Each topic area carries learning objectives and assigned reference readings. The authors note the areas "are very similar to those proposed by Yeung and Greenwalt" and consistent with ACGME and CAMPEP recommendations.
requirements: Topic selection must be tailored to the limited time available in a 24-month medical physics residency, drawing on published recommendations for focus areas.
constraints: The article states Table 1 "should not be taken as an exhaustive list"; for example, statistical process control is not included.
target_learning_goals: patient safety and quality of care in radiation oncology
examples: The one-month rotation schedule (Table 2) assigns readings and lectures week by week across these topic areas, culminating in an FMEA rotation project.

citation: Joubert Lanae; Kilgas Matthew; Riley Alexandrea; Gautam Yuba; Donath Lars; Drum Scott. (2017). In-Class Cycling to Augment College Student Academic Performance and Reduce Physical Inactivity: Results from an RCT. title: FitDesk stationary cycle desks deployed in a college lecture classroom
description: Stationary cycle desks (FitDesks®, FD Products, Kernersville, NC, USA) placed randomly throughout a lecture classroom so students could pedal during class, contrasted with "standard tables and chairs". Each desk carried an attached odometer and notebook for recording pedal time, mph and RPE each class period; two weeks of familiarization preceded the intervention.
requirements: Two weeks of familiarization with the cycle desks before the intervention begins
Attached odometer and per-class log for pedal time, mph and RPE
constraints: Physical confines of an academic classroom limit feasibility, per the article's limitations
target_learning_goals: enabling physical activity during lectures without disrupting course learning
