article_title: Assessing the Impact of Early Learning Programs in Africa.
citation: Gove, A., Brunette, T., Bulat, J., Carrol, B., Henny, C., Macon, W., Nderu, E., & Sitabkhan, Y. (2017). Assessing the impact of early learning programs in Africa. New Directions for Child and Adolescent Development, 158, 25–41. https://doi.org/10.1002/cad.20224
title: The "5 Ts" framework: five comprehensively addressed ingredients for effective early literacy programs
description: The article presents the "5 Ts" (Gove & Cvelich, 2011) as RTI's framework for effective early literacy programs: "effective teaching, access to high‐quality texts (materials), appropriate use of mother tongue languages, efficient use of instructional time, and use of formative and summative tests (assessments, including the Early Grade Reading Assessment [EGRA])". The framework holds that programs must comprehensively address all five ingredients rather than in isolation. The country case studies are organized around how each T was implemented, and the discussion identifies these as "the key ingredients to fuel success". Instruction combines explicit instruction in foundational skills with holistic reading and writing experiences.
requirements: Programs must comprehensively address all five Ts together rather than any single ingredient
constraints: The article notes determining the best mix of professional development should be locally contextualized to each country
target_learners: Early grade primary students (grades 1–4) in low- and middle-income African countries
Preprimary children in Kenya and Tanzania
target_learning_goals: Early grade reading fluency and comprehension
School readiness
examples: Each country case study documents adaptation of the model: scaffolded teacher guides and student books in Kenya, Liberia, and Ethiopia; mother-tongue materials in 12 Ugandan local languages; EGRA monitoring in Malawi and Tanzania

article_title: A survey of pharmacists' perception of foundation level competencies in African countries.
citation: Udoh Arit, Bruno Andreia, Bates Ian. (2018). A survey of pharmacists’ perception of foundation level competencies in African countries. Human Resources for Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12960-018-0280-1
title: FIP Global Competency Framework v1 (GbCF v1) for foundation-level pharmacy practitioners
description: The GbCF v1 is a competency framework developed by FIPEd in 2012 using evidence-based methodologies, designed as "a source document containing the core competencies expected of foundation level pharmacy practitioners" (pharmacists with less than 5 years practice experience). It comprises 100 behavioural statements (B1–B100) grouped under 20 competency domains and four broad clusters: pharmaceutical public health, pharmaceutical care, organisation and management, and professional and personal. It has been used to design pre-service curricula and country-specific in-service frameworks. This survey evaluated its relevance to practice in African countries.
requirements: Designed for foundation level practitioners, i.e. pharmacists with less than 5 years practice experience
constraints: Prior 64-country validation survey included only 12.3% respondents from Africa
target_learning_goals: Core pharmacy practice competencies across public health, pharmaceutical care, organisation and management, and professional and personal domains
examples: The survey questionnaire fully reproduced the GbCF v1 as 105 questions, with 100 behavioural statements rated on a 4-point relevance scale.

article_title: Learning through a virtual patient vs. recorded lecture: a comparison of knowledge retention in a trauma case.
citation: Courteille Olivier, Fahlstedt Madelen, Ho Johnson, Hedman Leif, Fors Uno, von Holst Hans, Felländer-Tsai Li, Möller Hans. (2018). title: Three-dimensional finite-element cervical spine model with dynamic injury simulations for biomechanics education
description: A detailed three-dimensional finite-element model of the cervical spine developed at the KTH Royal Institute of Technology, consisting of vertebrae, ligaments, facet joint, discs, muscles and skull. It visualizes kinematics and stress distribution at the time of impact, with dynamic imaging sequences "designed to enhance the understanding of the biomechanics behind an injury". It was embedded in both the lecture and the VP format, preceded by a short introduction to the finite-element method.
requirements: A short introduction to the finite-element method is given before the three-dimensional simulations
constraints: The visualization modality had previously shown face validity and increased self-efficacy in medical students, per the authors' cited prior work
target_learning_goals: biomechanical understanding of cervical spine trauma
examples: Both teaching formats featured a demonstration or interactive exploration of accident reconstruction from a biomechanical perspective using this model
